block.cue: Leaving BSÍ — no window required.
block.hook: Before we point at a single thing, pocket three names: **a painter no bishop would bless, a brewer who named his beer after a Viking, and a farm boy who won the Nobel Prize.** Their stories are about to keep crashing into each other.
block.point: One valley — **Mosfellsdalur, my literature valley** — ties a Viking's buried silver, a rejected painting and a Nobel medal into the last twenty minutes of our drive home.
block.mic: Keep the three names in your pocket. By the time we come back through the valley at the end of the day, you'll know why the painting, the beer and the book all end up in the same house.

bullets: **Kjarval** — the painter. His story opens the tour two minutes from now — and the **elf-filled altarpiece the church refused to bless** will be waiting for us in a valley at the end of our day.

title: Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval
subject: jóhannes sveinsson kjarval

block.title: Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval
block.sub: the cod fisherman who became legal tender
block.cue: Look left at 9 o'clock — Klambratún Park.
block.hook: How do you fund art school in 1900s Iceland? Your shipmates **pass a hat round a freezing cod trawler**. Not a GoFundMe — an actual hat.
block.point: Most artists travel the world for inspiration. Kjarval found a whole country in the **dirt under his boots** — then handed it back, one canvas at a time.
block.mic: In Iceland, the landscape looks back — and sometimes files a complaint with the bishop.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the park is grey and half empty, that is exactly the Iceland Kjarval painted. He was never interested in the sunny version."
bullets: Born **15 October 1885** at **Efri-Ey** in **Meðalland**, south Iceland — **9th of 13 kids** (his parents clearly had stamina). Fostered east to **Geitavík** in **Borgarfjörður eystri**, where the fjord still calls him **“Jói í Geitavík.”** Too poor for paint, he drew with **calf blood, soot and wool dye** — then went to sea.

Crew saw his sketches, **passed the hat**, the fishermen's union topped it up. **1911**: **London's Royal Academy slammed the door.** The rejection was the redirect — **1912** to **Copenhagen** and the **Royal Danish Academy** (graduated **1917**).

Home again he painted Iceland knelt over the **moss and lava three inches from his nose**, swearing he saw **elves and hidden folk** in the cracks. (In Iceland, that's not a diagnosis — that's a career.)

**1914**: his **Bakkagerði** altarpiece shows Christ preaching from **Álfaborg**, the elf-rock, **Dyrfjöll** behind. The bishop refused to bless it — **too many elves, not enough Jesus** — so it still hangs there, gloriously **unconsecrated**. A second altarpiece, dismissed as “crude and ugly,” was bought by **Halldór Laxness** for **Gljúfrasteinn** (we pass it later). One man, two altarpieces, **zero bishops convinced.**

In **1968** he handed the city a huge part of everything he owned — the museum's Kjarval collection runs to **thousands of works** — and he died **owning almost nothing.** That grey block in Klambratún is **Kjarvalsstaðir**, Iceland's **first purpose-built art museum** (1973); since **1995** his face is on the **2,000-króna note** — the only cod fisherman ever **promoted to legal tender.**

title: 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson
subject: ölgerðin egill skallagrímsson

block.title: 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson
block.cue: Look right at 3 o'clock — Egils Brewery.
block.hook: How do you run Iceland's most famous brewery when beer is **illegal for 74 years**? Name it after a Viking — and brew beer that technically isn't beer.
block.point: Tómas didn't outrun Prohibition. He **outlived it** — 74 years on near-beer and a royal warrant.
block.mic: Name your company after a Viking and you don't follow the rules. You wait them out.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If you cannot see the brewery you can usually smell the malt. That counts."
bullets: Founded **17 April 1913** by **Tómas Tómasson** in two basement bedrooms of a rented Reykjavík house — at first just **1%-alcohol malt extract** — and named after **Egill Skallagrímsson**, the warrior-poet who once rhymed his way off an executioner's block (the *Höfuðlausn*, "Head-Ransom") and could drink a whole hall under the table. Aspirational branding.

Two years later Iceland bans **all alcohol** (1915) — so Tómas sails to **Copenhagen and Germany (1915–17) to learn brewing anyway**, training up for a product his own country just outlawed. Wine creeps back in **1922**, spirits in **1935**, but **beer stays illegal until 1989**. Beer alone, because it read as **Danish** — and sipping a Danish lager while fighting Denmark for independence felt like treason.

So Ölgerðin cheats: brews **Egils Pilsner kept just under the legal 2.25%** — beer that technically wasn't beer. A loophole in a glass. (The orange **Appelsín**, drowned in malt every Christmas, came later — **1955**.)

The irony peaks in **1926**: after a state visit from King **Christian X**, Ölgerðin wins the right to style itself the **"royal brewery"** — a Danish royal blessing, in a country half-banning beer for being too Danish.
Real beer returned **1 March 1989** — now **Bjórdagurinn, "Beer Day."** Egils didn't fight for shelf space; they already owned it.

One more thing: hold the name **Egill Skallagrímsson**. In about an hour we park in the middle of his family's saga — mounds, headlands, a drowned foster-mother and all. The beer is the trailer; Borgarnes is the film.

title: 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur
subject: elliðaárdalur

block.title: 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur
block.sub: The Valley That Runs the City
block.cue: Look right at 2 o'clock — Elliðaárdalur.
block.hook: Most capitals get a grey, sad little river. Reykjavík's hands you **dinner, drinking water, electricity — and the country's first parliament.** Show-off.
block.point: Looks like a dog-walking park. It's where the capital gets **fed, watered, powered — and first learned to argue in public.**
block.mic: Reykjavík didn't get a postcard river. It got a **Swiss Army knife.**
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The valley looks its best wet. That river is the reason anything in this city is green."
bullets: Meet the **Elliðaá** — one of the only **capital-city rivers on Earth with a wild Atlantic salmon run**. About **2,500** shove upstream past the joggers every summer to spawn — and the city was so smitten it **bought the whole river in 1906**. (Your city buys parks. We bought a river.)
The **pure tap water** your hotel keeps bragging about? Springs in this same catchment, up by the lake **Elliðavatn** — the city first drew its drinking water here in **1909**.

The lights? In **1921** they dammed it for **Elliðaárstöð** — **Reykjavík's** first power station and **Iceland's second** hydro plant, switched on by King **Christian X** in person on **27 June 1921** and still running a century later.

Iceland's *actual* first hydro plant was humbler: in **1904** a Hafnarfjörður carpenter, **Jóhannes Reykdal**, wired a generator to his workshop stream and lit **15 houses — the school and the Good Templars' hall among them — plus four street lamps**: officially "Iceland's first power station," realistically a shed with big dreams.

Upstream, on a low spit in **Elliðavatn** called **Þingnes**, sits the ground identified since **1841** as the **Kjalarnesþing** — **Iceland's first assembly**, held by **Þorsteinn Ingólfsson** (the first settler's son) before the national **Alþingi** of **930**. **Ari fróði** put that þing on **Kjalarnes**; the ruins are here, fourteen kilometres away, and nobody has ever closed the gap. The old ground now lies **partly underwater** since the river was dammed. Very Icelandic: invent democracy, mislay it, then flood it. (More on parliaments shortly.)

The heat, too. Reykjavík's hot water did not start with volcanoes, it started **inside the city** — **low-temperature fields at Laugarnes and here in Elliðaárdalur**, plus **Mosfellsbær** out of town. Those wells are still working, and neighbourhoods get deliberately swapped between sources **so the reservoir under the city can rest.** (Yes, the ground gets a lie-down.)

There is even a chemical reason your shower behaves oddly here: water from the **Laugarnes** wells is **high in silica**, which deposits on taps and tiles as it cools, while water from **Nesjavellir and Hellisheiði** is heated groundwater and **low in silica.** Same tap, different geology.

The old ground now lies **partly underwater** since the river was dammed. Very Icelandic: invent democracy, mislay it, then flood it. (More on parliaments right at the end of the day — hold that thought.)

title: ⛰️ Mount Esja
subject: mount esja

block.title: ⛰️ Mount Esja
block.cue: Look left and ahead — the long striped wall of Esja.
block.hook: That ridge isn't a mountain — it's a **volcanic range** with **11 ice ages** stacked inside it. Reykjavík's **weather forecast, written in stone** — and unlike the app, it's never wrong.
block.point: Dark = warm, pale = frozen. One glance up and you've read **11 ice ages** before the lights change.
block.mic: Reykjavíkers don't check the weather app — they check if they can still see Esja. If Esja's gone, your phone is the least of your problems.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If Esja has gone, you are getting the honest version. Locals judge the whole day by how much of it they can see."
bullets: **Esja** rose between **3.2 and 1.8 million years ago**, west end oldest — it's been weathering longer than humans have existed, and it isn't one mountain but a whole **volcanic range**.

The stripes are climate you can read from your seat: **dark basalt** flowed in **warm, ice-free** spells and cooled in peace; **pale móberg** (tuff) is lava that picked a fight with a glacier and lost — shattered to rubble under the ice.
Count the bands and you're counting cold snaps: geologists read **at least 11 separate ice ages** in there. Makes this winter look like a warm-up.

True summit is **Hábunga (914 m)** — which almost nobody bothers with. The crowd-pleaser is **Þverfellshorn (~780 m)**, where a boulder called **Steinn**, about **200 m below the top**, is the official "close enough, take the selfie" turnaround. Touch the rock, you climbed Esja. We don't ask questions.

block.title: ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing
block.cue: Out to your right at 3 o'clock across the bay — Kjalarnes, under the foot of Esja, five kilometres off.
block.hook: Iceland's world-famous parliament at Þingvellir? Not even the first. The original ran over there on Kjalarnes — set up by the founder's son. Nepotism: also a Viking value.
block.point: Þingvellir wasn't Kjalarnes moved house — it was something new and national. Kjalarnes just proved Icelanders could hold a parliament without a king.
block.mic: Kjalarnes did the homework. Þingvellir took the credit, the fame, and the tourists.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Nothing to see even on a clear day — it is a field. The story is the thing, not the view."
bullets: **Þorsteinn Ingólfsson** — son of **Ingólfur Arnarson**, Iceland's first settler — held the **Kjalarnesþing** before the national **Alþingi of 930**. Our only near-contemporary source is **Ari fróði**, writing around **1122–33**: *"en áðr var þing á Kjalarnesi"* — before that, the þing was on Kjalarnes. Tradition even credits Þorsteinn with **consecrating** that later national parliament — so the founder's son didn't just build the prototype, he blessed the sequel.

**Here's the catch: nobody has ever found it on Kjalarnes.** **Jónas Hallgrímsson** went looking in **1841**, examined **Leiðvöllur** on the farm **Esjuberg**, and decided it was a footpath. The national register still lists that spot as *sést ekki* — nothing to see. What he found instead was **14 km away, at Þingnes on Elliðavatn**: around **20 booth foundations** and a **judgement ring 43 feet across** with a heap of stones in the middle. He proposed that was the Kjalarnesþing, and in **1930** the state made it official — the protection order calls Þingnes *hinn forni Kjalarnessþingstaður*. **Thirteen ruins are protected there today**, last surveyed in **June 2025**. The join between Ari's Kjalarnes and Jónas's Þingnes has **never been proven** — so Iceland's first parliament is a place we can name and can't quite find.

To write proper laws, the chieftains didn't reinvent the wheel — they sent one man, **Úlfljótr**, to **Norway for three years** to study the **Gulating law** and adapt it for home. He came back with **Úlfljótur's Law**, Iceland's **first law code** — but with one radical twist the Norwegians didn't have: a parliament with **no king**. That part was all theirs.

Nothing was written down — Iceland had no writing worth the name — so **Úlfljótur carried the whole code home inside his head.** He was sent **shortly before 930** and spent **three winters** in Norway, landing home in time for the founding of the **Alþingi in 930**. What he recited is **Úlfljótslög**, the oldest law this country has. Úlfljótur supplied the text. Þingvellir only supplied the venue.

**Iceland's first legal draftsman has a lake, a farm and a church carrying his name** — **Úlfljótsvatn**, Úlfljótur's water — and almost nobody stops at any of the three. (The church is the fun one: open a guidebook and it was built in **1914**, open the national heritage register and it was built in **1863**, by **Eyjólfur Þorvarðsson**, *forsmiður frá Bakka*. When two dates disagree, take the one with the carpenter in it.)

The famous line **"með lögum skal land byggja"** — with laws shall the land be built — gets hung round Úlfljótur's neck constantly, and **he almost certainly never said it.** It arrives in Iceland with **Járnsíða**, a Norwegian king's code imposed between **1271 and 1274**, in the fuller form **"með lögum skal land vort byggja en eigi með ólögum eyða"**, and the phrasing traces back to Norway's **Frostaþingslög**. That makes it about **three hundred and fifty years too young** to be his.

the first settler's son, who set it up around 900 CE
the man sent to Norway for three years to bring back Iceland's first law code
the lake it later moved to, at Þingnes, which we passed this morning
the Norwegian law code Úlfljótr studied and adapted

block.title: 🎵 Mosfellsbær
block.sub: A Town That Punches Above Its Weight
block.cue: All around — Mosfellsbær.
block.hook: A commuter town of **~13,700** — smaller than a single Reykjavík suburb — that exported **two global music acts** at opposite ends of the volume knob.
block.point: A town this size shouldn't manage one global act. Mosfellsbær made two — whisper-quiet piano and stadium blues, from the same patch of moss.
block.mic: Two acts, one small town, zero chill.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Low cloud suits this valley. Half the music that came out of it sounds like this weather."
bullets: **Ólafur Arnalds**, born here **1986**: **won the 2014 BAFTA TV Craft Award** for scoring ITV's *Broadchurch*, and picked up **two Grammy nominations** at the 2021 awards besides. For his *Island Songs* project (2016) he wrote **seven tracks in seven weeks at seven spots** around Iceland — one, *"Particles,"* with **Nanna Bryndís** of Of Monsters and Men.
🎵 *Now playing — "Particles," Ólafur Arnalds feat. Nanna Bryndís Hilmarsdóttir*

Loud end of the dial: **Kaleo**, the blues-rock band formed here in **2012**, whose *"Way Down We Go"* hit **No. 1** on the US alternative chart. Their *"Vor í Vaglaskógi"* is a smoky cover of an Icelandic classic about a forest up north.
🎵 *Now playing — "Vor í Vaglaskógi," Kaleo*

There is a second history under the music. After the British landed on **10 May 1940** the Americans took over in **July 1941**, and the US Army's own medical history puts **80% of the entire American force in Iceland** in a coastal strip **centred on Álafoss** — this town. In **April 1942** the **167th Station Hospital** moved into fresh **Nissen huts at Álafoss**, and they plumbed the **hot springs** in to heat the wards. A field hospital, warmed by the ground.

It is still in the soil. Minjastofnun's **2022 survey at Lágafell** records a circular **gun-pit, 3.5 by 3.1 metres**, and an intact **34-metre trench** — both still there. **Lágafell Camp** itself, a depot and vehicle workshop on land requisitioned from **Thor Jensen**, has vanished completely under later housing. The camp went. The hole somebody dug to shoot from did not.

Up the coast at **Hvalfjörður** the Royal Navy ran **HMS Baldur** at **Hvítanes** from 1940 to the end of the war, and the Americans built a fuel depot of **44 oil tanks**. **Convoy PQ17 sailed out of that fjord on 27 June 1942** — **35 merchant ships** bound for **Arkhangelsk**. **Eleven arrived.** And a myth worth killing: **HMS Hood did not sail from Hvalfjörður** on her last voyage — she was on her way *to* it when she was turned west for the Bismarck.

title: 🪶 Mosfellsdalur

block.title: 🪶 Mosfellsdalur
block.sub: A Valley of Buried Silver and a Nobel Prize
block.cue: All around — Mosfellsdalur.
block.hook: Two famous residents, a thousand years apart: one **buried a fortune here and killed the witnesses**; the other won the **Nobel Prize**.
block.point: A buried fortune no-one's ever found, and a Nobel written five minutes up the road from it.
block.mic: One man hid his fortune. The other left his on the shelves.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the valley has closed in, so much the better. Laxness wrote most of it looking at exactly this."
bullets: **The silver (from Egil's saga):** in old age the warrior-poet **Egill Skallagrímsson** — sitting on two chests of silver gifted by **King Æthelstan of England** (the same Egill the brewery back in town is named after) — slipped off during the Alþingi with the silver, a horse and two slaves. The horse came back. Egill came back. The slaves and the silver didn't — he killed them to keep the spot secret. A thousand years of treasure hunters later: score **zero**. (Saga, not survey — treat it as legend.)
**The dig:** archaeologists have excavated nearby at **Hrísbrú**, where the saga says Egil's bones were later moved to the church his descendants built.

**The Nobel:** born **Halldór Guðjónsson** in **1902**, raised from age three at the farm **Laxnes** just here in the valley — when he needed an author's name, **he took the farm's**. **Nobel Prize for Literature, 1955** — Iceland's only laureate, largely for ***Sjálfstætt fólk*** (*Independent People*).
Two stops in the next kilometre: **Laxnes**, the farm that gave him his name — then **Gljúfrasteinn**, the house he built with the proceeds. Both coming up on the left.

title: 🎬 Laxnes Horse Farm
subject: laxnes horse farm

block.title: 🎬 Laxnes Horse Farm
block.cue: Look right on Route 36 — Laxnes, about 400 metres up the side road.
block.hook: That farm on the right started with **six horses and one stranger asking for a ride.** Its horses have since turned up in *Game of Thrones* — and the boy who grew up on this land carried the farm's name all the way to Stockholm.
block.point: One small farm exported a breed to Hollywood **and** a surname to Stockholm.
block.mic: Some of these horses grazing by the road have better screen credits than most working actors. Don't ask for autographs — they only sign with a hoof.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The horses do not mind, and they will be out in it. They were bred for days like this."
bullets: **Ragnheiður Gíslason** and **Þórarinn "Þóri" Jónasson** moved onto the run-down farm in **1967** and started the riding business in **1968**, after a visitor asked out of nowhere whether they'd take him out on horseback. Six horses, summers only. It grew into **Iceland's oldest continuously running riding-tour company** — **120 horses** and around **15,000 riders a year** by **2018**, **85% of them from abroad**.

Their horses work on screen too. The Mosfellsbær local paper *Mosfellingur* puts it plainly: **"hestar frá Laxnesi birst í nokkrum bíómyndum eins og Game of Thrones"** — horses from Laxnes have appeared in several films, *Game of Thrones* among them. In **1992** Þóri shipped Icelandic horses to the **United States** to show them off near Hollywood and ended up on **CBS and CNN**.

And the name. **Halldór Guðjónsson** was raised on this farm from the age of **three**. When he started publishing he took the farm's name — **Laxness** — and in **1955** that name won Iceland's **only Nobel Prize in Literature**. **Gljúfrasteinn**, the house he built, is the white one we passed **600 metres back up the valley**.

block.title: 🪶 Gljúfrasteinn
block.cue: Look right — the white house by the river Kaldakvísl, just off Route 36.
block.hook: On **17 June 1945** — the young republic's first birthday — a woman sat down and typed the building contract for that white house. **Ten years later there was a Nobel Prize in it.**
block.point: Iceland's only Nobel came home to a quiet valley — to a house that doubles as the country's smallest gallery of rejected art.
block.mic: A Nobel on the shelf, a rejected altarpiece on the wall — Gljúfrasteinn is where Iceland keeps the things the gatekeepers got wrong.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "A white house in grey rain is very Icelandic literature. He would have approved."
bullets: The typist was **Auður Sveinsdóttir**, born at **Eyrarbakki on 30 July 1918**, and she didn't just type it — she ran the build. She married **Halldór Laxness** that **Christmas Eve, 1945**. The architect was **Ágúst Pálsson**; the house was home from **1945** until Halldór died on **8 February 1998**. Auður outlived him by fourteen years, dying **29 October 2012**, aged **94**.

**1955:** Halldór takes Iceland's **only Nobel Prize in Literature** — *"for his vivid epic power which has renewed the great narrative art of Iceland."* Auður marked it the way a textile artist would: she made **Maríuklæðið**, "Mary's Cloth", to commemorate it.

**Kjarval's altarpieces, chapter one:** in **1914** he painted one for **Bakkagerði** church out east — Christ preaching from **Álfaborg**, the elf-rock, **Dyrfjöll** behind. The bishop refused to bless it — **too many elves, not enough Jesus**. It still hangs there, gloriously **unconsecrated**.

**Chapter two:** his second altarpiece (*John the Baptist, Christ at his feet*) was rejected outright as **"crude and ugly"** — so **Halldór bought the reject and gave it a wall in this house.** One man, two altarpieces, **zero bishops convinced** — and the painter, the brewer's Viking and the novelist, the morning's three pocket names, all tie off in this one valley.

The **Icelandic state bought the house and its art in 2002**, a hundred years to the year since Halldór was born, and opened it to the public on **4 September 2004**. His **typewriter is still on the desk**.

title: 🚢 The Norse Expansion (793–1066 CE)

block.title: 🚢 The Norse Expansion (793–1066 CE)
block.cue: Approaching Þingvellir.
bullets: **Social** — competition among ambitious young men (polygyny, inheritance); population outgrew the land.
**Economic** — silver, silk, spices, and a profitable **slave trade**.
**Political** — retaliation against Christian encroachment; warfare brought status and new land.
**🌊 Expansion routes**
**Raids & trade — who, why, what moved**
| **Region** | **Main targets** | **Why they came** | **Took/traded (N→S)** | **Got back (S→N)** |
| England | Monasteries, towns | Wealth, slaves, land | Furs, amber, slaves, timber | Silver, gold, weapons |
| Ireland | Monasteries, towns | Wealth, slaves, trade towns | Furs, amber, slaves, timber | Silver, gold, weapons |
| Scotland | Islands, towns | Land, cattle, slaves | Furs, amber, timber | Silver, weapons |
| France | River towns, Paris | Ransom, loot, settlement | Furs, amber, timber, slaves | Silver, silk, weapons |
| Spain/Portugal | Coastal cities | Slaves, spices, plunder | Furs, amber, timber, slaves | Silver, gold, silk, spices |
| Low Countries | Coastal towns | Trade control, markets | Furs, amber, timber, slaves | Silver, gold, luxury goods |
| Baltic | Trading centres | Furs, amber, slaves | Furs, amber, timber, slaves | Silver, silk, spices |
| Eastern Europe | River trade towns | River-route control, silver | Furs, amber, slaves, timber | Silver (Arab coins), silk, spices |
| North Atlantic | Islands, new land | Farmland, resources | Furs, amber, timber, walrus ivory | Silver, weapons, exotic goods |
| Morocco | Nekor (c. 859) | Gold, silver, fame | Slaves, furs, amber, timber | Gold, silver, spices, textiles |
**🗺️ Patterns**
**North → South:** furs, amber, slaves, timber, walrus ivory → Europe, Byzantium, the Islamic world.
**South → North:** **silver** (Islamic dirhams), **silk**, spices, weapons, luxury goods.
**Reach:** sea + river networks linking the Arctic to the Mediterranean — **6,000+ miles**, Baghdad to Ireland.
**🌏 What they achieved**
Trade network: Volga → Islamic world, Dnieper → Byzantium, Atlantic → West Europe & N. America.
Arabic silver coins in Scandinavia; deep slave networks; new market integration.

**Vínland — the one hard proof:** the Norse site at **L'Anse aux Meadows**, Newfoundland (excavated **1960**, UNESCO **1978**) is the only confirmed Norse settlement in North America — ~500 years before Columbus.
Legacy: English law & language, the sagas, the world's oldest parliament (**Alþingi, 930**), the birth of **Normandy** and **Kievan Rus'**.
**⏳ How it ended (1066)**
**Battle of Stamford Bridge** — Harald Hardrada's defeat closes the Viking Age.
Why: political consolidation, Christianization, stronger defences, climate cooling, a shift to legal trade.
**🗝️ Key dates**

**North → South:** furs, amber, slaves, timber, walrus ivory — raided and traded out of monasteries, river towns and coastal cities from **Ireland to Morocco** (yes, Morocco — the **Nekor raid, c. 859**).

Trade network from the **Volga to Vínland**: Islamic silver in Scandinavia, Byzantium via the Dnieper — and the one hard proof in the west, **L'Anse aux Meadows**, Newfoundland (excavated **1960**, UNESCO **1978**), ~500 years before Columbus.

block.title: 🏘️ Landnám
block.sub: Sixty Years to Build a Country
block.cue: Crossing the Settlement Era.
block.hook: By tradition, in **874 CE** Iceland was all but empty. By **930**, it was full. Settled, mapped and **booted up with a national parliament** — in a single human lifetime.
block.point: Most countries are built over centuries by armies. Iceland was built in **two generations**, by farmers with notebooks.
block.mic: Founding-fathers? We've got 400. We named them all. They're still in the book.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "No view required. This is the chapter you listen to rather than look at."
bullets: The **Landnám** ("Land-Taking") is the **~60-year window** when 9,000-plus Norse, Celtic and other settlers grabbed every habitable bay and valley on the island. (**874 is the traditional date**; Ari the Wise points nearer **870**, and a nationwide ash layer — the **871 ± 2 tephra** — timestamps the whole business to the second.)
The textbook source is **Landnámabók** (*The Book of Settlements*) — **400 settlers** named, their farms, feuds and home-towns mapped in detail no other Viking-age country can match.
The trick: Iceland had **no locals to fight** — just a handful of Irish monks (the **Papar**) who legged it the moment longships appeared.
By **930** the population (and the feuds) were big enough that the chieftains met at **Þingvellir** to launch the **Alþingi**, the world's oldest parliament still in use.
say: the Land-Taking, the sixty years when settlers filled the island
The Book of Settlements, which names 400 settlers and their farms
the Irish monks already here, who left when the longships appeared
the parliament the chieftains launched at Þingvellir in 930

block.title: 🌍 Almannagjá
block.cue: We are walking down inside the crack. The wall on your left is the edge of North America.
block.hook: You are in the **gap between two continents** — and no, they do not meet here. They are tearing **apart**, at the speed your fingernails grow, and this valley is the hole they have left behind.
block.point: Most plate boundaries sit invisible under two kilometres of ocean. Here you can **walk into the one the planet is tearing open.**
block.mic: Hand on the wall to your left: North America. It is going that way. You are going that way. Slowly, and there is no hurry — it is about as fast as your fingernails grow.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Rain in the rift is normal. The wall does not care, and neither did the men who argued under it."
bullets: Forget the postcard version where you "touch two continents at once." **Þingvellir** sits on the **Mid-Atlantic Ridge**, and what you are standing in is a **seven-kilometre-wide graben** — a strip of valley floor **sinking between two fault walls** as the plates pull apart about **2 cm a year**. The plates never touch here. The valley **is** the gap.

The cracks have names. **Almannagjá**, the big one you are walking through, is the **torn edge on the North American side**; its twin **Heiðargjá** marks the far side of the rift. The floor between them belongs to **neither continent** — it is the seam, still ripping.
The plain is **Þingvallahraun**, a **9,000-year-old** shield lava that spread down from **Skjaldbreiður**. Since then the floor has sunk **over 40 m** and the rift has pulled open by about **70 m**.

It does not creep smoothly — it locks, strains, then lets go. The last big pulse came in **spring 1789**, dropping the valley floor about **2.5 m in roughly ten days** and flooding the paths around the assembly ground.
Since **930** the assembly ground itself has dropped some **3–4 m.** The parliament you are about to stand in met noticeably higher up than the ground you are on.

🎬 **On screen:** this gorge is the pass to the **Bloody Gate** in *Game of Thrones* — the gate was added digitally above the Öxarárfoss trail — and the park doubled as an otherworldly realm in ***Thor: The Dark World*** (2013).
say: the big crack you walk through; its west wall is the edge of the North American plate
the fault marking the far side of the rift
the 9,000-year-old lava plain the valley floor is made of
the shield volcano that poured it out

block.title: ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi
block.cue: At the Law Rock — the wall behind you is the reason this spot was chosen.
block.hook: The **world's oldest parliament still in use**. Set up in **930 CE** in a literal **crack in the earth** — because the acoustics were better than anyone's farmhouse.
block.point: No royal palace. No marble columns. Just a rock, a cliff wall, and the world's first national parliament held outdoors.
block.mic: Britain calls itself the home of parliament. Iceland was running one **300 years before the Magna Carta** — in a hole in the ground.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "They met here for two weeks every summer in whatever the sky was doing. So can we."
bullets: In **930 CE**, Iceland's chieftains gathered here and founded the **Alþingi** — the national assembly. They picked the spot because the **Lögberg** ("Law Rock") cliff wall **carried the spoken law** across the valley.
For two weeks every summer the country **shut down** and came here: laws made, marriages arranged, murderers tried, beer drunk.

The **Lögsögumaður** (Law-Speaker), elected for a **three-year term**, had to recite **a third of the entire legal code from memory each year** — three years to deliver the lot. Drop one clause and you could change a verdict.
And there was **no king** — roughly **36 goðar** (chieftain-priests) ran the whole thing by consensus. One law, one people, zero crowns.

They chose this ground carefully: reachable from north, south and west inside about **seventeen days' travel**, a natural stage of cliffs and level floor, and **common land confiscated after its owner was outlawed for murder.** Practical, dramatic and pointedly neutral.

It met here every summer until **1798**, sat two more summers in Reykjavík, and was then **abolished outright by royal decree on 6 June 1800.** Re-established on **8 March 1843**, it sat again on **1 July 1845** — in Reykjavík, in a school building. So not a thousand unbroken years. A thousand years with a **43-year hole** that Denmark put there.
say: the national assembly founded here in 930
the Law Rock, the cliff wall that carried the spoken law across the valley
the Law-Speaker, who recited a third of the whole legal code from memory each year
the chieftain-priests, about 36 of them, who ran it by consensus

block.title: ⚖️ Kristnitaka
block.sub: The Day Iceland Changed Religion, Lying Down
block.cue: Standing at Lögberg. This is the exact ground where it was decided.
block.hook: Around **the year 1000**, Iceland changed its national religion **without a single sword being drawn** — right here. No army. No martyrs. Just one pagan chieftain, one cloak, and a really long nap.
block.point: Most national religions are imposed by kings or won by armies. Iceland's was decided **on this rock, by a man having a lie-down.**
block.mic: Calmly, collectively, and after a really good night's sleep. That is how Iceland became Christian — standing where you are standing. Most countries were not given the option.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Þorgeir lay under a fur cloak for a day and a night. In this, you can see why."
bullets: By **999** the country was split — Christian districts against pagan strongholds — and Norway's King **Ólafur Tryggvason** was squeezing hard: he welcomed Christian traders into his ports, barred the pagans, and **held Icelandic hostages** as leverage. Convert, or lose the trade route you cannot live without.
Persuasion had gone badly. One Saxon priest, **Þangbrandur**, allegedly **fought duels and killed poets** who mocked his sermons. Not a charm offensive.

By **AD 1000** (the sources wobble between 999 and 1000) the **Alþingi** met on this spot facing two religions, two law codes and one looming civil war — so both sides handed the verdict to one man: **Þorgeir Ljósvetningagoði**, the *pagan* Law-Speaker.

He lay down under his cloak **a full day and a night**, then stood up on this rock and ruled: **one law, one people, one faith — Christianity** — so the young commonwealth would not split in two. Private sacrifice, horse-meat and infant exposure were quietly tolerated at first, then dropped. Food is food.
say: the pagan Law-Speaker who lay under his cloak a day and a night, then chose Christianity
the Saxon priest who fought duels with the poets who mocked his sermons
Norway's king, who squeezed Iceland with port bans and hostages

block.title: ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur
block.sub: A Westminster Abbey With Two Occupants
block.cue: The white church and the five-gabled farmhouse on your right, at the bottom of the wall.
block.hook: There has been a church on this spot since **1017**. Beside it is a **national burial ground built to hold Iceland's greatest artists** — and in eighty-five years it has managed to bury exactly **two people**.
block.point: A thousand-year-old church, a Prime Minister's summer house, and a national shrine containing two poets — one of whom may not be the right man.
block.mic: They built this to hold the greatest Icelanders who ever lived. Two people went in. Then everyone thought about it a bit more and decided, actually, we'd rather be buried at home.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The white church against a grey sky is the photograph everybody takes anyway."
bullets: The church first went up around **1017**, the present building dates from **1859**, and the bell tower was added in **1907** — the date is on the weather vane. It has no resident priest; the one who serves it **comes out from Skálholt**, which we pass later today.

The five-gabled farmhouse beside it is **Þingvallabær**, built in **1930** for the Alþingi millennium festival by **Guðjón Samúelsson**, the state architect. He turned its face deliberately toward **Almannagjá** — the older turf farmhouse it replaced had looked out at the lake. It began with **three gables**; two more were added after a **1970 fire** destroyed the king's house next door. Since **1974** it has been the **Prime Minister's summer residence.** One gable belongs to the church.

Behind the church is **Skáldareitur**, the poets' plot — and it exists because of an argument over a corpse. When **Einar Benediktsson** died in **January 1940**, his ex-wife and his companion could not agree who had the right to bury him. **Jónas Jónsson frá Hriflu** saw the opening and proposed a national honour ground here, modelled on **Westminster Abbey**. Einar went into it on **27 January 1940**.

The second and last arrival was **Jónas Hallgrímsson**, Iceland's national poet, who had died in Copenhagen on **26 May 1845** of blood poisoning after breaking his leg on a staircase. His bones came home and were buried here on **16 November 1946** — over the objection of the man who dug them up, who wanted him in **Öxnadalur** where he was born. The Prime Minister, **Ólafur Thors**, overruled him. The government's position was that **Jónas's bones were state property.**

And nobody is sure they are his. Two other people had been buried on top of him in **1875** and **1900**, and both had to be lifted out first. The doubt has never gone away — there are still calls to open the grave and test what is in it.

Two graves. That is the whole national pantheon. **Halldór Laxness**, whose house we passed this morning, is not here. **Kjarval**, who opened this tour, is not here either. Iceland built itself a Westminster Abbey and then quietly stopped using it.
say: the five-gabled farmhouse, the Prime Minister's summer residence
the church, on this spot since 1017
the poets' plot behind the church
the poet whose disputed funeral created the place, buried 1940
the state architect who built the farmhouse in 1930

block.title: 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá
block.sub: The Waterfall, the Drowning Pool and the Fake Wishing Well
block.cue: Follow the Öxará. The waterfall ahead, the still green pool below it, and the coin-filled crack by the bridge.
block.hook: A waterfall that was **moved here on purpose**, a pool where **at least eighteen women were drowned**, and a wishing well invented by **a sign put up in the 1930s.**
block.point: The law was spoken up on the rock. It was carried out down here, in the water.
block.mic: People throw coins in and make a wish because a sign in the 1930s told them to. Icelanders have been quietly watching tourists do it ever since and saying nothing.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Rain makes the falls louder and the pool darker. Neither improves the story of this place."
bullets: The **Öxará** comes over the wall at **Öxarárfoss** and runs down through the assembly ground. It is the main open river feeding the whole valley — and it is doing a job it was very probably given, diverted to bring water to the assembly.

Below the falls the river widens into a still green pool: **Drekkingarhylur**, the drowning pool. After the Reformation Iceland adopted a severe moral code, **Stóridómur**, in **1564**, and Þingvellir doubled as an execution ground — men **beheaded, hanged or burned**; women convicted of **adultery, incest, perjury or infanticide** were **drowned here**.

Court records point to **at least eighteen women killed at this pool between about 1618 and 1749.** A memorial plaque now names them. Two weeks a year this place made the law. It also carried out the sentence.

And then there is **Peningagjá** — the crack full of coins by the bridge, properly the southern end of **Nikulásargjá**. The coins have nothing to do with the sagas. The **bridge went up in 1907** for the visit of the Danish king **Frederick VIII**, who is said to have thrown the first one in.

The wish came later, and from a signpost. In the **1930s** somebody put up a board reading **"to the wishing well"** — and that is the entire origin of the tradition. The national park's own record is blunt about it: **no older Icelandic folk tale or story about wishing here exists.** An ancient custom, ninety years old, invented by signage.
say: the waterfall coming over the rift wall
the 1564 moral code that made the drownings law
the coin crack, properly the south end of Nikulásargjá

block.title: 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra
block.sub: The Cleanest Water on Earth, and Four Fish That Are One Fish
block.cue: The lake filling the rift ahead of you, and the clear pools off to the side.
block.hook: Meltwater that left a glacier **thirty to a hundred years ago**, filtered through lava the whole way — **drinkable from your cupped hand**, with **120 m** of underwater visibility. And one fish in it that has quietly become four.
block.point: Two continents pulling apart, the cleanest drinking water on the planet running through the gap, and a fish quietly turning into four other fish while nobody watches.
block.mic: Iceland's answer to a tectonic disaster: turn it into a reservoir, then drink it.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the far shore has gone, that is the rift you cannot see across — which is rather the point."
bullets: **Þingvallavatn** is Iceland's largest natural lake: about **84 km²**, up to **114 m deep**, averaging **34 m**, sitting at roughly **100.5 m above sea level** — and its bed lies **below sea level** because of the rifting.

About **nine-tenths of everything entering it arrives from below**, seeping up through porous lava at **3–4°C**. Only about a tenth comes in as visible surface water, most of that the **Öxará**. The catchment runs to some **1,300 km²**, of which the lake is only about **six per cent** — the rest is plumbing you cannot see.

The water begins as snow on **Langjökull** and spends **thirty to a hundred years** underground before it surfaces. Clear pools like **Silfra** are that meltwater arriving. The water in front of you fell before some of you were born.

In that lake, one Arctic charr arrived after the ice left and split into **four separate forms in about 10,000 years.** **Kuðungableikja**, the snail charr. **Dvergbleikja**, the dwarf. **Murta**, the small open-water one. **Sílableikja**, the fish-eater. Two feed on the bottom, two feed in open water — and they are **all one species**, *Salvelinus alpinus*. They can interbreed and produce fertile young. They largely decline to.

**Three of the four are genetically distinct.** The fourth, sílableikja, comes out muddled — some read as murta, others as crosses. Vísindavefurinn's assessment is that this may be **sympatric speciation**, one population dividing with no physical barrier between the halves, and that another **10,000 years** could produce genuinely separate species. Evolution has not finished tidying up.

That island out in the lake is **Sandey**, a **tuff cone** built by **Hengill** about **1,900 years ago** — the same eruption that laid down **Nesjahraun** at the north end. An eruption happened in the middle of a lake and built itself an island out of it.
say: Iceland's largest natural lake, filling the rift floor
the clear pool you can drink from, visibility up to 120 m
the glacier the water left 30 to 100 years ago
the small open-water charr, one of the lake's four forms
the tuff-cone island Hengill built about 1,900 years ago

block.title: 🇮🇸 17 June 1944
block.cue: Back at the Law Rock. This is where the country stopped belonging to anybody else.
block.hook: On **17 June 1944** Iceland declared itself a republic — not in the capital, but **here**, in the rain, in front of tens of thousands of people standing in this valley.
block.point: A thousand years after the first assembly, on the same ground, the country finished the job.
block.mic: It absolutely poured. Tens of thousands stood in it for hours. If you want one image of how much this particular field means to Icelanders — that is the one.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "It poured on the day itself. Thousands stood in it anyway."
bullets: They could have done it in Reykjavík, in a building, dry. They chose this ground instead: **the place the nation first assembled in 930**, and the place Denmark had shut down in **1800**.
The date was not an accident either — **17 June** is the birthday of **Jón Sigurðsson**, the man who led the independence campaign and who did not live to see it.
It rained. It rained hard, the whole way through. Nobody left. The photographs of that day are mostly a valley full of soaked people refusing to go home.
say: the independence leader whose birthday, 17 June, became the national day
republic; the word they were there to say

title: 🕳️ The Cave People
subject: the cave people

block.title: 🕳️ The Cave People
block.cue: Ahead and right at 2 o'clock — Laugarvatnshellir, a little over two kilometres off the road.
block.hook: The last family to call an Icelandic **cave** home moved out in **1922** — no electricity, no plumbing, but **their own front door** and a cow tied up next door.
block.point: Twentieth-century Europe had jazz, cars and radio. It also had **a family raising kids in a cave**, because that's what was available.
block.mic: Legend says a shepherd here was repeatedly **dragged out of the cave by invisible hands** — right before a blizzard that would have killed him inside. In Iceland, even the hidden folk do their own weather warnings.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Low cloud is the right weather for this. They lived in a cave because of days like this."
bullets: **Laugarvatnshellir** is a pair of man-made caves hacked out of soft **palagonite tuff** (solidified volcanic ash) on the Lyngdalsheiði heath, between Þingvellir and Laugarvatn.

First in, **1910**: the carpenter **Indriði Guðmundsson** and **Guðrún Kolbeinsdóttir**, who lasted about **eleven months** and ran a **coffee-bread-and-cakes tent** for passing Golden Circle travellers — Iceland's original roadside café, carved edition.

Then **1918–1922**: **Jón Þorvarðsson** and **Vigdís Helgadóttir** raised **three children** in the rock. When a blizzard blocked the midwife, Jón **delivered his own daughter Ragnheiður** himself — cave dad of the century.
Not medieval, either: this was **the same decade as the Model T Ford**. Reopened to visitors in **2017** — original door back in place, coffee pot and all.

block.title: 🌋 Hekla
block.cue: Look right at 1 o'clock — Hekla, sixty kilometres out on the horizon. Clear days only.
block.hook: In medieval Europe, this was officially **the front door of Hell** — and the prison of **Judas Iscariot**. Iceland didn't argue. We just charged tourists.
block.point: Most volcanoes get a Wikipedia entry. Hekla got a **theological one** — used to scare medieval Europe straight for 800 years.
block.mic: Welcome to the gateway to Hell. It gives you barely **an hour and a half's notice** to send the postcards.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Hekla is out sixty kilometres and hides most days. Medieval Europe thought that was deliberate."
bullets: **Hekla** — **1,491 m**, erupted **20+ times since the Vikings**; the **1104** blast (**VEI 5**) dropped ~**2 km³ of tephra over 55,000 km²**, one of the biggest in Iceland's record and the one that started the legend.
When word of 1104 reached Europe, **Cistercian monks** ran with it — by **1180** Herbert of Clairvaux wrote that next to Hekla, Etna was "a small furnace."
Through the 12th–13th centuries the Church named Hekla the **literal mouth of Hell** and a prison of **Judas Iscariot**.
Last erupted **February 2000** — and Hekla is so eerily quiet beforehand that seismographs picked up its run-up only about **80 minutes** before it blew.

On a very, very clear day this same sightline stacks up **three more ice-capped volcanoes** toward the coast: **Tindfjallajökull**, then **Eyjafjallajökull** — of 2010 ash-cloud fame — then **Mýrdalsjökull** behind it.

She is a great deal older than her CV suggests. The story of the Hekla we would recognise today begins **just over 7,000 years ago** — she was already in business long before anyone was here to take notes. **1104** was her **first eruption after the settlement of Iceland** — and it is still **her own largest explosive eruption in historical time.** (The bigger explosive eruption in Iceland's historical record belongs to a rival: **Öræfajökull in 1362.**) She had been quiet for roughly **three centuries** beforehand, which means nobody then alive had the faintest idea what she was capable of.

The ash of 1104 went north, and the farming districts of **Þjórsárdalur** and **Hrunamannahreppur** were **abandoned** because of it. Iceland got a thousand years of European publicity out of that eruption and **wrote none of it** — the people actually living underneath were otherwise engaged, emptying two districts.

The Judas story has a date and a document. **Within ten to twenty years of 1104** an **English poem** was already asserting that **Judas** — the arch-traitor himself — was imprisoned inside Hekla, and European clergy positively welcomed eruption reports, because to their minds an eruption **proved that Hell existed.** The image that fixed it was a woodcut in the history of the Northern Peoples by the Swedish churchman **Olaus Magnus (1490–1557)**, published in **Venice in 1555**, showing Hekla with a set of tunnels running down out of the mountain. **Vesuvius and Etna never acquired the same reputation** — and Vísindavefur offers the driest explanation available. They were **too close to civilisation.** A volcano safely off the edge of Europe made a far more convincing front door.

Her longest eruption began on **5 April 1766** and continued with breaks until **May 1768** — **just over two years**, including a **six-month pause** in the middle that must have felt to everyone like the end of it.
say: the 1,491 m volcano at one o'clock that medieval Europe called the gateway to Hell
volcanic ash and fragments; the 1104 blast dropped about 2 km³ of it
the first of the three glaciers visible on a very clear day
the 2010 ash-cloud volcano, second in the stack
the third glacier in the stack, furthest toward the coast

title: 🛁 Laugarvatn & Apavatn
subject: laugarvatn & apavatn

block.title: 🛁 Laugarvatn & Apavatn
block.cue: Look left at 9 o'clock — Laugarvatn.
block.hook: What happens when you put the leaders of an entire country into the **same hot tub** to argue policy? Iceland's been finding out for **1,000 years**.
block.point: Most countries hold political summits in glass towers. Iceland held one in a hot lake.
block.mic: The Vikings invented hot-tub diplomacy a thousand years before Davos.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Steam shows better in the cold. If the lake has gone grey, look for where it is smoking."
bullets: **Laugarvatn** ("Pool Lake," ~260 people) sits on the **Hreppar block** — geothermal springs at **35–40°C** feed the lakebed, so even in winter parts of the shore run bath-warm.

Its moment came around **1000 CE**: with Christianity already voted through at Þingvellir, the newly-Christian northerners and southerners rode over so they could be **baptised in the warm spring** rather than the freezing river. The spring — once **Reykjalaug** — was renamed **Vígðalaug, the "Consecrated Pool,"** for the event. (Westerners had their own warm spring at Krosslaug. Iceland ran baptisms by postcode.)

Neighbour lake **Apavatn** ("Marsh Lake") is where the "cold politics" happened. In **spring 1238**, during the Sturlung Age, **Sturla Sighvatsson** (Sturlungar) ambushed and captured his rival **Gizur Þorvaldsson** (Haukdælir) right here — forcing him to swear on the Bible to give up power and sail to Norway.

Gizur had his fingers crossed. He broke the oath, teamed up with **Kolbeinn ungi**, and five months later — **~1,700 men against ~1,000** — crushed the Sturlungar at **Örlygsstaðir (21 August 1238)**, the largest battle ever fought on Icelandic soil. Sturla's ancient family spear **Grásíða kept bending in his hands** as the tide turned; Gizur is said to have struck the fatal blow. So much for hot-tub diplomacy at the lake next door.
Today Laugarvatn has the **Fontana** geothermal baths — the same warmth that converted the pagans, now with a bar.

Neighbour lake **Apavatn** ("Marsh Lake") is where the "cold politics" happened — it staged one of the dirtiest ambushes in Icelandic history. Hold that thought: the whole blood-soaked story is coming up just past the next river.

title: 💙 Brúará
subject: brúará

block.title: 💙 Brúará
block.sub: The River That Lost Its Bridge
block.cue: Crossing Brúará.
block.hook: A river whose name literally means **"Bridge-River"** — except the bridge was a **natural stone arch**, and in **1602** the church **smashed it on purpose** to keep the starving out.
block.point: A river named after a bridge — that lost the bridge because the church was tired of the poor arriving.
block.mic: The cheapest border policy in Icelandic history: knock down the only bridge and let the river do the rest.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Rivers do not need good weather. This one is loudest when the sky is worst."
bullets: **Brúará** ("Bridge-River") is a clear, spring-fed river feeding the Hvítá; its showpiece is the electric-blue waterfall **Brúarfoss**. For centuries a natural **stone arch** here was the only crossing for miles.

In the famine year **1602**, the steward of **Skálholt**, the great church estate we'll visit this afternoon — with the knowledge of the bishop's wife, **Helga Jónsdóttir** — had the arch **deliberately destroyed** to stop displaced, starving people crossing to reach the estate's fertile land. Charity, Skálholt-style: demolish the bridge so the hungry can't walk over it.

The river had form: back in **1433** the disgraced bishop **Jón Gerreksson** was **drowned in it in a sack** as an execution. Not a lucky river to owe a bishop money. Keep both stories in hand — we reach the estate itself this afternoon.

title: ⚖️ The Sturlung Age
subject: the sturlung age

block.title: ⚖️ The Sturlung Age
block.sub: The Civil War That Ended the Republic
block.cue: *The 13th-century chapter most tours skip.*
block.hook: Iceland ran itself as a republic for **300 years**. Then **one family** decided that wasn't working — and burned the whole thing down. Literally.
block.point: Iceland didn't lose its independence to an army. It **lost it to itself**.
block.mic: The world's oldest parliament was killed by the same families it was built to control.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "No view for this one — it is thirteenth-century politics, and it is grim enough without the rain."
bullets: The **Sturlungaöld** ran roughly **1220–1262** — Iceland's longest, ugliest internal war.

Power had pooled in a few big clans, especially the **Sturlungar** (yes, saga-writer **Snorri Sturluson**'s family). Disputes stopped going to the Althing and started going to **swords, fires and assassinations**.

**Spring 1238, at Apavatn** — the lake we just passed — **Sturla Sighvatsson** ambushed his rival **Gizur Þorvaldsson** of the Haukdælir and forced him to **swear on the Bible** to give up power and sail to Norway. Gizur had his fingers crossed.

Five months later the oath came due at **Örlygsstaðir (21 August 1238)** — Gizur, teamed up with **Kolbeinn ungi**, brought **~1,700 men against ~1,000** to the **largest battle ever fought on Icelandic soil**. The northern Sturlungar were wiped out in an afternoon; Sturla's ancient family spear **Grásíða kept bending in his hands** as the tide turned, and Gizur is said to have struck the fatal blow.

Snorri himself — the man who wrote down Norse mythology — was **murdered in his own cellar at Reykholt on 23 September 1241**, on the orders of the Norwegian king, by a raiding party led by **Gizur Þorvaldsson, his own former son-in-law**. His last words: ***"Eigi skal höggva!"*** — "Don't strike!" They struck.
The low point: the **Burning of Flugumýri (1253)** — a wedding ambush, the hall torched with the family inside. (Often linked to *Game of Thrones'* Red Wedding — a pop claim; see verify list.)
By **1262**, exhausted, the chieftains signed the **Old Covenant**, handing the country to the King of Norway. The 300-year republic was over.

Power had pooled in a few big clans, especially the **Sturlungar** (yes, saga-writer **Snorri Sturluson**'s family). Disputes moved from the Althing to **swords, fires and assassinations**. At **Örlygsstaðir (1238)**, the largest battle on Icelandic soil, the northern Sturlungar were wiped out in one afternoon.

title: ⚖️ Haukadalur
subject: haukadalur

block.title: ⚖️ Haukadalur
block.cue: At the geothermal field of Haukadalur.
block.hook: One farm in this steaming valley bred a **dynasty**: Iceland's first bishop's family, the schoolmaster who trained the nation's memory — and the man who **ended the republic**. Meet the **Haukdælir**.
block.point: One valley, one family: the first bishop's line, the schoolroom that preserved Iceland's memory — and the earl who signed the republic away.
block.mic: The hawks of this valley taught Iceland to read, write and pray — then one of them sold the whole country to Norway. Family legacies are complicated.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Steam and low cloud look identical from here. Both mean the ground is warm."
bullets: **Haukadalur** means **"Valley of the Hawks"** — known now for steam, but for two centuries this was a **chieftain's seat**: the home farm of the **Haukdælir**, one of the great power families of the Icelandic Commonwealth.

**Teitur Ísleifsson** — son of **Ísleifur Gissurarson, Iceland's first bishop** — settled this farm and became the **patriarch of the Haukdælir**. He ran a famous school here in the 11th century, and one of its boarders, from about **age seven**, was **Ari fróði Þorgilsson** ("the Wise," c. 1067–1148) — who grew up to write **Íslendingabók**, the reason Iceland has any firm early dates at all. (The *first*-school crown belongs to **Skálholt**, down the road — we'll get there.)

The family stayed at the top for two centuries — bishops, lawmen, and finally **Gizur Þorvaldsson**, the oath-breaker of Örlygsstaðir from the last stop: a **Haukdæling**, made **Iceland's first and only earl in 1258**, four years before the republic he helped bury was handed to Norway.
The valley also holds the **Geysir** and **Strokkur** hot springs — the original "geyser" that gave the word to the world — on the **Hreppar block**, where superheated water reaches the surface.
**Haukadalur** means **"Valley of the Hawks"** — known now for steam, but historically one of Iceland's great **education centres**.

In the 11th century the farm was home to **Teitur Ísleifsson** — son of **Ísleifur Gissurarson, Iceland's first bishop** — who ran a **famous school** at the farm (the *first*-school crown belongs to **Skálholt**). One of its boarders, from about **age seven**: **Ari fróði Þorgilsson** ("the Wise," c. 1067–1148), who grew up to write **Íslendingabók**, Iceland's foundational history and the reason we have any firm early dates at all.
So the alphabet, the legal training and the historical record of a whole country came out of **one farm**.

But steam is only the valley's modern job: this was also a **chieftain's seat** — the home farm of the **Haukdælir**, one of the great power families of the Icelandic Commonwealth, with schoolmaster **Teitur Ísleifsson** as their patriarch.

block.title: ⛲ Geysir
block.cue: At the geothermal field — Strokkur and Geysir.
block.hook: Iceland gave the world the word **"geyser"** — from one hot spring, in one field, on one farm.
block.point: Every other geyser on the planet is named after **this one**. Yellowstone, New Zealand, Chile — all geological cousins of one Icelandic hot spring.
block.mic: Iceland exported the word "geyser" before it exported the cod.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Wind decides which way you get soaked. Stand upwind of Strokkur and watch everyone else learn that."
bullets: The original **Geysir** is first recorded in **1294**, when earthquakes reshaped the field's springs — at its peak it threw water **60–80 m** up. It's mostly **dormant** now, but its reliable cousin **Strokkur** ("the Churn") goes **every 6–10 minutes**, **15–20 m** high (occasionally 40).
Watch the **dome** bulge just before it fires: a thin layer of cooler water over near-boiling water below, pressure building until it punches through.
The field sits on the **Hreppar block** — water seeps down, hits **200°C+ rock**, flashes to steam, shoots back up.

**Geysir runs on earthquakes.** Born in the annals after the **1294** quakes, it roars back after every big southern shake — **1630**, **1896**, most recently **June 2000** — then dozes off again between them, sometimes for decades.

Icelanders never quite accepted the naps: they used to **shovel rocks and turf in** to provoke it, and from **1963 to 1981** the official trick was **soap** — lower the surface tension and the superheated water boils over. The country literally **washed its geyser into performing**. (We've since let it sleep with dignity.)

The name **Geysir** (from *geysa*, "to gush") first appears in writing in **1647** — and as Enlightenment scientists took an interest, the word spread to **every language on Earth**, all from this one field.
At its most active it took **8 to 10 hours** to refill between eruptions. In **1896** it came back erupting **several times a day**, then fell dormant around **1915**.
A **channel was cut in 1935** to lower the water surface and restart it, then **re-cut and deepened in 1981**.

**Strokkur** is straight thermodynamics: **one metre down the water is 90–95°C**, at **ten metres 112°C**, and at the bottom of the **23-metre shaft about 130°C** — held liquid only by the weight of water above it. Take the lid off and it flashes to steam.
Measured eruptions in **2000** threw between about **270 and 425 litres** of water, or **300 to 500 litres** once you count what leaves as steam.

**Strokkur's** reliability is younger than most of its audience. Its nineteenth-century performances are said to have **lasted an hour and reached up to 60 metres** — then it fell silent for decades. In **1963** the decision was taken to **drill about 40 metres into the gosskál**, the eruption basin, and it has been **extraordinarily active** ever since. The most dependable natural spectacle in this country is not entirely natural.

One more number for the shaft: a **cold vein comes in at about 13 metres** down. That is part of why height, duration and interval all vary — and why nobody will ever hand you a timetable, so keep looking at the water rather than at your phone.
say: the original hot spring that gave every language the word geyser; mostly dormant now
"the Churn", its reliable cousin that fires every 6 to 10 minutes

block.title: 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss
block.sub: Meltwater and the Falls One Woman Saved
block.cue: At Gullfoss.
block.hook: In **1907** an investor tried to dam this waterfall — and a farmer's daughter, **Sigríður**, fought it all the way to Reykjavík. She **lost in court** — and the falls are still here anyway.
block.point: The world's most famous Icelandic conservation story — lost in the courtroom, saved in the end, by a woman who never had a vote.
block.mic: An investor showed up with engineers. A farmer's daughter showed up and lost every legal round — and the falls are still here.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Rain makes it bigger, spray makes it wetter, and the rainbow needs sun. Two out of three today."
bullets: **Gullfoss** ("Golden Falls") drops the **Hvítá** down two staircase tiers, **32 m** total, in a narrow canyon — spray throwing rainbows so consistently it looks staged.
The Hvítá is **glacial meltwater** from **Langjökull**, silt-laden enough to glow gold in summer light.

In **1907** an Englishman leased the falls from farmer **Tómas Tómasson** for a **hydro plant**. His daughter **Sigríður Tómasdóttir** spent her own savings on a Reykjavík lawyer — **Sveinn Björnsson**, later Iceland's **first president** — and fought for years to void the lease. The famous "walked barefoot to Reykjavík / threatened to jump" details are **romanticised**; she genuinely **lost in court**, but the lease then **lapsed because the developers stopped paying the rent**.
Gullfoss survived, became a **nature reserve in 1979**, and Sigríður — remembered on a memorial above the falls — is now called **Iceland's first environmentalist**.
The gorge below runs about **2.5 km long and 70 m deep**, and mean flow over the lip is **109 m³/s**.

The Englishman's offer, early in **1907**, was **50,000 krónur** — and Iceland passed a law that same year restricting **foreign ownership of waterfalls**, after which foreign parties obtained rental rights anyway.

**Sigríður Tómasdóttir**, **1871 to 1957**, came from the farm **Brattholt** above the falls, and what she spent years trying to void were the agreements **her own father had signed**. The judgement went against the Brattholt family.

What actually saved it was duller than the legend: in **1928** the rental payments stopped and the agreement fell void. The reserve declaration was signed on **9 March 1979** and covers **164.2 hectares**.
Her lawyer was **Sveinn Björnsson**, who went on to become Iceland's first president, **1944 to 1952**. (Losing that case turned out to be quite good for his CV.)

🎬 **On screen:** Gullfoss shows up in *Vikings* (later seasons) and Netflix's *Lost in Space* — and it's the "Argentina" in the *Smallville* episode "Zod" (2006), where the final shot is captioned *Iguazú Falls* but is pure Gullfoss.
say: "Golden Falls," the 32 m two-tier waterfall we are standing at
the glacial river that makes it, meltwater off Langjökull
the farmer's daughter who fought the dam, and is now called Iceland's first environmentalist
her Reykjavík lawyer, later Iceland's first president
the glacier the Hvítá's meltwater comes from

block.title: 🎧 Iceland Through the Years
block.cue: Leaving Ytri-Tunga, last stop of the day. Playlist on, mic live between the stops.
block.hook: Forty-three tracks in three acts, and the whole story of how a country with fewer people than most cities ended up on everybody's playlist. We get through the first two today.
block.point: The exact moment a country stops importing pop and starts exporting it — and you can hear it happen.
block.mic: Everything from here is Icelandic. Listen out around track twenty-one: that is this small, cold, sheep-heavy island going from copying everybody to being copied.
bullets: **ACT I — Borrowed clothes.** Iceland still working out who it sounds like. Five of the biggest singalongs here are secretly Anglo-American hits in Icelandic disguise — *Mambo Italiano*, *California Dreamin'*, *I Will*, Ray Sharpe rockabilly, and a Brita Borg banger out of Stockholm. The mambo arrived secondhand, via 1950s Manhattan. Post-war crooners, dancehall ballads, and Keflavík kids who saw The Beatles in Bournemouth and ran home to start a band.

**01 · Jeg vil ha' morfor med mig ud på sjov** — *Raquel Rastenni*. Plot twist — the Danes nicked it. The song is actually “Jag ska' ta' morfar med mej ut i kväll,” a 1949 Brita Borg banger out of Stockholm, dressed up in a Danish coat a year later. Same writers (Peter Spar / Jessup Sandy), different *morfar*.  [Secret-cover thread]

**02 · Litla flugan** — *Sigfús Halldórsson*. Iceland's most beloved earworm started as a bar bet. December 1951, Reykhólar farm — the manager Sigurður Elíasson tells Sigfús he can't turn that poem into a tune in ten minutes. Ten minutes later: a national standard. Drinks were *not* on Sigurður.

**03 · Ísland farsælda frón** — *Karlakór Reykjavíkur*. The melody Icelanders actually sing is the wrong one. Helgi Helgason's tune gets the credit — but the version everyone knows is centuries older, a Lydian-mode chant from medieval manuscripts that got married to Jónas Hallgrímsson's 1835 lyric long after the wedding bells. A 600-year-old tune wearing 19th-century words.
**04 · Bláu augun** — *Haukur Morthens*

**05 · Vor við flóann** — *Ragnar Bjarnason*. Two-for-one. The 1959 7″ gives you Ragnar singing “Vor við flóann” on the A-side — flip it over and **Guðbergur Auðunsson** takes the mic for “Hvítir svanir.” Same record, two singers, no warning.  [Recorded somewhere unusual]

**06 · Æskuminning** — *Alfreð Clausen*. 1953. Iceland's first-ever ballad recorded with a full orchestra, Carl Billich on the baton. Walked it into the SKT dance-song competition the year before — and *lost*. The audience promptly overruled the judges and handed it the people's prize. Iceland figuring out who runs music: the people. Always the people.

**07 · Lilla Jóns** — *Guðbergur Auðunsson*. It's a Ray Sharpe rockabilly tune in Icelandic drag. Jón Sigurðsson took the American melody, dressed it in his own words, and out came “Little Jónsi.”  [Secret-cover thread]

**08 · Hæ Mambó** — *Haukur Morthens*. Yes — *that* Mambo Italiano. The Rosemary Clooney one. Loftur Guðmundsson Icelanded the lyrics and Reykjavík caught the mambo bug secondhand via 1950s Manhattan.  [Secret-cover thread]
**09 · Sveitapiltsins draumur** — *Hljómar*. California Dreamin'. With Icelandic lyrics. About a country boy. Yes, really.  [Secret-cover thread]

**10 · Sveitin milli sanda** — *Elly Vilhjálms*. There are no lyrics. None. Elly sings the entire thing on one open vowel — wordless, weightless, pure *Aaaaaa*. It started life as the score to a 1962 Ósvaldur Knudsen documentary; Magnús Blöndal Jóhannsson never bothered to add words and nobody ever asked.

**11 · Vor í Vaglaskógi** — *Vilhjálmur Vilhjálmsson*. Akureyri, February 1966. Two lovers go camping in Vaglaskógur — a 300-hectare birch forest in Fnjóskadalur — and Iceland gets its forever-song. The hook line every Icelander mouths on first beat: *Draumar þess rætast, sem gistir Vaglaskóg* — “the dreams of those who sleep in Vaglaskógur come true.” Kaleo dragged it onto the global stage in 2016. The forest has not stopped collecting tourists since.

**12 · Kling Klang** — *Dátar*. 1966 Keflavík teen-rock — fine. But the keyboard player? **Þórir Baldursson.** Twelve years later he'd be playing organ on Donna Summer, Giorgio Moroder and ABBA records. Pop is a small world. Iceland is an even smaller one.

**13 · If you knew** — *Thor's Hammer*. Recorded on Parlophone — *the Beatles' label* — in London, 1966. The “Umbarumbamba” EP that houses it now goes for thousands at auction; among 60s garage-rock collectors it's the white whale, the holy grail, the EP they'll remortgage their flat for.

**14 · Tætum og tryllum** — *Stuðmenn*. From the soundtrack of *Með allt á hreinu* (1982) — Iceland's biggest film of all time. 120,000 tickets. In a country of 230,000. Half the country watched it. Half the dialogue was improvised on the day, and the rival on-screen girl-band “Gærurnar” was actually Grýlurnar (skip ahead to track 19) — meaning the battle of the bands was real on screen *and* in the bar afterwards.

**ACT II — Finding the voice.** Iceland stops borrowing and starts getting copied. *Með allt á hreinu* eats half the country's box office — **120,000 tickets, 230,000 people**. Grýlurnar weaponise punk, and the band rivalry becomes the actual plot of the film. The Sugarcubes go global. Björk goes solo. GusGus turn out to be a twelve-person filmmaking collective who picked up instruments halfway through.

**15 · Reyndu aftur** — *Magnús Eiríksson, Mannakorn*. Track 2 of Mannakorn's January 1977 sophomore LP *Í gegnum tíðina*. The voice you're hearing? Pálmi Gunnarsson — same Pálmi who'd open Iceland's Eurovision account in Bergen 1986. Track 21 is also him. The man gets around.

**16 · Skólaball** — *Brimkló*. Plot twist confirmed by RÚV in 2021: *Skólaball er um stúlku sem síðar varð konan mín* — “the girl in the song became my wife.” Magnús Kjartansson met her at an actual school dance and wrote the actual song. The most romantic Reykjavík origin story that doesn't involve a horse.  [Song about someone]

**17 · Gáta dagsins** — *Spilverk þjóðanna*. Twenty seconds. *Twenty.* “Today's Riddle” clocks in shorter than a cigarette break — a deliberately cryptic micro-piece slipped in among the album's full-length songs. Blink and you've missed it.

**18 · Á Sprengisandi** — *Þú og ég*. A 19th-century Grímur Thomsen *ghost poem* turned into a 1980 disco track. Yes. The placename comes from *sprengja* — “to ride a horse to death” — because the highland route was so brutal travellers were said to kill their mounts crossing it. Now picture that on a glitterball.  [Debut-LP opener]

**19 · Sísi** — *Grýlurnar*. It's not about anyone. The whole song is laughter and “vo-oh-oh”s and the name “Sísí” chanted as a hook — pure rhythm, no narrative. From *Mávastellið*, 1983. (The band's name means “the Grýlas” — Iceland's child-eating troll-mother, the lady who shows up at Christmas to scare your kids straight. Sweet branding.)  [Song about someone]

**20 · Svart-hvíta hetjan mín** — *Dúkkulísurnar*. Forty years and she still won't crack. Gréta Sigurjónsdóttir wrote both words and music in 1986 and Icelanders have been begging ever since: *who is the black-and-white hero?* Not telling. “Their best-kept secret.” Stop asking.  [Song about someone]

**21 · Þorparinn** — *Magnús Eiríksson, Pálmi Gunnarsson*. The song is about its own singer. Magnús Eiríksson watched his friend Pálmi Gunnarsson hauling fish in Vopnafjörður before fame found him — and wrote it down. The voice you're hearing is the voice of the song's own subject. Meta-loop activated.  [Song about someone]

**22 · Deus** — *The Sugarcubes*. “Deus does not exist… but if he does, he lives in the sky above me.” Sing-songed like a kindergarten chant. Delivered in fluent Icelandic blasphemy. Whole band straight-faced through the entire thing. The Sugarcubes never did anything halfway.

**23 · Venus As A Boy – 7″ Dream Mix** — *Björk, Mick Hucknall, Gota Yashiki*. Now for the most-WTF production credit on this entire playlist — the 1993 “Dream Mix” was produced by **Mick Hucknall.** As in: Simply Red. As in: *Holding Back the Years* Mick Hucknall. He had a side production company called Dream that year and Björk used it. Pop is so weird.

**24 · Lög unga fólksins** — *Unun*. Title nicked straight from RÚV — *Lög unga fólksins* is Iceland's long-running pop-request show, “Songs of Young People.” Naming your 1994 alt-rock single after the state-broadcast request show is the indie equivalent of calling your album *Top of the Pops*.

**25 · Oh – Edit** — *GusGus*. Hidden inside this slick Reykjavík club banger: a 1959 *tiki-bar* instrumental. Hawaiian exotica composer Arthur Lyman's “Taboo Tu,” sampled in. GusGus reached back forty years and pulled out a luau.

**26 · Sá ég spóa** — *Savanna tríóið*. Authorship: nobody. It's a *þjóðlag* — an anonymous Icelandic folk song that Savanna tríóið nailed down in the now-definitive arrangement. The lyric is twelve seconds of pocket-sized natural history: a curlew on the marsh, a golden plover singing “bí-bí-bí,” and that's it — that's spring, officially clocked in by the *lóa*.

**27 · Serenade** — *Emilíana Torrini*. Album closer of *Fisherman's Woman* (Rough Trade, 2005). Torrini said the entire album was “a letter I wrote to a person that I lost at that time. I coped by thinking I was with a fisherman.” Serenade is the dream-state final page of that letter — the bit where she lets him go.

block.title: ⚡ Tungufljót
block.sub: The Quiet Tributary & Brú Power Plant
block.cue: Crossing the Tungufljót river.
block.hook: A river you've never heard of, **powering a country you have** — quietly.
block.point: Iceland's most-photographed waterfall is Gullfoss. Its most useful one is **this tributary you're crossing**, doing the actual work of keeping the lights on.
block.mic: Gullfoss gets the photos. Tungufljót gets the electricity bill paid.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "A working river in working weather. It does not stop for either of us."
bullets: **Tungufljót** ("Tongue-River") drains the highlands into the **Hvítá**, and its showpiece is **Faxi** (Vatnsleysufoss) — a broad, low **~7 m** curtain of a waterfall with a **salmon ladder** built into it.

Its water now spins **Brúárvirkjun**, a small **Landsvirkjun** hydro station damming the upper river — a modern plant opened in the early **2020s**. Tiny globally; big enough to help keep this stretch of the south on the grid.
Iceland runs on **~70% hydro** plus geothermal — a grid that's **~99.9% renewable**, one of the cleanest on Earth. Quiet little rivers like this are the majority behind that number.
