title: 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar
subject: reykholt & friðheimar

block.title: 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar
block.cue: Passing Friðheimar, Reykholt.
block.hook: We grow **tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers and strawberries** at the latitude of **Fairbanks, Alaska** — heated by hot water that **costs us almost nothing**.
block.point: Just south of the Arctic you shouldn't be able to grow a tomato — so Iceland grows a big share of its own on volcano heat and skips the shipping.
block.mic: At our latitude, you shouldn't be able to grow a tomato. So we built a farm on a volcano and flew in Dutch bees to run it.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The greenhouses do not care what the sky is doing. That is the entire business model."
bullets: **Reykholt** ("smoky hill") in **Bláskógabyggð** is the village — a whole cluster of geothermal greenhouses (**Friðheimar, Espiflöt, Jarðarberjaland** — literally "strawberry land," and more). **Friðheimar** is the headliner: a working tomato greenhouse where you eat lunch **among the vines**, soup ladled three feet from the plant that grew it.

The crop drinks the volcano: **~95°C geothermal water** piped straight from a borehole heats the glasshouse, **LED grow-lights** fake a summer through the black winter, and the vines fruit **12 months a year — about 370 tonnes**, roughly **a tonne a day**, a serious slice of every Icelandic tomato. The same volcanic heat that warms Reykjavík's living rooms, just aimed at lunch.

No native insect can pollinate a tomato flower this far north, so Friðheimar **flew in Dutch bumblebees** — a striped workforce knocking out **up to 2,000 flowers a day**. Iceland outsourced its pollination department to the Netherlands and never looked back.

Iceland's **first geothermally heated greenhouse went up in 1924**, over in **Mosfellssveit**, once growers worked out that geothermal water could both **heat the glasshouse and steam-sterilise the soil**. Here at Reykholt the first greenhouse went up at **Reykholtshver in 1932**, and the **first proper horticultural station followed in 1938**.

**Knútur Rafn Ármann** and **Helena Hermundardóttir** took Friðheimar over in **1995**, built the first large house between **1995 and 2001**, and switched to **year-round tomatoes in 2002**. Before that, Icelandic tomatoes simply stopped in winter.
**Reykholt** ("smoky hill") in **Bláskógabyggð** is the village; **Friðheimar** is its star farm — a working geothermal greenhouse complex where you can eat lunch among the vines.

Inside, roughly **ten thousand tomato plants** grow under LED lights on **geothermal water** piped straight from the ground, pollinated by **imported Dutch bumblebees** — Iceland has no native pollinator strong enough for tomato flowers, so it flew in a workforce.
The signature dish is **unlimited tomato soup eaten three feet from the plants that made it**. Same volcanic heat that warms Reykjavík's homes, just aimed at lunch.

Here's the bit most guides get wrong: **geothermal energy gives you heat, not light.** At this latitude the sun effectively resigns in November, so the plants run on **electric grow-lights** through the dark months. Heat **plus** light, never heat alone.
**Reykholt** is a whole cluster of these operations — **Friðheimar**, **Espiflöt**, **Jarðarberjaland**, literally **strawberry land** — in a village of about **100 people**.

block.title: 🐎 Icelandic Horses
block.cue: Look at the horses in the field.
block.hook: The horse in that field is a **direct descendant of a Viking horse** — a bloodline effectively **closed for ~1,000 years**. Just don't call it a pony. That's the one hill Iceland will genuinely die on.
block.point: A horse breed Vikings would still recognise — kept intact for a millennium by isolation, hard winters, and a one-way export door.
block.mic: You can take an Icelandic horse out of Iceland. You just can't bring it back. The country runs a one-way door for its own livestock.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "They will be standing in it, tails to the wind, entirely unbothered. Take the lesson."
bullets: The **Icelandic horse** is small (**~132–145 cm**), shaggy, long-lived (often **30 years**), tough and frankly opinionated — and by breed convention and national insistence, **always a "horse," never a pony**.

No new bloodstock has arrived since roughly the year **1000**, so it's essentially a **closed, disease-naïve population** — one of the purest native breeds on Earth. Tradition says the **Alþingi** slammed the import door around **982**; the documented ban dates to **1882** — and it still stands.

Most breeds have three or four gaits; the Icelandic has up to **five**, including the famous **tölt** — a four-beat running walk so smooth you could carry a full beer and not spill it. The extra gaits trace to a **single gene mutation**.

Population ~**78,000** in Iceland and ~**195,000 abroad** across 30+ countries — the diaspora outnumbers the home herd two to one, and **not one of them is ever allowed back** (biosecurity enforced by MAST, the food and veterinary authority).
say: the smooth four-beat running walk this breed has and most others don't

title: ⛪ Skálholt
subject: skálholt

block.title: ⛪ Skálholt
block.cue: At Skálholt.
block.hook: For **700 years**, this farm was Iceland's **capital, university and cathedral** rolled into one. Then a **1784 earthquake** ate the lot — and the country never gave it back.
block.point: Iceland's centre of power didn't fall to an invasion. It fell to a fault line — and politics finished the job.
block.mic: A 700-year capital, ended by a single earthquake and a Danish administrative form.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Grey and windswept is how this place looked for most of its eight hundred years."
bullets: **Skálholt** was Iceland's first **episcopal see**, founded **1056** — for 700 years the country's brain: bishops, Iceland's **first school** (Skálholtsskóli, 1056), a scriptorium and a library, all bankrolled by a guaranteed **church tithe from 1097**.

It gave Iceland its **only saint** — **Þorlákur Þórhallsson**, declared holy by the Alþingi in **1198** and formally made **patron saint of Iceland by the Vatican in 1984**; his feast on 23 December still anchors the Icelandic Christmas.

The **Reformation** arrived on **7 November 1550** with the beheading here of **Jón Arason** — the Catholic bishop of *Hólar*, the northern see — and two of his sons. The Lutheran takeover, sealed in blood on this lawn.

A **~magnitude-7 earthquake** (South Iceland Seismic Zone) in **1784** levelled the cathedral; the Danes used it to abolish the bishopric and shift the see to a fishing village called **Reykjavík** — formally, in **1801**. (The last bishop to live at Skálholt, **Hannes Finnsson**, died here in **1796**; the lights went out slowly.) The current church is a **1963 reconstruction** — where the blues-rock band **Kaleo** later recorded a track live, because Iceland.
Its first bishop, from **1056**, was **Ísleifur Gissurarson** — whose son ran the school up at **Haukadalur**.

The district around it is **Biskupstungur**, **the bishop's tongues** — the wedge of land between the **Hvítá** and the **Tungufljót**. A **tunga** is a tongue of land between two rivers, and the bishop in the name is the one on that hill.

The church came before the bishop. **Gissur hvíti** — Ísleifur's own father — is said to have raised the **first church at Skálholt** after the conversion at the **Alþingi in the year 1000**, and **Ísleifur Gissurarson was consecrated the first bishop of Iceland in 1056** and took his seat there. Minjastofnun's phrase for the place is the **head place of Iceland for about 700 years**, and the bishopric ran **continuously from 1056 to 1801**, moving to **Reykjavík** only in the wake of the great natural disasters at the end of the eighteenth century.
The school ran from **the later eleventh century until 1785**, with short interruptions. Seven centuries of teaching, on a farm.

The 1550 beheading has names and a run-up. **Jón Arason** was executed here on **7 November 1550** together with his sons **Ari** and **the Reverend Björn** — and two years earlier, in **1548**, the Skálholt men had thrown up a **fort east of the churchyard** to hold off his attack, the remains of which are still identifiable on the ground. In **1912** an Englishwoman, **Disney Leith**, paid for a **monument** to him at what is taken to be the execution spot.

The site carries **ten protected archaeological monuments** and **well over a hundred** further age-protected remains. The cathedral standing there now was designed by the state architect **Hörður Bjarnason** and consecrated in **1963** — and Skálholt got a bishop back, a **vígslubiskup**, in **1992.** (Seven hundred years as the centre of the country, ended by an earthquake rather than by politics.)

**Skálholt** was Iceland's first **episcopal see**, founded **1056** — for 700 years the country's brain: bishops, Iceland's **first school** — **Skálholtsskóli**, a school from Ísleifur's time — a scriptorium and a library, all bankrolled by a guaranteed **church tithe from 1097**.
The school ran from **Ísleifur's time until 1785**, with short interruptions. Seven centuries of teaching, on a farm.

title: 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið
subject: grímsnes & kerið

block.title: 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið
block.sub: Red Walls, Blue Lake, Björk on a Raft
block.cue: At Kerið crater.
block.hook: A **red volcanic crater** with a **bright blue lake** at the bottom — that **Björk once performed on**, from a **floating raft**.
block.point: A crater that doubles as the world's most exclusive natural amphitheatre — built by a volcano, booked by an opera singer and a young Björk.
block.mic: Most countries put concerts in arenas. Iceland puts them in volcanoes.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The crater water goes a deeper green under cloud, so this is not the day to feel short-changed."
bullets: **Kerið** is a **5,000–6,000-year-old volcanic crater** — about **270 m long, 170 m wide and 55 m deep**: enough to swallow a **17-storey building**.

The walls are **red scoria** — iron-rich basalt cinders whose iron has **oxidised to hematite**, rust essentially, helped along by groundwater; give it a few thousand more years and it'll blacken like its neighbours. The lake is **groundwater** (7–14 m deep) with **no inlet or outlet** — it just tracks the water table, turquoise because the water absorbs red light first against a dark floor. There's even life in it: a **2014 study found 10 kinds of zooplankton**.
**Kerið** is a **gjallgígur** — a scoria crater, built up from cinder. It is **not** an explosion crater. The eruption that made it took its time about it.

Kerið is **privately owned** — by **Kerfélagið**, an association of the local landowners — and has charged a small **admission fee since 2013**, which is unusual in a country where walking into a landscape is normally free. The money goes on the path and the **stairway down the north wall**, which is how you get to stand at the water's edge.

It sits in the **Grímsnes** volcanic field on the western rift — the northernmost of a four-crater row, and the work of **one of a dozen or so Grímsnes eruptions** that built the **Grímsneshraun** lava field. (No single big bang, then — this one was built up slowly, the way Iceland does most things.)

The bowl's acoustics are superb, so it's hosted **concerts on a floating stage**. The famous first, in **August 1987**, drew ~**5,000 people** and was headlined by the operatic bass **Kristinn Sigmundsson**; a 21-year-old **Björk** (then in the early Sugarcubes) was on the bill too — real, but not the headliner the postcards promise.

title: ⚡ Sog River
subject: sog river

block.title: ⚡ Sog River
block.cue: Crossing the Sog.
block.hook: A river that's only **20 km long** — and powered **half of Iceland** for **50 years**.
block.point: Three small hydro plants on one short river — and they kept the country running for half a century.
block.mic: Big rivers get the postcards. The Sog quietly ran the lights.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Spring-fed, so it looks the same today as it did in the sunshine last week."
bullets: The **Sog** flows out of **Þingvallavatn** (Iceland's biggest natural lake) and joins the Hvítá to form the Ölfusá.
Short but huge in volume — **Iceland's largest clearwater (spring-fed) river**, ~**110 m³/s** of glacier-filtered, lake-clear water, perfect for hydro.

Three plants — **Ljósafoss**, **Írafoss** and **Steingrímsstöð**, built **1937–1959** — a combined **~90 MW** that together ran roughly **half of Iceland's electricity** through the 1960s and 70s, until the bigger highland plants on the **Þjórsá** took over.

And where did Iceland's electric age actually start? Not here — in a **carpenter's workshop in Hafnarfjörður**: on **12 December 1904**, **Jóhannes Reykdal** switched on the country's **first power station**, lighting **15 houses — the school and the Good Templars' hall among them — plus his own workshop and four street lamps**, in time for Christmas. From one carpenter's stream to all of this, in a single lifetime.

The consequence was entirely domestic. **Ljósafoss quadrupled the electricity available to the capital region**, and **Reykjavík households swapped their coal ranges for electric cookers.** A whole city stopped smelling of smoke because of a drop in a river almost none of them had ever visited. **Steingrímsstöð** very nearly did not happen either — its dam **gave way during construction in the storm of 17 June 1959.** Losing a dam on the national day is not a detail Icelanders bring up often.
Also one of Iceland's best **brown trout** rivers.

**Ljósafossstöð** was built between **1935 and 1937**, and opened with **two machines totalling 8.8 MW** (two of **4.4 MW**). A **third machine of 5.8 MW** was added in **1944**, taking it to its **14.6 MW** installed — about **105 GWh** a year. Scale was never the point. **Being first was.**

The reason the engineers loved this river: the **Sog is the only river draining Þingvallavatn**, and that lake behaves like an enormous header tank — it refuses to flood and it refuses to dry. That makes the Sog **one of the steadiest rivers in the country**, which is exactly what a turbine wants.

Three plants: **Ljósafoss (1937, 14.6 MW)**, **Írafoss (1953, 48 MW)** and **Steingrímsstöð (1959, 26 MW)** — a combined ~**90 MW** that ran roughly **half of Iceland's electricity** through the 1960s–70s, until the bigger highland plants on the Þjórsá took over.

title: Ölfusá
subject: ölfusá

block.title: Ölfusá
block.cue: Look right at 1–2 o'clock — Ölfusá.
block.hook: One of the **shortest** rivers in Iceland — but it moves **more water than any other**. Four rivers in disguise, sharing a name only for the last **25 km**.
block.point: Every drop that fell on the Golden Circle — glaciers, geysers, lakes — eventually squeezes through this one 25 km channel.
block.mic: The Golden Circle gets the postcards. This river is where the whole day quietly ends.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Rain makes it bigger. Everything I am about to tell you about this river is more true today than it was yesterday."
bullets: Only **~25 km long**, yet **Iceland's largest river by discharge** — about **400 m³ every second** off a **~5,760 km² basin**. Not the longest; just the one you absolutely could not cross.

It's **four systems in one**. The glacial **Hvítá** runs south from **Langjökull** past **Gullfoss**, gathering **Tungufljót** and **Brúará**; the spring-fed **Sog** drains **Þingvallavatn**, Iceland's biggest natural lake. They meet just above **Selfoss** and from there run as one — the **Ölfusá**.

It follows the **South Iceland Seismic Zone**, zig-zagging along fault lines. Beside it lies **Þjórsárhraun** — about **8,700 years** old, roughly **1,000 km²**, the **longest lava flow in Iceland**. Vísindavefur puts it higher than that (id=87471, Haraldur Sigurðsson, January 2025): *“Þjórsárhraun er stærsta hraun sem runnið hefur á jörðinni síðan ísöldinni lauk”* — the largest lava flow to have run anywhere on Earth since the Ice Age ended.

For centuries the **ultimate obstacle**: unfordable, no bridge, just a ferry at **Laugardælir** paid in **cattle or cod** to reach the harbour at **Eyrarbakki**. When it flooded catastrophically in **1623**, a bishop blamed a giant river serpent — an “ice worm.” (It was an **ice-jam flood**; the serpent just got the better press.)

That lava has a proper name and a frankly silly scale: **Þjórsárhraunið mikla**, the Great Þjórsá Lava. It erupted **about 8,700 years ago** from a **fissure 20 to 30 km long** in the **Veiðivötn swarm of the Bárðarbunga system**, well up in the interior, then ran **about 130 km to the sea**, reaching the coast **between the Þjórsá and the Ölfusá.** Total volume: **25 cubic kilometres.**

On the magnitude scale Vísindavefur rates it **MS-9 — the largest Icelandic eruption by volume of erupted material** — ahead of **Eldgjá at MS-8** and a long way ahead of **Laki 1783 at MS-6.5.** That scale is logarithmic, so the gaps are wider than they look. Keep one distinction straight, though: largest by volume is not the same as **most powerful**, and that title goes to **Eldgjá**. The same system gave us **Vatnaöldur in 871** and **Veiðivötn in 1477.** (The biggest eruption this island ever produced is shaped like a field. You cannot see it, and that is exactly how large it is.)
The glacial **Hvítá** runs south from **Langjökull** past Gullfoss, gathering **Tungufljót** and **Brúará**.

The spring-fed **Sog** drains **Þingvallavatn**. The two trunk rivers meet just above Selfoss — and from there the combined flow is the **Ölfusá**, **Iceland's biggest river by discharge** (~**400 m³/s**, draining a basin of ~**5,760 km²**).

For centuries this was the ultimate obstacle: no bridge anywhere, just a ferry at **Laugardælir** paid in **cattle or cod** to reach the harbour at **Eyrarbakki**. When it flooded catastrophically in **1623**, a bishop blamed a giant river serpent — an "ice worm." (It was an ice-jam flood. The serpent got the better press.)

Ölfusá is **Iceland's largest river by discharge — about 400 m³ a second** off a **5,760 km² basin.** Not the longest; just the one shifting the most water, which is the number that mattered when nobody could get across it.

block.title: Hveragerði
block.cue: Look left at 9–10 o'clock — Hveragerði.
block.hook: A town of **about 3,350 people** (3,344 at the start of 2026) where the ground occasionally rearranges itself — so the locals **built an exhibition around the crack in their floor**.
block.point: Pizza baked by a volcano, salad grown on steam, a museum built on an earthquake crack — all in the same town.
block.mic: Most towns hide their disasters. Hveragerði put theirs in the lobby and charged admission.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Cannot see the town? Look for the steam instead. The town is wherever the ground is smoking."
bullets: Hveragerði sits on a **three-way tectonic junction** on the edge of the **Hengill volcanic system** — geothermal *and* seismic, a rough combination for a postcode. Fumaroles and boiling mud pots vent **between the houses.**

Veðurstofa Íslands logged it to the minute — **fimmtudaginn 29. maí kl. 15:45**, **2008** — epicentre at **Ingólfsfjall in Ölfus, about 5 km north-west of Selfoss**, with a very large number of aftershocks behind it. It was a **doublet**: **Mw 5.8 beneath Ingólfsfjall** set off **Mw 5.9 on the Kross fault about 5 km to the west** **within 3 seconds**, for a **composite Mw 6.1**. (Moment adds, magnitude doesn't — 5.8 plus 5.9 comes out at Mw 6.06. The **6.3** you will still see quoted was the figure announced in Iceland that same day, a teleseismic estimate.) It shook the town at up to **~0.88 g** (near 1 g: the earth shoving as hard as gravity), split buildings and re-plumbed the hot springs. (Two quakes, one bang; nobody in town stopped to count.)

Cheap volcanic heat made it a **greenhouse town** from the 1920s (Iceland's **first geothermally heated greenhouse** went up in **Mosfellssveit in 1924**) and Iceland's **market garden**: tomatoes, cucumbers, flowers — and, at the horticultural college, **experimental bananas** planted ~**1950**: about **a tonne a year, never commercial**. Iceland is *not* a banana republic — just the most over-hyped tonne of fruit in Europe.

The town has a birthday. It began in **1929**, on land belonging to the farm **Vorsabær** in Ölfus: that summer the milk station went up at **Breiðumörk 26**, and the first two houses appeared — **Varmahlíð**, and a summer house at **Fagrihvammur** where **ylrækt**, growing under glass on geothermal heat, started in Hveragerði. A milk station, two dwellings and a greenhouse. That is the whole origin.

The **Garðyrkjuskóli ríkisins** at **Reykir** — the state horticultural college — turned out **its first qualified horticulturists in the spring of 1941**, and most of them went straight out and built nurseries of their own here. The count tells it better than any adjective could: **seven horticultural stations in Hveragerði by 1940, twenty by 1950.** Flower growing took off across the forties and the place became **blómabærinn**, the flower town.

For scale: **about 140 people at the end of 1941**, **about 400 by 1946** — the year the district was formally constituted — and **about 3,350 today, 3,344 at the start of 2026** (Hagstofa MAN02005; the town passed 3,000 in 2023). The name is far older than the town. **Hveragerði first appears in Fitjaannáll shortly before 1700**, in an account of an erupting hot spring that **shifted position during earthquakes in 1597**, and by the description of Ölfus written in **1703** the springs were already in daily use for **bathing, boiling and washing.**

block.title: 🎧 Rícharður's Mix
block.cue: Through Borgarnes — my own playlist from here to BSÍ.
block.hook: Sixteen tracks, sequenced for exactly this road: quiet while you are tired, warm as the light changes, loud by the time the city shows up.
block.point: Sixteen tracks that go quiet, then loud, in exactly the shape of a good day ending.
block.mic: Right — that is me done talking. My own playlist from here into town: sixteen tracks, all Icelandic, all picked for this exact stretch of road.
bullets: **ACT I — Silence.** You have been awake since six and the whole day is in your bones. Piano, strings, glass-cool modern classical, and a lullaby to close it. That lullaby, track three, is — heads up — technically about infanticide. We will not dwell.

**01 · Sofðu unga ástin mín** — *Hafdís Huld*. Heads up — Iceland's most beloved lullaby is, technically, *about infanticide*. The lyric is from Jóhann Sigurjónsson's 1911 play *Fjalla-Eyvindur*: outlaw's wife Halla sings it to her own baby seconds before throwing the child into a waterfall so she and her fugitive husband can keep running across the highlands. Icelandic parents have nonetheless been singing this to their toddlers ever since. Hafdís Huld cut this version on *Vögguvísur* (2012) at home — while pregnant with her own daughter Arabella. Sleep tight, kids.  [Lullaby thread]

**02 · Flight from the City** — *Jóhann Jóhannsson*. Opening track of *Orphée* (2016) — Jóhann's first solo album for Deutsche Grammophon, and the last solo album he ever made before he died in Berlin in February 2018. The whole record traces the Orpheus myth — death, rebirth, looking back — and was tied directly to his own move from Copenhagen to Berlin. *Flight from the City* is the literal opening of that journey out. Listen to it knowing he never made another.

**03 · Bambaló (feat. Steiney Sigurðardóttir)** — *Gabríel Ólafs*. Plot twist — that “traditional Icelandic lullaby” is actually an *Irish* folk tune that hitchhiked north centuries ago. The word *bambaló* is essentially Icelandic for “rock-a-bye.” Gabríel cut this version with cellist Steiney Sigurðardóttir for *Lullabies for Piano and Cello*. Iceland: still wearing imported clothes, still pulling it off.  [Lullaby thread]

**ACT II — Eyes Open.** The warmth creeps in. Laufey waltzes. **Elín Hall** sings about her dad running *toward* the lava — not a metaphor, in a country built on the stuff. **Ásgeir's** actual father writes his son a song called *The Journey Home*, and the bus suddenly knows where it is going. Then BRÍET, Friðrik Dór and Jón Jónsson, and Valdimar lift it up off the floor.

**04 · Bewitched** — *Laufey*. Title track of the 2023 album that won Laufey the Grammy for Best Traditional Pop Vocal Album in 2024. She wrote it as a “guitar voice waltz” about the moment of falling helplessly into new love after a perfect first date — then asked the **Philharmonia Orchestra** to score the inside of her head. She calls it the song that “sets the sound of the album.” One song. One orchestra. One Grammy. Done.

**05 · Twice** — *Little Dragon*. The piano line you're hearing wasn't supposed to be a Little Dragon song. It was written for a *children's collage book*. Yukimi Nagano walked into the studio, heard drummer Erik Bodin's friend's kids'-book melody, and started scribbling lyrics on the spot. It became Little Dragon's debut single (2007) and got them signed to Peacefrog. Robert Glasper Experiment later covered it. Bedtime story to indie classic, in one studio drop-by.

**06 · Pretty Face** — *Sóley*. Track 2 of Sóley's 2011 debut *We Sink*. The lyric obsesses over the narrator's own reflection in someone else's eyes — validation, identity, choosing to disappear into a dream rather than stay. Listen for the eerie under-hum; that's the song quietly unraveling around you.

**07 · Tachylite** — *Elín Hall*. *Tachylite* is volcanic glass — basaltic lava that cooled too fast to crystallise. Elín Hall calls it “failed lava.” The song is a quiet tribute to her father — an **Icelandic geophysicist who works as a first responder during eruptions**. He runs *toward* the lava. She wrote a song called Failed Lava about him. Released January 2026.

**08 · Heimförin** — *Ásgeir*. *The Journey Home.* The lyrics are by **Ásgeir's dad** — Einar Georg Einarsson, a poet from the village of Laugarbakki — and most of the original Icelandic words on the 2012 debut *Dýrð í dauðaþögn* are his father's. A song called The Journey Home, written by Dad, set to music and sung by son. The album went on to become the best-selling Icelandic debut *of all time*. Family business.  [Family wrote it · Homecoming]

**ACT III — Bags Packed.** Reykjavík widens ahead and the volume comes up. Of Monsters and Men, then **Una Stef** singing *Like Home* — her father wrote track 39 of the other playlist. Agent Fresco blow the doors off. Reykjavík's own mystery woman finally gets a name, seventy years late. Quarashi, and then **Ingó Veðurguð** has the last word.

**10 · Á Sama Tíma, Á Sama Stað** — *Friðrik Dór & Jón Jónsson*. The brothers Jónsson. (Yes — actual brothers.) The song was the official 2018 *Þjóðhátíðarlag* — the festival anthem of Þjóðhátíð on the Westman Islands, where every August Iceland packs into a lava-walled valley called Herjólfsdalur and sings whatever song the year's commissioned writer hands them. 2018: the brothers' turn. The country's biggest weekend, scored by two siblings sharing a mic.

**11 · Á Flug** — *Valdimar*. *In Flight.* Valdimar are from **Keflavík** — i.e. the literal airport town this coach just left. From their 2010 debut *Undraland*, released on Geimsteinn, the Keflavík label founded by Rúnar Júlíusson. A song about flight, made by guys you flew over.  [Homecoming]

**12 · Tuna in a Can** — *Of Monsters and Men*. Yes — the song is actually about **canned tuna**. The image — *tuna in a can, sticky from the brine / I thought I'd gone bad, you thought I was fine* — is reportedly Nanna's nod to her **mum's tuna salad**. It became the visual anchor of the entire 2025 album *All Is Love and Pain in the Mouse Parade*; the cover is built around it as “a quilt of familial stories.” Best self-portrait-as-expired-canned-fish in modern indie pop.

**13 · Coming Home** — *Sjonni's Friends*. Sjonni Brink wrote the music. **His wife Þórunn Erna Clausen wrote the lyrics.** So in effect, this is her words sung back to her. He was due to perform it in Iceland's Eurovision semi-final on 29 January 2011 — and died of a brain aneurysm on **17 January 2011, age 36**. Twelve days before the show. Six of his musician friends formed *Vinir Sjonna* / Sjonni's Friends to perform it in his place at Eurovision in Düsseldorf, finishing 20th with 61 points. The song's message — *never know when your time's up, so live and love hard* — was written before he died. Then performed after.  [Family wrote it · Homecoming]

**14 · Howls** — *Agent Fresco*. Track 6 of *Destrier* (2015) — the concept album frontman Arnór Dan Arnarson wrote after **two men attacked him late one night and left him with a broken eye socket and concussion**. The whole record is grief and adrenaline. *Howls* sits at the nostalgic end — *howls of youth, when life would run with lawless legs to race the sun* — the memory of pre-violence freedom the rest of the album is trying to claw back. (A *destrier* is the medieval warhorse bred for battle.)

**15 · Fröken Reykjavík** — *Ríó Tríó / Stórsveit Reykjavíkur*. For seventy-odd years nobody knew who the red-shoed woman walking down Austurstræti actually *was*. Mystery solved in 2023 — director Björn Brynjúlfur Björnsson revealed in *Vísir* that she was his mother, **Jóna Sigurjónsdóttir**. Reykjavík kept its secret for seven decades. Then it broke. **16 · Jungle Drum** — *Emilíana Torrini*. Co-written with producer Dan Carey, released as a single in March 2009. **17 · Mr. Jinx** — *Quarashi*. The earworm hook is sampled from a 1973 American soul cut — **New York City's “Sanity”** — laundered through Reykjavík rap. block.title: 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun
block.cue: Look right at 2 o'clock — Hellisheiði geothermal plant.
block.hook: In most countries, a volcano is a disaster plan. In Iceland, it's the **light switch**.
block.point: While the world debates carbon capture, Iceland dissolves the problem in water, files it under "rocks," and moves on.
block.mic: Your shower in Reykjavík tonight was heated by the same volcano that's currently filing CO₂ as gravel under your feet.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If you cannot see the plant you will see the steam, and on a day like this the steam is the whole show."
bullets: We're on the **Hengill volcanic system**, a rare **plate-boundary triple junction on dry land**. Water goes down, returns at nearly **300°C**, and spins turbines — the white plumes are **steam**, not smoke. Built up in stages 2006–2011 to **303 MW**, it's **Iceland's largest geothermal power station**.
After the electricity, the leftover hot water pipes off to heat **more than half of the capital region** — nothing wasted.

Via **CarbFix**, CO₂ is dissolved in water and pumped into hot basalt, where **~95% turns to solid rock within about two years** (Matter et al., 2016). Next door, **Climeworks' Mammoth** plant (2024) sucks CO₂ straight from the air — up to **36,000 tonnes a year** — for the same rock treatment.

Both gases go up the same **scrubbing tower** and both end up as stone — but not at the same speed. **Over 95% of the CO₂ is mineralised inside two years**, while **the bulk of the H₂S is done in about four months** (Sigfússon et al., 2018). Carbon takes its time. Sulphur is in a hurry.

The plant has a neighbourhood: **Jarðhitagarður**, the **Geothermal Park** — **103 hectares** where companies plug straight into its outputs. **VAXA Technologies** grow **spirulina** there in vertical farms, on the plant's own electricity, heat and water. Algae farmed off a volcano, next door to the turbines.

The trick that makes the whole thing work: the geothermal fluid under us is **hot, corrosive and loaded with dissolved minerals**, and it never goes anywhere near your radiator. It is used to **heat clean groundwater through heat exchangers**, and that clean heated water is what travels to the city. **You get the heat without the chemistry.**

Hellisheiði's quieter half is the hot water: **200 MW of thermal output**, about **950 litres per second** down the pipe. Over the ridge sits its older sibling **Nesjavellir** — **Reykjavík bought the farm in 1965** and production still did not begin until **1990**, which is **twenty-five years** of drilling, testing and arguing before one useful litre went anywhere. It now runs at **up to 120 MW of electricity** and **up to 300 MW of thermal**, or as Orka náttúrunnar puts it in the only unit a household understands: **1,640 litres of hot water every second.**

Nesjavellir has grown hard. In the late **1990s** the same station was being reported to Alþingi at **60 MW of electricity and 200 MW of heat** — **the electrical output has since doubled and the heat output is up by half**, on the same hillside, with the same rock. Between the two stations, **Orka náttúrunnar supplies roughly 60 per cent of all the hot water in the capital region.**

**Hengill** is not a peak, it is a **volcanic system 50 to 60 kilometres long** and **5 to 10 kilometres wide**, running from **Selvogur** in the south-west all the way up to **Þingvallavatn**. Its most recent eruptions, about **1,900 years ago**, produced **Nesjahraun** and part of **Hellisheiðarhraun**; an earlier round **5,700 to 5,800 years ago** produced **Hagavíkurhraun**. It is **classified as active** — and this power station was built on that basis, not in spite of it.
Nationally, **about 90 per cent of the energy used to heat Icelandic homes comes from geothermal** — that is Orkustofnun's figure for **2020.** The comparable British number is effectively **zero.**

block.title: ⛰️ Kristnitökuhraun
block.cue: Look left at 9 o'clock — Kristnitökuhraun, the Christianity Lava.
block.hook: Can a volcano vote? Around **the year 1000**, one sort of did. One chieftain out-thought it with a single question.
block.point: A whole country's religion settled by a single, calm geology question.
block.mic: The pagans claimed a volcano was voting. Snorri pointed out the ballot box was older than the religion.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Lava in fog is the honest version. This is roughly what the year 1000 looked like from a distance."
bullets: Remember **Þorgeir under his cloak** at Þingvellir this morning? Same assembly, same knife-edge year — two faiths, two law codes, one looming civil war. This lava field is where that story grew teeth.
At peak tension a messenger reported **lava flowing on Hellisheiði**. Pagans cried "the gods are angry!"

Chieftain **Snorri Goði** pointed at the ancient lava underfoot: *"What were the gods angry about when this rock was made?"* Silence — and Iceland chose Christianity to keep **one law** for the whole island. *(Kristni saga)*

**And here's the thing — look left: the dark field out your window IS that lava.** It's the fresh top of the three-flow **Svínahraun** stack, radiocarbon-dated to around **1000 CE**, so it **inherited its name** from the conversion it coincided with. Fitting footnote: today the **CarbFix** project uses this very basalt to turn CO₂ into stone — the rock that once "proved" divine anger now mops up industrial emissions.

Fitting footnote: today the **CarbFix** project uses this very basalt to turn CO₂ into stone — the rock that once “proved” divine anger now mops up industrial emissions.

title: ⛰️ Rauðhólar
subject: rauðhólar

block.title: ⛰️ Rauðhólar
block.cue: Look ahead — Rauðhólar, the red crater hills.
block.hook: A line of perfect little volcanoes — and **not one of them is real**. NASA can't get enough.
block.point: Two armies and one city carved up Iceland's Mars lab and paved it into a runway.
block.mic: Eighty cones. One Mars classroom. Half of it now under your runway.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The red goes deeper in the rain, so a grey day actually makes the craters easier to pick out, not harder."
bullets: These are **pseudocraters** (Icelandic *gervigígar*) — properly, **rootless cones**: no magma pipe, no roots. Fake volcanoes.

**~5,000 years ago** lava from the **Leiti** shield volcano rolled over the **Heiðmörk** wetland; trapped water flashed to steam and, in a **phreatomagmatic** blast, **punched back out** through the molten lava — frozen mid-explosion in red scoria (iron oxide — rust).

Originally ~**80 cones**. Because a rootless cone only forms where lava met water, geologists read Iceland's as a template for **Mars** — the rootless cones of **Athabasca Valles** are cited as evidence of buried water on the Red Planet.
Then, practically, the British army mined the field for gravel to build **Reykjavík airport** in WWII; digging continued for years. Protected in **1974**.

One full-circle glance before the city: behind the cones lies **Elliðavatn** — and on a low spit in it, **Þingnes**, the only ground anyone has ever dug an assembly out of from this era: around **20 booth foundations** and a **judgement ring**, protected since **1930** as *the ancient Kjalarnesþing site*. Whether it really is the þing **Ari fróði** put on **Kjalarnes**, fourteen kilometres that way, nobody has ever proven — so you're leaving the Golden Circle past the country's first parliament grounds. Probably.

And the electricity story closes here too: the **Elliðaár** valley below held **Reykjavík's first power station (1921)** — seventeen years after **Reykdal's carpentry-shop plant** lit the nation's first bulbs in Hafnarfjörður. From a workshop stream to a volcano filing CO₂ as gravel: one century of Icelandic power, and you've just driven the whole arc.
These are **pseudocraters** — no magma pipe, no roots. Fake volcanoes.

**~5,000 years ago** lava from the **Leiti** volcano rolled over the **Heiðmörk** wetland; trapped water flashed to steam and **blew back out** through the molten lava, frozen mid-blast in red scoria (iron oxide — rust).
Originally ~**80 cones**. NASA compared them to shapes on **Mars** as "Earth analogues" for buried water.

Just before the cones, that shallow lake on the right is **Rauðavatn**, “Red Water” — and the scruffy belt of trees beside it is the **oldest deliberate woodland in the Reykjavík area**. In **1901** around eighty shareholders founded **Skógræktarfélag Reykjavíkur**, bought **six hectares** by the lake, and put the Danish forester **C. E. Flensborg** in charge of the summers. (How do you find your way out of an Icelandic forest? Stand up. This is where somebody first tried to ruin that joke.)

**Ari the Wise** wrote in *Íslendingabók* that at settlement Iceland was **viði vaxið milli fjalls og fjöru** — wooded from the mountains to the shore; today woodland covers about **1.5% of the country.** They dug **8,600 holes** here in **1902** and planted about **8,000 rowan** the next summer — frost killed nearly all of it, and the fence never held (a newspaper in **1918** grumbled that the livestock **gengur þar inn og út**, in and out as they pleased). Only after the Second World War, with **close to 60,000 plants**, did it stick. The oldest **mountain pines** by the lake are now **over 100 years old** — a national repair job running since 1901.

Then, practically, the British army mined the field for gravel to build **Reykjavík airport** in WWII; digging ran for years. Protected in **1974**.

block.title: 🏔️ Langjökull
block.cue: Heading up onto Langjökull — Iceland's second-largest ice cap.
block.hook: That waterfall you just photographed at Gullfoss? It's **this glacier crying.** Now we're going to ride snowmobiles across the thing doing the crying — a **580-metre-thick bank of ice, currently in overdraft.**
block.point: You are riding a snowmobile across a **1,400-metre-high freshwater reservoir that sits on two volcanoes and is quietly melting on a deadline.** Nowhere else does "just a bit of snow" carry that much backstory.
block.mic: We put you on a snowmobile on top of the very glacier that feeds every waterfall, geyser pool and fissure you've admired all day. Ride gently — you're on the source code.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the ice cap has gone into the cloud, that is normal. It makes its own weather up there."
bullets: **Langjökull** means **"Long Glacier"** — Icelandic place-naming at its most ruthlessly literal, like nicknaming a tall bloke "Tall Man." It's **Iceland's second-largest ice cap** (after Vatnajökull): roughly **870–900 km²**, about **50 km long, up to 20 km wide**, holding on the order of **190 km³ of ice** up to **~580 m thick** and topping out just over **1,400 metres**. You'll be snowmobiling on more frozen water than most countries own.

**Fire directly under the ice:** this isn't just frozen scenery — it's a **lid on two active volcanic systems**, **Prestahnúkur** and **Hveravellir**. The calm white surface you're carving across has a temper it simply hasn't used lately.

**The waterworks of the whole Golden Circle:** Langjökull's meltwater feeds the **Hvítá** — the river that becomes **Gullfoss** — plus the **Ölfusá** system, and, via groundwater filtered through porous lava, the eerily clear **Silfra** fissure back at Þingvellir. Everything wet you've seen today drained off the glacier under your skis.

**The timer:** Langjökull has been **losing mass steadily for decades**, and Institute of Earth Sciences modelling projects it could be **largely gone within about 150 years** on present warming — the fastest-shrinking of Iceland's big caps. Snowmobiling here is less "extreme sport," more "**visiting a patient you'll outlive.**"

For the fully indoors version, the **"Into the Glacier"** ice tunnel — the world's largest man-made bore into a glacier, **~500 m** long, opened **1 June 2015** from the Húsafell side — lets you walk *inside* Langjökull past ice older than the settlement of Iceland. A museum you have to dig.
say: the "Long Glacier" under your skis, second-largest ice cap in Iceland
the Icelandic word for glacier or ice cap
one of the two active volcanic systems under this ice
the second volcanic system under the ice
the only Icelandic ice cap bigger than the one under your skis
the meltwater river off this ice that becomes Gullfoss

block.title: ♨️ Gamla Laugin
block.sub: The "Secret" Lagoon That Taught Iceland to Swim
block.cue: At Flúðir — the Secret Lagoon.
block.hook: A "secret" lagoon that's **135 years old** and printed on every Golden Circle coach map. Some secret. It's the **oldest swimming pool in Iceland** — and the spot where the whole country first learned not to drown.
block.point: The oldest pool in the country, the classroom where Iceland learned to swim, and a live geyser for a tap — all in one steaming field off the Golden Circle.
block.mic: Iceland's worst-kept secret: a 135-year-old bath that taught a nation to swim, took a 67-year nap, and woke up still warm.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "You are getting in the water anyway. The forecast stops mattering at the changing rooms."
bullets: **Gamla Laugin** ("the Old Pool") at **Hverahólmi** by Flúðir was **built in 1891** — **Iceland's oldest surviving swimming pool**, older than the national grid, the republic, and your great-grandparents. The "Secret Lagoon" branding was bolted on 120-odd years later; the water never went anywhere.
Before it was a pool it was a **parliament**: the local Flúðir assembly met on this exact patch until **1894**. Iceland's founding instinct, again — find a warm bit of ground and hold a vote on it.

In **1909** it hosted **Iceland's first formal swimming lessons** — **32 men** in the debut course, girls following by **1911** — and taught the district every summer until **1947**. In a country ringed by a lethal North Atlantic, teaching the nation to swim in a hot bath was a genuinely brilliant life-hack.
Then it was **abandoned for nearly 70 years** — the village built a modern pool and left the old one to the algae. Scrubbed up and reborn on **7 June 2014**, history intact.

The water sits at **38–40°C year-round**, sulphur-rich, kept topped up **100% by the surrounding hot springs** — including a **baby geyser, Litli Geysir**, that fires every few minutes just off the deck. The one hot tub on Earth plumbed straight into a working geyser.
say: "the Old Pool", a.k.a. the Secret Lagoon, built 1891
the geothermal spot by Flúðir it sits on
the greenhouse-and-mushroom village beside it, whose assembly met here until 1894
the baby geyser off the deck that fires every few minutes

block.title: 🌊 Ölfusá Intro
block.cue: Look right at 1–2 o'clock — Ölfusá, ahead in the lowlands.
block.hook: The big drain, ahead in the lowlands. It gathers a huge slice of the highlands and ends at villages now best known for **a prison and a lost harbour**.
block.point: From up here it's just a pale line on the flats. Down at Selfoss, it's the biggest river in the country.
block.mic: At the far end of that pale line: two harbours that lost their trade, and one address nobody checks out of early.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Rain makes it bigger. Everything I am about to tell you about this river is more true today."
bullets: That pale line across the lowlands ahead is the **Ölfusá**. Every drop of water we'll see today ends up in it — but save the numbers, we'll be standing on its bank at Selfoss.
What's worth knowing from up here is what sits at the far end of it — the two villages where it meets the sea, and the prison just inland.
It empties by **Eyrarbakki** and **Stokkseyri** — once among Iceland's busiest harbours, until the deeper port at Þorlákshöfn stole the trade.
Just inland sits **Litla-Hraun**, Iceland's main maximum-security prison.

block.title: 🫧 Öskjuhlíð & Perlan
block.sub: The Lid On The City's Hot Water
block.cue: Look right at 3 o'clock — the wooded hill with the glass dome on top.
block.hook: That dome is a **lid.** Under it sit **six steel tanks**, each **ten metres tall and twenty-three across**, each holding about **four million litres** of water at **eighty degrees** — so Reykjavík can run a bath at seven in the morning.
block.point: A hill they quarried away, occupied, then filled with the city's hot water and put a restaurant on.
block.mic: Every building you will see today is heated by water like that. Iceland does not burn anything to keep warm — it just pumps up what is already hot.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the dome has gone in the murk, you are not missing much of a view today either — which is rather the point of the tanks underneath it."
bullets: **Öskjuhlíð** is **61 metres** high and made of **Reykjavíkurgrágrýti** — grey basalt erupted from Mosfellsheiði late in the Ice Age, then scraped smooth by glaciers. About **ten thousand years ago it was an island.** The old shoreline round here sits **42 metres** above today's sea.

From **1913** they blasted the north face out and ran it down to the harbour on a **purpose-built railway** — one of the very few stretches of railway Iceland has ever had. **The stone became the harbour. The hole became the bowling alley.**

The **Allies took this hill in 1940** and built all over it once the airfield went into Vatnsmýri in **1941.** It is now **the best-preserved military ground in Reykjavík** — pillboxes, command bunkers, trenches, blast walls, and the floors of hundreds of Nissen huts still in the trees.

The first hot-water tank went up in **1940**, more followed, two more in **1966**, and the lot was **demolished in 1986 to 87** and rebuilt. **Perlan** went on top — architect **Ingimundur Sveinsson**, opened **21 June 1991.** The steel frame does two jobs: it ties the tanks together and it is the dome.

The wood is deliberate. Planting started **after about 1950** on a council scheme, and the tallest conifers now clear **15 metres** — birch, mountain pine, Sitka spruce, Alaska poplar. In a country with almost no forest, somebody had to decide to put one here.
say: the 61 m basalt hill the tanks stand on
'the pearl', the dome over six hot-water tanks, opened 1991
the grey Ice Age basalt the hill is made of

block.title: 🧺 Þvottalaugarnar
block.sub: Why The Main Shopping Street Is Called Laundry Road
block.cue: Look left — the green valley of Laugardalur opening up.
block.hook: Reykjavík's main shopping street is called **Laugavegur.** Everyone translates it as something romantic. It means **the road out to the washing pools** — and they are in that valley, and this is the road.
block.point: The hot water that ended the washerwomen's walk is the same hot water heating every building you will see today.
block.mic: So when a guidebook tells you Laugavegur is Reykjavík's Oxford Street — it is, but it started as the route to the launderette.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "On a day like this you can see the steam from the valley better than anything else, which is how they found the place to begin with."
bullets: Out there are the **Þvottalaugarnar**, hot springs the town did its laundry in. First written down in **1672** by the physician **Þorkell Arngrímsson Vídalín**, who reckoned the water healed people. **By about 1830 nearly every household in Reykjavík was using them.**

Women carried the washing out, boiled it, beat it, and carried it home wet. The town council finally voted in **1885** to build them a proper road, and it was laid in **1886.** That road is **Laugavegur.** By **1900** it was the most populous street in town with over **700 residents** — a laundry track that turned into the high street.

The name runs the other way from what people assume. The **pool** is the oldest name. **Laugardalur**, **Laugarnes**, **Laugalækur**, **Laugavegur** — all of them are named after the *laug*, not the other way about.

In **1928** they drilled the first borehole beside the pools and got **87 degree** water. In **1930** they ran a **three kilometre pipe** from there to **Austurbæjarskóli** — **Iceland's first municipal district heating.** By **1937** it warmed 58 houses.

**The same year the pipe was switched on, 1930, the laundry stopped.** The springs did not run out. They got promoted. There is a sculpture in the valley, **Þvottakonan** by **Ásmundur Sveinsson**, 1958, for the women who made the walk.
say: 'the valley of the pools', off to the left

title: Elliðaárdalur & Paradísardalur
subject: elliðaárdalur & paradísardalur

block.title: Elliðaárdalur & Paradísardalur
block.sub: the park that's really a crime scene
block.cue: Look right at 2 o'clock — Elliðaárdalur.
block.hook: To joggers it's a postcard. To a geologist, it's a **crime scene** — 10,000 years of Iceland trying, and failing, to stay quiet.
block.point: It looks like a Sunday-stroll park. It's a 5,000-year-old construction site nobody ever closed.
block.mic: A volcano split the river. The Vikings claimed it. The British fortified it. The river is still working overtime to undo all of it.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The valley looks its best wet. That river is the reason anything in this city is green."
bullets: The whole valley was redesigned **~5,000 years ago** when **Leiti** erupted: lava poured down, hit the river and **split it in two**. Before, one river; after, two. Every waterfall here is the river's **5,000-year project** to saw back through solid basalt to the sea.

The Elliðaá is one of the only **capital-city rivers on Earth with a wild Atlantic salmon run** — around **1,500–2,500** shove upstream past the joggers each summer. Reykjavík was so smitten it **bought the whole river in 1906.** (Your city buys parks. We bought a river.)

One kilometre of valley has hosted a **1750s wool mill**, a **drowning pool at Skötufoss** for women convicted of “moral crimes,” outlaws in the lava tubes, **British WWII Quonset huts**, and a century-old hydro plant — **Elliðaárstöð (1921)**, still humming.
Most Icelandically of all: a **1998 burst pipe** flooded the valley and, in a single weekend, **washed 10,000 years of buried history back into daylight.** Even the plumbing does archaeology here.

block.title: 🗻 Vífilsfell
block.sub: The Mountain Named After A Slave
block.cue: Look ahead at 1 o'clock — the stepped mountain with the flat shelf.
block.hook: There is a mountain out that window **named after a slave** — and the naming is recorded in Iceland's founding text itself.
block.point: Two eruptions, two ice ages, one mountain — and it is named after a freed slave rather than the man who freed him.
block.mic: Ingólfur got a statue and a hill in the middle of Reykjavík. Vífill got 655 metres of it.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the top is in cloud you are still seeing the shelf, and the shelf is the older mountain — so you are getting the first eruption and missing the second."
bullets: **Landnámabók** puts it in seven words: ***"við hann er kennt Vífilsfell"*** — the mountain is named for him. **Vífill** was one of **Ingólfur Arnarson's** two slaves, sent along the coast to hunt for his high-seat pillars. **Ingólfur gave Vífill his freedom.** The other one, **Karli**, said they had crossed good country only to settle an outlying headland, and walked off. **Only Vífill was freed** — and only Vífill got a mountain.
It is **655 metres**, the highest ground in Kópavogur. And that shelf halfway up is the interesting part.

**It is two mountains stacked.** The shelf is a **stapi** — a tuya — móberg built under ice and then capped with lava once the eruption melted through and the meltwater could no longer reach the vent. **The summit above it is a second, younger móberg mountain sitting on top of the first**, from a separate eruption in **probably a different ice age.**

That younger top sits on a **north-west to south-east fissure**, which is odd. Almost every crack in South Iceland runs **north-east to south-west.** This one is at right angles to the grain of the country.
say: 655 m, named for Ingólfur's freed slave Vífill
a tuya, a flat-topped mountain built under ice then capped with lava
the brown rock made when lava erupts under a glacier

title: 🌊 Þjórsá
subject: þjórsá

block.title: 🌊 Þjórsá
block.cue: Look right at 1–2 o'clock — Þjórsá and its floodplain.
block.hook: Up ahead we cross **Iceland's longest river** — a **230 km** glacial spine that founding fathers held parliaments beside and engineers turned into the country's **biggest power supply**.
block.point: Every crossing passes over the main drain for a big chunk of Iceland's backbone — and its biggest battery.
block.mic: Selfoss had its milk-truck drama. Þjórsá is the **patient heavyweight** — moving a whole highland's worth of water, and half the national grid, to the sea.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Weather barely touches this river. It comes off an ice cap, so it runs much the same in sun or sleet."
bullets: **Þjórsá** ("Bull River") rises off the **Hofsjökull** ice cap and runs **230 km** to the sea — **Iceland's longest** — draining a **7,530 km²** catchment at roughly **383 m³/s**. Not a river you paddle absent-mindedly.

Midstream sits the island of **Árnes**, which in the settlement era hosted its own **Þing** — a local assembly. Give an Icelander a defensible rock in a fast river and their first instinct is to hold a meeting on it.

It does **more electrical work than any river in Iceland**: **six power stations** on the Þjórsá–Tungnaá system (Búrfell first, 1969) feed the grid — chiefly the **aluminium smelters** that are the reason a country of 380,000 makes so much power.
Those wide braided channels in the fields are **floodpaths**: when the glaciers melt fast, Þjórsá spreads across its plains rather than politely staying in one channel.

And a kilometre or so below the bridge sits **Urriðafoss** — **Iceland's most voluminous waterfall.** Not the tallest, not the most powerful. The most *water*. It is only about **six metres high** and it carries roughly **358 cubic metres a second** — about **1.7 times Dettifoss** up north. Dettifoss is the most **powerful**, which is height times flow, and the two get swapped so often that the University of Iceland has had to correct it in print.

Every winter the river builds an ice jam here called the **Urriðafosshrönn.** Landsvirkjun's own survey measured up to **40 million cubic metres** of ice and slush, a sheet up to **20 metres thick**, burying the waterfall completely — and in some years it backs up past the bridge we are crossing. Iceland's most voluminous waterfall spends part of most winters entirely out of sight, under its own ice.

People have wanted to dam it since **1927**, when the poet **Einar Benediktsson's** company Titan won a licence it never found the money to use. The modern version is **Urriðafossvirkjun**, **140 MW**. On **17 February 2026** Alþingi left it in **biðflokkur** — the hold category — while everyone waits to see what the two dams upstream do to the **Þjórsá salmon**, one of Iceland's largest wild stocks at around **ten thousand fish.** Landsvirkjun's own assessment says the falls would run at **10 to 15 cubic metres a second** in winter instead of 350, and it proposes **no mitigation.**

One last thing, about the name. **Landnámabók** says Þjórsá is 'bull river' because a settler sailed into the mouth with a bull's head on his prow. Iceland's place-name scholars are not convinced. **Þórhallur Vilmundarson** argued it was originally **Þjótsá** — 'the roaring river' — and the roar it was named for is this one, at Urriðafoss. There is a farm on the bank still called **Þjótandi**, 'the one that roars.'

**Þjórsá** rises off the **Hofsjökull** ice cap and runs **230 km** to the sea — **Iceland's longest river** — draining **7,530 km²** of highland and pushing about **383 m³ a second** past its mouth. Not a river you paddle absent-mindedly.

Midstream sits the island of **Árnes**, which in the settlement era hosted its own **Þing** — a local parliament. Given a defensible spot in a fast river, the Icelandic instinct was, of course, to hold a meeting on it.
Its valley, **Þjórsárdalur**, is farm country that neighbour **Hekla has buried more than once** in ash.

block.title: Hella
block.cue: Coming up ahead — the caves of Hella, cut into the bank of the Ytri-Rangá.
block.hook: Long before the Vikings arrived with longships, someone else may already have been here — **literally hiding in the walls**.
block.point: Some of the oldest, strangest archaeology in the country — proof that in Iceland, history isn't just on the surface. Sometimes it's dug into the hillside you're driving past.
block.mic: Most towns keep their history in a museum. Hella keeps a chunk of it in the basement — and isn't sure who moved in first.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "You will not see the caves from here in any weather. They are cut into the bank, which is rather the point of them."
bullets: Carved into the soft sandstone beside the **Ytri-Rangá** river is a cluster of **man-made caves**, some with simple **crosses** and **stone benches** cut into the wall.

A popular theory ties them to the **Papar** — the Irish monks that **Íslendingabók** and **Landnámabók** both say were in Iceland *before* the Norse and legged it the moment longships appeared. Tempting, but honest: the dating is **disputed** and **no archaeology has confirmed a pre-Norse origin** — treat it as suggestive, not settled.

The town itself is a newcomer: **Hella was founded in 1927**, when a man built a general store *and* a slaughterhouse by the river bridge — because nothing anchors a settlement like buying your groceries and butchering your lamb in one stop.
Today it's the pit-stop with **volcanoes on the skyline** (Hekla up the road), **horses in the fields** (**Rangárvellir** horse country), and possibly **monks in the basement**.

block.title: 🐟 Ægissíðufoss
block.sub: The Best Salmon River In Iceland Is Not A Salmon River
block.cue: Look ahead at 12 o'clock — the Ytri-Rangá going over its lower falls.
block.hook: In **2022** this river was **the top-producing salmon fishery in the whole of Iceland** — **5,112 fish.** And before the 1970s it had **essentially no salmon in it at all.**
block.point: A cold, clear, gravel-poor river that had no salmon, engineered into the best salmon fishery in the country.
block.mic: It shares its name with the caves we just passed at Ægissíða — same farm, completely different story. One is a river cutting rock. The other is people cutting sandstone.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "You will hear it before you see it in this. The Rangá never runs low, which is the whole point of a spring river."
bullets: The **Ytri-Rangá** is a **60 km spring-fed river** rising in Rangárbotnar north of Hekla, running at about **50 cubic metres a second** and barely changing — the springs come out at **4 to 6 degrees** all year, so it does not flood in summer and it does not freeze.

**And that is exactly why it had no salmon.** The bed is too fine, the water too cold, and salmon fry could never get a grip. **These were trout rivers.** Then people started releasing smolts by the hundred thousand.

In **1982** they cut a **fish ladder** into this waterfall, and another into Árbæjarfoss upstream in **1985.** Both carry **fish counters**, and the one here is the river's census point. In **2024** it logged **6,400 salmon** going up, from which the river reckoned about **twelve thousand** came in off the sea.
The state fisheries institute is careful enough about it that **when it publishes Iceland's wild salmon figure, it subtracts these rivers first.**
The falls also mark a line in the ground. The old **interglacial shield lavas** that make up all the flat farmland north of here **stop right at Ægissíðufoss.** Everything past it is younger.

block.title: Vestmannaeyjar
block.cue: Look right, out to sea at 3 o'clock — the Westman Islands.
block.hook: In **1973** this archipelago was almost wiped off the map — and the only reason it survived is that **a storm hit the night before**.
block.point: One of the few places on Earth where a town fought a volcano **with seawater and pumps** — and came out with a better harbour.
block.mic: The volcano tried to close the harbour. The locals replied: “we'll take the upgrade, thanks.”
block.weather: Weather pivot: "No islands today? They are twenty-seven kilometres out. On a clear day they look close enough to swim to, and that is the illusion."
bullets: Just after midnight on **23 January 1973** a **1.6 km fissure** tore open barely 200 m from town on **Heimaey**, and a brand-new volcano — **Eldfell**, “Fire Mountain” — began throwing lava through the eastern streets.

The lucky break was weather: a storm the day before had kept the **whole fishing fleet in harbour**, so of about **5,300 residents, roughly 5,000 were evacuated in around eight hours** — Iceland has **no army**, so the fishermen ran the evacuation themselves.

The eruption ran **five months** and buried about **400 buildings** — Iceland's own Pompeii, some houses now dug back out at the **Eldheimar museum**. To save the harbour, crews pumped **millions of litres of North Atlantic seawater** onto the advancing flow for weeks, and the cooled lava left the entrance **deeper and better sheltered than before.**

block.title: 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull
block.cue: Look left at 10–11 o'clock — Eyjafjallajökull and Þorvaldseyri farm.
block.hook: In **2010**, this innocent-looking glacier volcano shut down **air travel for millions of people** who couldn't even say its name.
block.point: Up there: peaceful glacier above a postcard farm. In memory: the mountain that turned Europe's airports into campgrounds.
block.mic: A farmer here was digging ash out of his drinking water while airline CEOs were melting down 2,000 km away.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Cannot see it? Neither could the pilots in 2010, and that was rather the problem."
bullets: **Eyjafjallajökull** — an ice cap over a **1,651 m** stratovolcano — sits there now, white cap over green fields, looking harmless.

Here's the twist: **the 2010 eruption was tiny** — only **~0.27 km³** of ash. But it punched an **8–9 km plume straight into the jet stream**, and the glassy particles turned jet engines into expensive sandblasters. A small volcano in exactly the wrong spot.
The first hit was local, not global: as meltwater poured off the ice, **500–800 people were evacuated overnight** from the farms below, and the ash fell thick enough to turn day into night.

At farms like **Þorvaldseyri** at its foot, people **milked cows in respirator masks** and scraped ash off the roofs — then built a visitor centre, because if a volcano rewrites your year you may as well sell the story back.

Then the global bill: the **worst aviation shutdown in Europe since WWII** — **104,000 flights cancelled over eight days, 15–22 April**, **48% of expected European traffic**, about **10 million passengers** who simply could not fly, and some **20 countries'** airspace closed. At the peak, **18–19 April**, that was roughly **19,000 cancellations a day**, and **US$1.7 bn** of airline revenue gone. Airport floors turned into campgrounds; Europe learned volcanoes don't read timetables.

Guest question, every time: does it trigger **Katla** next door? Historically the 920, 1612 and 1821 eruptions each were — but in **2010 Katla stayed shut.** Eyjafjallajökull is a **warning light, not a trigger.**

title: 🪨 Drangurinn

block.title: 🪨 Drangurinn
block.cue: Look left at 10 o'clock — Drangurinn, under the cliffs of Eyjafjöll.
block.hook: A rock that **forgot to leave** when the rest of the mountain eroded away — and became a barn, a film set, and an elf hotel.
block.point: A single stone that lets you flip between two ways of seeing Iceland — geology and saga — at the same time.
block.mic: Geologists see a volcanic leftover. Storytellers see a giant's throw. The farmers just saw a free barn with elf staff.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The rock sits right by the road, so this is one you get whatever the sky is doing."
bullets: **Drangurinn** stands alone in the field like a stubborn leftover — a block of **palagonite tuff (móberg)**, the same subglacial-eruption stuff that built **Pétursey** further along the coast, left standing when the softer cliff around it weathered away. That's the geology.
It sits about **130 m north of the road**, at the foot of the **Eyjafjöll** cliffs, in the home field of the farms of **Drangshlíð** — which is why it looks dropped there rather than built there.
The saga version: the strongman **Grettir the Strong** supposedly **ripped it out of the Hrútafell cliff** and dropped it here, leaving a chasm still visible above Skarðshlíð. Show-off.

Locals didn't waste a rock this size — they **built turf barns and cowsheds right up against it**, and the folklore says **elves live inside**, quietly minding the farmers' cows and even **milking them at calving time.** The most useful neighbours in Iceland, if you believe it.
It later starred as a location in the Viking film *Hrafninn flýgur* ("When the Raven Flies") — even the movies knew a dramatic rock when they saw one.

block.title: Sólheimajökull
block.cue: At Sólheimajökull glacier.
block.hook: This is where the glacier stops being “a nice view from the bus” and turns into a **giant, melting history book.**

block.mic: You don't have to give a climate lecture here. You point at where the ice used to be — and the **missing glacier** does the talking.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Cloud sits low on the ice. If the top has gone you are still seeing the snout, and the snout is the part that has been moving."
bullets: A gravel path pulls you toward **Sólheimajökull**, an outlet tongue of **Mýrdalsjökull** — **Iceland's 4th-largest ice cap** — wedged between the volcanoes **Katla** and **Eyjafjallajökull**, with Katla buried right underneath.
Up close the ice isn't white — it's streaked with **black ash bands** from both volcanoes' past tantrums, like a sooty paintbrush dragged across a layered record of the neighbourhood.

In front sits a **blue-green proglacial lagoon** with small icebergs calving off; the colour is **glacial flour**, rock ground so fine it turns the water to liquid stone-dust. That lagoon is **new** — the tongue has been **retreating around 40 m a year**, about a bus-length a summer, and the walk to it keeps getting longer.
Signs along the path mark where the front *used* to reach: “here… and here… and here.” You've just walked **decades of retreat in a few minutes.**

block.title: ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
block.cue: Look right at 2 o'clock — far out on Sólheimasandur.
block.hook: Somewhere out there in the black void is a silver ghost that **Justin Bieber made world-famous** — and that half the internet gets the name of wrong.
block.point: It's a **modern layer on the geology**: Katla built the sandur, the US Navy accidentally parked a plane on it, and social media did the rest.
block.mic: From the bus you mostly see empty blackness. The real story: a crew that iced up over a glacier, glided to the coast, and **lived** — on a plane everyone insists on calling by the wrong name.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "You would not see the wreck from the road on the clearest day of the year. That is what the photograph is for."
bullets: Everyone calls it a "DC-3." It isn't. It's a **US Navy Super DC-3 (a Douglas R4D-8 / C-117D)** — same family, buff cousin who went to the gym. It's worn the wrong name for fifty years like a stag-do lanyard.

On **21 November 1973** it was flying from **Höfn to Keflavík** when **ice choked both carburettors over the Vatnajökull ice cap** and both engines quit. The tourist story that it "ran out of fuel" is false — it iced up and became, in the co-pilot's words, "a massively overweight glider."
The pilot turned **south for the coast** and put it down on the black sand. **All seven crew walked away.** The Navy stripped the useful parts and left the shell.

For decades it was a quiet local landmark; then a **Bieber video (2015)** and Instagram turned it into a pilgrimage. Cars were banned in **2016**, so now you walk **4 km each way** across old ocean floor just to touch a plane with no wings.
⚠️ Not a joke in bad weather: the plain has no shelter at all, and two visitors died of hypothermia near the wreck in a January 2020 storm.

block.title: ⛰️ Pétursey
block.cue: Look right at 1–2 o'clock — the steep, isolated mountain.
block.hook: A **275-metre lump of frozen explosion** — submarine volcano, offshore island, saint's shrine, Sturlung-era fort, **WWII lookout post**. **Most mountains never have a CV that long.**
block.point: Geology, saga, saint and soldier — all stacked on one piece of frozen ash.
block.mic: Most mountains have a Wikipedia stub. **Pétursey has a CV.**
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the mountain is in cloud you are seeing what it was for. It was a sea mark, and sailors mostly needed it in bad visibility."
bullets: **Pétursey** is **móberg** — ash-and-rubble rock formed when a volcano **erupted underwater** in the last Ice Age; hot magma met cold sea, shattered mid-blast, and cemented into these steep walls.
For much of the Holocene the Atlantic surrounded it and it was a true **island** and sailors' landmark — until **Katla**'s black sand slowly swallowed the gap and stranded it inland.
The name comes from a **medieval shrine to Saint Peter** on top, a Catholic pilgrimage site before the Reformation.

In the **Sturlungaöld** (the civil-war era) armed men fortified the summit; **Þórðar saga kakala** records it as a refuge. In **WWII** the British reused that same 360° summit as a **lookout post** over the south coast. At the base today sit two farms, **Eystri-** and **Vestri-Pétursey.**

The cliffs still work as a **seabird colony** — fulmars and **puffins** circle it as if it never stopped being an island — and, this being Iceland, the mound is thick with **hidden-folk and elf legends.**

block.title: Skeiðflatarkirkja
block.cue: Look left — small red-roofed church in the fields.
block.hook: This tiny country church is the **DNA** of some of Iceland's most famous modern buildings.
block.point: The story of Reykjavík's iconic architecture doesn't start in the city. It starts on **farms like this**, under the shadow of volcanoes.
block.mic: If you squint, you can almost see Hallgrímskirkja **hiding inside** this little red-roofed church — it just needed a son with a big imagination and a State Architect's salary.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Small red roof, big grey sky. It is the roof you are looking for, not the church."
bullets: This modest church was designed and built by the master carpenter **Samúel Jónsson** (born 1864) — one of those simple, sturdy rural churches built to shrug off wind, rain and ash.

His son **Guðjón Samúelsson** (born **1887**) grew up here and became **Iceland's first State Architect** — the man behind **Hallgrímskirkja**, the basalt-column church on the Reykjavík hill, plus the **National Theatre** and the **University's main building.**
Callback for later today: Guðjón also designed the **1927 lighthouse at Dýrhólaey**, the headland we'll pass near Vík. Father built the little church; son built the skyline.
Hallgrímskirkja was **commissioned in 1937** but took a marathon to raise — finally **consecrated in 1986, 36 years after Guðjón died in 1950.** He never saw his own masterpiece finished.

block.title: 🚪 Dýrhólaey
block.cue: Look right at 2 o'clock — the high headland with the lighthouse.
block.hook: Ahead on the right is the **front door of the South Coast** — and for a thousand years the **southernmost point of the mainland**, until a volcano moved the finish line. With a hole big enough to **fly a plane through.** Someone did. Three times.
block.point: A teaching stop par excellence: glacial plains, old islands and active coastal erosion all visible in **one slow spin of your head.**
block.mic: Dýrhólaey is the hinge where the **volcanoes, the sandur and the ocean** all shake hands — and argue about who built this coastline.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the headland has gone you may still catch the light blinking, which is the entire reason it is up there."
bullets: **Dýrhólaey** was born underwater ~**100,000 years ago** in a submarine eruption — half tuff (**Háey**), half basalt (**Lágey**) — then hammered by waves into a huge natural **sea arch**. In **October 1993** a pilot flew a small plane clean through it **three times** (once could've been luck).

On top sits a **castle-like lighthouse** — Iceland's **first landfall light and brightest**, seen **43 km** out to sea; the current 1927 tower was designed by state architect **Guðjón Samúelsson** (yes — the same man behind that little church back down the road, and Hallgrímskirkja).

From the top you can read the whole **Katla Corridor** — the sandur behind, the **Reynisdrangar** needles ahead, and the Atlantic hurling itself at the basalt. Parts close in summer for **nesting puffins**: this is a full **seabird city**, a **protected reserve since 1978** under **100 m cliffs** — the birds were here first, and the reserve rules say so.
The flyers have names: pilot **Arngrímur Jóhannsson** and MP **Árni Johnsen**, who took a light aircraft through the arch in **October 1993** — three passes, to prove the first wasn't luck.
The name is literal: **Dýrhólaey** means **door-hill island** — the hill with the doorway through it. The first light went up here in **1910**; the tower you can see replaced it in 1927.

Footnote for the pedants: it's long been called the **southernmost point of the mainland** — until **Katla's 1918 flood built Kötlutangi**, which took the title off it **for several decades**, before the sea carried that sand west again. The volcano moved the goalposts; the Atlantic moved them back.

block.title: 🌊 Reynisfjara & Reynisdrangar
block.cue: Step off at Reynisfjara — and before anything else: stay high on the sand, well back from the water.
block.hook: Black sand. A basalt pipe-organ. Sea stacks standing offshore. Iceland's most beautiful beach — and its most dangerous. Never turn your back on these waves.
block.point: The most beautiful beach in Iceland is also the one that asks for the most respect — awe first, but feet planted well back from the water.
block.mic: Black sand, stone trolls, a basalt cathedral — and a sea that has taken lives. Look all you like; just do it from up here.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Bad weather makes this beach more dangerous, not more atmospheric. Stay well back from the water today."
bullets: ⚠️ **Safety first, always:** the "sneaker waves" (laumualda) here are lethal and unpredictable — they surge far higher up the beach than the sea in front of you suggests, the water is freezing, and the undertow drags. People have drowned here, several in recent years. Stay well back, keep off the wet sand, and never turn your back on the ocean for a photo.

The cliff is stuðlaberg — hexagonal basalt columns formed as thick lava cooled slowly and cracked into near-perfect pillars; the Hálsanefshellir cave folds them into a natural pipe-organ you can walk into when the tide allows.

Offshore stand the Reynisdrangar sea stacks. The old story: two night-trolls were hauling a three-masted ship to shore when the sun came up and caught them — and trolls turn to stone in daylight. They're still out there, mid-heist, a few thousand years on.
In summer the Reynisfjall cliffs above fill with nesting seabirds — puffins, fulmars, guillemots — so bring the zoom as well as the wide angle.
🎬 **On screen:** this black coast plays the Eastwatch-by-the-Sea shore in *Game of Thrones*, and the beach and stacks have appeared in *Rogue One*, *Star Trek Into Darkness* and *Noah*.
Under your feet: fine **black volcanic sand** — basalt that met the sea, shattered, and got ground to grains. **No shells, no coral, just pulverised volcano.**

To one side, **Hálsanefshellir** — the shallow cave with its pipe-organ wall of **hexagonal columns** under the **Garðar cliff**: lava that cooled so slowly it contracted and cracked into neat six-sided pillars, same trick as the Giant's Causeway.

Out in the surf stand the **Reynisdrangar sea stacks**, the last of an old headland where tough basalt held while the softer cliff was chewed away — the "stack" at the end of the crack-cave-arch-stack sequence. The cliffs above are a **puffin colony** in summer.
In the legend, those stacks are **two trolls and a ship**, caught by sunrise mid-theft and turned to stone. Trolls in Iceland are strictly nocturnal; daylight is their kryptonite.

🎬 **On screen:** Hollywood's favourite black beach — *Rogue One: A Star Wars Story* (2016), *Star Trek Into Darkness* (2013, standing in for an alien planet), *Noah* (2014), and *Game of Thrones* as the Eastwatch coast, plus several Indian films (*Aadhavan*, *Naayak*).

Out in the surf stand the **Reynisdrangar sea stacks**, the last of an old headland the sea otherwise chewed away. In the legend, those stacks are **two trolls and a ship**, caught by sunrise mid-theft and turned to stone — because Icelandic trolls are strictly nocturnal, and daylight is their kryptonite.

The serious bit stays serious: the **sneaker waves here have killed at least five people since 2007**, with another death in 2025, which is why the **traffic-light warning system** went in in 2022. The folklore is the safer attraction.
