block.title: Katla
block.sub: The Sleeping Giant Under the Ice
block.cue: Look right at 2 o'clock — Mýrdalsjökull, and Katla under it.
block.hook: We've said her name half a dozen times today — under Sólheimajökull, off Dýrhólaey, at the church on the hill, in the cairn field, on Hjörleifshöfði. **Here's the volcano itself.** And the biggest threat on the South Coast doesn't look like a threat — it's a **white ice cap, peaceful and silent.**
block.point: The most dangerous volcano on the south coast doesn't look like a volcano. It looks like a glacier.
block.mic: Iceland's most polite warning: **the loudest thing she does is wait.**
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Cannot see the ice cap? Neither can the people living under it. That is the whole problem with Katla."
bullets: Under that ice sits **Katla** — a **~10 km-wide caldera**, summit **1,512 m** — one of Iceland's biggest, angriest volcanoes. The cap above is **Mýrdalsjökull**, Iceland's **4th-largest ice cap** — **520 km² as measured in 2019**, down from about **607 km² around the year 2000** and **736 km² at its Little Ice Age peak around 1890** — a **200–700 m** insulating blanket over a furnace. Being subglacial is the whole danger: she doesn't just throw ash, she **flash-melts the glacier into floods.**
She's produced **at least 21 eruptions in the last 1,100 years**, typically **VEI 4–5** — bigger than famous neighbour Eyjafjallajökull's 2010 show.

The gaps between her eruptions have run from **about 13 years to about 80, averaging just under 50** — and it is now **108 years since 1918, the longest quiet spell on record.** (Do that sum on the bus and watch the faces.) She also leaks so much CO₂ while dormant that one study ranked her among **Earth's biggest volcanic CO₂ sources.**

Erupting under ice, she makes a **jökulhlaup** — a glacial flood that can push **up to ~300,000 m³ a second** to the sea, faster than a galloping horse. The town ahead, **Vík**, has drilled for this for decades.

Her last full eruption began shortly before **3pm on 12 October 1918** and ran until **4 November** — twenty-four days — and the flood carried roughly **200 million cubic metres** of rock and ice to the sea, a cube **585 metres** on every side. It dumped so much sediment that it **pushed the shore south of Hjörleifshöfði out by more than 3 km.** A volcano that does land reclamation.

The ash of **1918** came to about **0.7 cubic kilometres** spread over **60,000 km²**, more than half the country, with the plume reaching **at least 14,300 metres** and the finest dust above **25 kilometres**.
Nobody died in **1918**, and the Icelandic record is blunt about why — *"sennilega olli tilviljun"*, probably just coincidence. The flood came down where nobody happened to be standing.

Her system's **Eldgjá** was not a day but a campaign: it **began in the spring of 939 and ran on, at least episodically, into the autumn of 940**, along a fissure **75 kilometres** long, and that flow ran **about 70 kilometres** to the sea. Vísindavefur rates it **VEI-6** — similar to **Laki** in lava volume, **about 20 km³ against Laki's 14.7** — but **a full magnitude and a half above it on the MS scale**, which is why Vísindavefur calls Eldgjá **the most powerful Icelandic eruption of the last ten thousand years.**

**VEI-6** is rare company. Across the whole of the last **10,000 years** only a handful of Icelandic eruptions have climbed that high — the **Saksunarvatn** tephra event of about ten thousand years ago, **Veiðivötn in 1477**, and this one. Vísindavefur puts Eldgjá **about 840 years before the Lakagígar eruption of 1783.**

The whole belt between **Mýrdalsjökull** and **Vatnajökull** is built out of these — the remains of **fissure eruptions tens of kilometres long**, some from the ice age and some from after it. **Lakagígar, Eldgjá, Veiðivötn, Vatnaöldur.** Four names, four gashes, one neighbourhood. And Vísindavefur states plainly that **another great fissure eruption in this belt is all but certain** — in the system of **Grímsvötn**, **Katla** or **Bárðarbunga** — and that it could come very soon or in many centuries. (Nobody will tell you which, which is the least reassuring answer available.)

The cap above is **Mýrdalsjökull**, Iceland's **4th-largest ice cap** — **520 km² as measured in 2019**, down from about **607 km² around the year 2000** and **736 km² at its Little Ice Age peak around 1890** — acting as a several-hundred-metre insulating blanket over a furnace.

She's produced **at least 21 eruptions in the last 1,100 years**, typically **VEI 4–5** — bigger than famous neighbour Eyjafjallajökull's 2010 show. The last one to come up through the ice, **1918**, ran **24 days** and dumped so much flood sediment — **about 200 million m³ (0.2 km³) of sand** — that it **pushed the shore south of Hjörleifshöfði out by more than 3 km.** A volcano that does land reclamation.

The gaps between her eruptions have run from **about 13 years to about 80, averaging just under 50** — and it is now **108 years since 1918, the longest quiet spell on record.** (Her system also produced **Eldgjá**, which began in the **spring of 939 CE** and ran on, at least episodically, into the **autumn of 940** — one of the largest lava floods of the last 2,000 years.)

Erupting under ice, she produces a **jökulhlaup** — a glacial flood that can push **up to ~300,000 m³ a second** to the sea, faster than a galloping horse. The town ahead, **Vík**, has drilled for this for decades.

block.title: Víkurkirkja
block.cue: Look left at 10 o'clock — the red-roofed church above the town.
block.hook: In most towns, the church is for Sunday service. In Vík, it's the **literal lifeboat.**
block.point: The town's most beautiful building is also its most practical piece of **safety equipment.**
block.mic: It's the only place in Vík where the view of the ocean feels peaceful — because you know you're standing on the only safe soil in the valley.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Even in cloud it is the highest thing in the village, which is precisely why it is the evacuation point."
bullets: **Víkurkirkja**, **consecrated in 1934**, sits high on the hill for one reason: **Katla.**
If the volcano erupts under **Mýrdalsjökull**, the resulting **jökulhlaup** could erase the whole village — and this church stands on the **only ground high enough** to stay above the water.

Every resident is trained to **run to this church** the moment the sirens sound, and the drills assume there may be **very little warning at all**. (You will see “about 15 minutes” quoted for the run-up; no Icelandic official source states it, so leave the number out and keep the instruction.) block.title: Vík í Mýrdal
block.cue: Look ahead at 12 o'clock — Vík over the hill.
block.hook: Over this hill is Vík: one small village, **a lot of black sand**, and a volcano that once shoved the coastline forward like it was rearranging furniture.
block.point: Vík is where coffee breaks, Coast Guard alerts and **thousand-year-old saga grudges** all share the same view of a volcano.
block.mic: Sleepy seaside town. If Katla starts shouting, swap the beach for the church and hope it's a drill.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The village is over the hill either way. You will know when we are there."
bullets: Iceland's **southernmost mainland village** — about **300 people** in the village, **~750** in the wider district — strung along the beach with **Víkurkirkja** parked safely up on the hill. With **no natural harbour**, this was historically a place you rowed boats out through the surf from an open shore.

It's also, **jointly with Vestmannaeyjar**, the **warmest place in Iceland** (**5.3°C** yearly mean) — Veðurstofa's own wording is *ásamt Vestmannaeyjakaupstað*. And it is properly wet, about triple Reykjavík. “Warmest” is doing heroic work in that sentence.
That shore we just talked about — the one **1918** shoved out past **Hjörleifshöfði** — is this town's front garden: everything out there is fresh Katla sand.

To the east, **Hjörleifshöfði** — a saga headland that once sat by open sea — is now stranded **inland**, the gap quietly filled by a century of Katla's black sand. The church above town is the official “**run here if Katla wakes**” point.

The weather station here was set up in **1925** and has observed continuously ever since. **Veðurstofa Íslands** gives the annual mean as **2,333 mm** over the standard period **1971 to 2000** — a lot of rain, but not a national record: Iceland's wettest year anywhere is **Kvísker, 4,630.4 mm in 2002.**

The wettest year on record is **1926 at 2,887 mm** — the station's second year of operation, which must have felt like a discouraging start. **1950** and **1959** are barely behind at **2,858** and **2,855 mm**, and the heaviest single day is **150.3 mm on 9 September 1933**.
The temperature extremes are **28.5°C on 11 August 1939**, which the Met Office itself marks as **doubtful**, and **minus 16.9°C on the night of 1 April 1968**, which nobody has ever queried.

None of that exists without **Guðný Helgadóttir**, who has been observing the weather at Vík **since 1972** — one person, one place, decades of readings taken by hand in whatever was falling that morning.

You'll see Vík — Iceland's **southernmost mainland village**, and with no natural harbour, historically a place you rowed boats out through the surf from an open shore — strung along the beach, with **Víkurkirkja** parked safely up on the hill.

block.title: Hjörleifshöfði
block.cue: Look ahead at 1 o'clock — the massive flat-topped mountain on the horizon.
block.hook: That massive rock ahead is a **1,100-year-old crime scene** — and the address of Iceland's most famous ghost.
block.point: Iceland's history didn't start with peace. It started with a **slave revolt, a blood feud** — and a vengeful housekeeper who lives in the ice.
block.mic: Most countries' founding stories are statues and speeches. Iceland's is a body, a fake bear — and a woman who became a volcano.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Twelve kilometres out on a wet day means you are not seeing it. It looks like a ship, and today it is a ship in fog."
bullets: **Hjörleifshöfði** — a **221 m móberg headland** — is named for **Hjörleifur Hróðmarsson**, sworn **blood-brother of Ingólfur Arnarson, Iceland's first settler**. The two **sailed here together around 874**, then split: Ingólfur let the gods choose his home, following his high-seat pillars to Reykjavík; Hjörleifur — who **refused to sacrifice to any god** — parked at the first headland. **His burial mound still crowns the summit.**

Come spring, says *Landnámabók*: **one ox** — so his **enslaved Irishmen dragged the plough**. They killed the ox and **blamed a bear**. Iceland **has no bears** — the newcomers just didn't know that yet. When the Norsemen scattered to hunt it, the thralls **ambushed them one by one**, Hjörleifur included, then fled with the women and boats to the islands offshore.

Ingólfur found the bodies, tracked the killers to those islands, and killed them all. His eulogy: **“A sad end for a good man, slain by slaves — that's what comes of refusing to sacrifice.”** Those islands became the **Vestmannaeyjar** — **“Isles of the West Men,”** the Norse name for **Irish Gaels** — **named after the enslaved men who did the deed.**

The ghost came **three centuries later**. **Katla**, a fearsome housekeeper at the nearby monastery of **Þykkvabæjarklaustur**, owned **magic breeches that never tired**. Shepherd **Barði** borrowed them; she **drowned him in the whey vat**. When sinking whey threatened to expose the body, she fled onto **Mýrdalsjökull** and **leapt into the chasm still called Kötlugjá — “Katla's rift”** — the volcano's vent. Soon after, a **glacial flood burst from the ice**. **The volcano is named after her** — and every eruption, they say, is her temper.
Like Pétursey, this cape **was once an island** — tethered to Iceland by miles of Katla's black sand.
**Hjörleifshöfði** is a **221 m palagonite (móberg) inselberg** named after **Hjörleifur Hróðmarsson**, the sworn **blood-brother** of Iceland's first settler **Ingólfur Arnarson**.

Per *Landnámabók*, Hjörleifur settled here around **874** and, **within a year (c. 875)**, was **murdered by his own enslaved Irish/Hebridean men** — one of the very few slave revolts the sagas record. Ingólfur tracked them to the islands on the horizon and killed them in revenge.

Here's the payoff on the map: those islands are the **Vestmannaeyjar** — the **"Isles of the West Men."** *Vestmenn* was the Norse word for the **Gaels of Ireland and the Hebrides** — so the archipelago out there is **named after the enslaved Gaels themselves.** The romantic image of free, self-made Viking farmers is missing a chapter.

At its base sits **Kötluklettur**, "Katla's Rock." The tale: **Katla**, a housekeeper at nearby **Þykkvabæjarklaustur** with **magic breeches** that made her run impossibly fast, killed the shepherd boy **Barði** for borrowing them and hid him in a **vat of skyr** — then, as the whey dropped and discovery loomed, threw herself into the glacier. Every eruption, they say, is her ghost. **The volcano is named after her.**
Like Pétursey, this cape **was once an island**, now tethered to the coast by miles of Katla's black sand.

🎬 **On screen:** This headland and the black sands around it (Hafursey, Mýrdalssandur) became the planet **Lah'mu** — Jyn Erso's childhood home — in *Rogue One* (2016). The famous "Yoda Cave" (Gigjagjá) is tucked into this very massif.

block.title: 🏞️ Skógafoss
block.cue: At Skógafoss.
block.hook: The waterfall that **looks like a fantasy backdrop** and sounds like someone left a giant tap on **since the Ice Age**.
block.point: One spot: ancient shorelines, modern sandur, old farms, a volcano trail, and a missing chest where somebody grabbed the wrong part.
block.mic: If this was anywhere else, it would be the main event. Here it's just **one more stop on a Tuesday**.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Rain makes it bigger. There is no bad-weather version of this waterfall."
bullets: The **Skógá river** skips the rapids and walks straight off the old sea-cliff — a clean **60 m drop, 25 m wide** — free-falling into a deep pool before racing across the sandur to the Atlantic.

At the base you have to **shout to be heard** — which is why most videos from here are people silently pointing. The metal staircase on the right is your free fitness test; at the top begins the **Fimmvörðuháls trail**, which climbs the river **between Eyjafjallajökull and Mýrdalsjökull** — the same gap the 2010 eruption first cracked open.

This cliff is the **coastline of thousands of years ago**: textbook waterfall geology — hard cap-rock over soft, undercut and collapsing, so the fall eats **upstream** and leaves a gorge behind it. The land then lifted, rivers dumped black sand, and the real shore marched several km south — Skógafoss never moved.

Behind the car park: **Skógar Museum** (turf houses, old church, farm buildings) and a **bonus waterfall, Kvernufoss**, hiding in a green gorge next door. Plus the legend of **Þrasi's treasure** — a settler's gold chest hidden behind the falls; would-be looters snapped off the iron ring, which ended up on the **church door**. The gold did not follow.

block.title: 💧 Seljalandsfoss & Gljúfrabúi
block.cue: At Seljalandsfoss car park.
block.hook: A waterfall you can **walk behind**. And a second one **hiding in a slot canyon** next door.
block.point: Same cliff. Same Ice-Age coastline. **One tiny change in the rock** = two completely different waterfall personalities.
block.mic: Stand in front of the old sea cliff. Walk behind the waterfall. If you have dry socks after Gljúfrabúi, you've done something wrong.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "You are getting wet either way. This is the one waterfall where the forecast is irrelevant, because you walk behind it."
bullets: **Seljalandsfoss** drops a clean **60 m** off Iceland's old sea-cliff, fed by the **Seljalandsá** river running off the **Eyjafjallajökull** glacier above.
A natural recess lets you walk **all the way behind the curtain** in summer — wet, slippery rock, so good boots, a waterproof and **one hand free**; in ice the path closes, so respect the barrier.

The cliff is an **old sea cliff from just after the Ice Age**, when the Atlantic reached the foot of the **Eyjafjöll**; rivers then filled the lowlands and the coast is now several km south — the same drowned-then-stranded coastline as Skógafoss down the road.
A short walk north, **Gljúfrabúi** ("the canyon-dweller") hides in a narrow mossy gorge — only its top peeks out; to meet it you **wade up the stream**, and **wet feet are non-negotiable.**

🎬 **On screen:** A proper film star too — *Beowulf & Grendel* (2005), Bollywood's *Dilwale* (2015) and a run of Indian blockbusters (*Namo Venkatesa*, *Aadhavan*), plus **Justin Bieber** getting thoroughly soaked here in "I'll Show You" (2015).

block.title: Rútshellir
block.sub: The Cave With a Murder Hole
block.cue: Look left at 10 o'clock — Rútshellir, the cave cut into the cliff by Drangshlíð.
block.hook: One of the oldest man-made homes in Iceland — and its first tenant was murdered through a hole drilled under his own bed.
block.point: A cave that's been a house, a byre, a fish-store, a murder scene and a Nazi wild-goose chase — all in one hole in the rock.
block.mic: Most farms have a shed. Drangshlíð has a thousand-year-old cave with a purpose-built assassination hole in the ceiling.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The cave is cut into the cliff, so it is there whatever the sky is doing."
bullets: **Rútshellir** is one of the **largest man-made caves in Iceland** — an arched hall roughly **20 m long and 2.5 m high**, hacked from the soft cliff of **Drangshlíðarfjall**, about **3 km west of Skógafoss.** Long claimed as Iceland's **oldest surviving man-made dwelling.**

The legend: a brute named **Rútur** — troll, looter or bad chieftain, take your pick — lived here, and his **slaves carved a hole under his sleeping ledge and speared him from below** as he slept. Even dead he terrified them: one killer, **Björn**, bolted to the mountain **Bjarnarfell**, which still carries his name.

It's in the record, not just the poetry — logged in **Árni Magnússon's land register (1714)** and the travel book of **1756**. A **cross carved in the ceiling** has people guessing at Irish monks before the Norse — unproven, so serve it as “some think.”
Weirdest chapter: in **1936 Himmler's Ahnenerbe** — the SS pseudo-science unit — searched here convinced they'd find an ancient Nordic temple. They found a barn.
say: Rútur's cave, one of the largest man-made caves in Iceland
the farm and cliff the cave is hacked into
the mountain the killer Björn fled to, which still carries his name
the SS pseudo-science unit that searched here in 1936

block.title: Laufskálavarða
block.sub: The Cairn Field of Good Luck
block.cue: Look left — the mossy lava ridge covered in stone cairns.
block.hook: Thousands of little stone stacks, and each one is a traveller buying insurance against a glacier.
block.point: A thousand years of nervous travellers, each leaving a rock and a prayer before driving into Katla's backyard.
block.mic: The cairns aren't decoration — they're the receipts of everyone who crossed here scared.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The cairns show better against low cloud than they do in sunshine, oddly."
bullets: **Laufskálavarða** is a low **lava ridge on the east edge of Mýrdalssandur**, by the river **Kúðafljót** — carpeted in **stone cairns.** The custom: anyone crossing this deadly black desert **for the first time** piled a cairn for a **safe journey**, and centuries of first-timers built the field you see.
The danger was real — **Mýrdalssandur is Katla's flood path**, swept by **jökulhlaups** without warning, so a little supernatural insurance made sense.

The name comes from **Laufskálar**, a big settlement-era farm here — tradition gives it **24 doors on iron hinges** — buried by **an early Katla eruption.** (You'll see a “894” date on the signs; the maths doesn't work, so just call it an early Katla eruption.)
Don't add to it: visitors are now **asked not to build new cairns** — the field is protected heritage, not a DIY project.

The green cones scattered across **Álftaver** just east of here are **gervigígar**, blown up through the **Eldgjá** lava from below where it sealed the wetland in — **Álftaversgígar**, a protected natural monument of **3,436.1 hectares**.
say: the low lava ridge carpeted in travellers' cairns
the black flood-desert it sits on the edge of, Katla's flood path

block.title: Eldhraun
block.cue: Look all around — the moss-black plain is Eldhraun, the Laki lava.
block.hook: That soft green moss you can't stop photographing? It's the lid on the **deadliest eruption in Iceland's history** — the one that nearly ended the country.
block.point: One fissure, one very bad year, a whole continent's weather rearranged. The prettiest thing out here is also the deadliest.
block.mic: Every other lava field is scenery. This one has a body count.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Moss in the wet goes an unreasonable green. This is the lava field at its best, not its worst."
bullets: In **June 1783** the **Lakagígar** fissure tore open — a **27 km rift of more than 140 vents** — and erupted for **eight months** (the **Skaftáreldar**, “Skaftá Fires”), laying down **14.7 km³ of lava across ~600 km².** That makes it **the second-largest lava flood in historical time, behind Eldgjá** and its **~20 km³** — larger still, but **8,700 years before anyone was here to see it**, is **Þjórsárhraunið mikla**. You're driving across the runner-up.

And yet the lava barely killed anyone — the **gas** did. The fissure breathed out **~122 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide** plus a fluorine fog that poisoned the grass, and the famine that followed has a name of its own: the **Móðuharðindin, “Mist Hardships.”** The haze even crossed **Europe**, wrecking harvests as far as France.
The green fuzz is **grámosi**, woolly fringe moss — **decades to grow, one boot-print to wreck.** Admire it through the window.
The **Skaftáreldar** began on **8 June 1783** and did not stop until **7 February 1784** — eight months to the day, near enough.

It did not spread politely across country, it went down the rivers: on **11 June** the **Skaftá** simply stopped, and on **3 August** the **Hverfisfljót** went the same way. Two rivers deleted, by something arriving down their own beds.

Landgræðslan measures that moss mat at an average **38 centimetres** thick, which is also why nothing else grows here — **well over two centuries on**, vascular plants are still sparse, because the mat smothers seeds before they germinate.

The arithmetic of the **Móðuharðindin**: roughly **10,000 dead — about a fifth of all Icelanders** — the population down from just under **50,000** to just under **40,000** by the end of **1786**, with **smallpox** taking another **1,500** and **earthquakes in August 1784** flattening about **400 farms**.

The haze formed a continuous cloud across the whole northern hemisphere, **30 to 90 degrees of latitude**, depositing **over a tonne of sulphuric acid per square kilometre**. Europe called it the dry fog and spent that summer wondering where it came from.

The national figure hides the local one. **Vatnajökulsþjóðgarður** puts the livestock loss at **around three quarters of every animal in the country** — and in the worst-hit districts, the ones we have just driven through, **about 40% of the people died.** (One in five is the headline. Out here it was two in five.)
say: the moss-black lava field we're driving across
the 27 km rift of more than 140 vents that erupted it
“Mist Hardships”, the famine that followed and killed a fifth of Icelanders
woolly fringe moss, the green fuzz on the lava

block.title: Kirkjubæjarklaustur
block.sub: The Convent on the Fire Road
block.cue: At Kirkjubæjarklaustur.
block.hook: A village so holy that, by legend, **sinners literally couldn't live here** — and then in 1783 a priest stared down a wall of lava and won.
block.point: A town that swears a priest out-argued a lava flow — with a natural basalt cathedral floor to set the scene.
block.mic: Most sermons just feel like they last forever. His actually stopped a volcano.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The sisters were here through eight hundred winters of exactly this."
bullets: Tradition (via *Landnámabók*) says the **Papar** — Irish monks — were here **before the Norse**, and the ground was so blessed no heathen could settle. In **1186** the Benedictines made it official: **Kirkjubæjar convent**, a nunnery that ran until the **Reformation in 1550.**

The place-names still gossip about the nuns: **Systrafoss** (“the sisters' falls”), lake **Systravatn**, and **Systrastapi** — the rock where, the darker tale goes, two sisters were burned for sin and only later cleared.
Nearby is **Kirkjugólf**, the “church floor”: a patch of **columnar basalt** worn flat so it looks like a tiled cathedral floor. Nobody laid it — **the volcano did the tiling.**

And this is where **Rev. Jón Steingrímsson** delivered his **Eldmessa — the “Fire Sermon” — on 20 July 1783**, preaching as the Laki lava bore down. It halted at the edge of the parish. He kept preaching.
The convent was founded by **Þorlákur helgi**, Bishop of Skálholt and later Iceland's patron saint, and its first abbess was **Halldóra**, about whom the record says almost nothing at all.

Behind the two-sisters legend sits one documented case: in **1343** a nun of this house — the sources cannot agree whether **Katrín or Kristín** — was **burned at the stake** for heresy and for having given herself to the devil in writing.

She is an outlier twice over. Iceland's actual burning age was the **17th century** — the **first burning for witchcraft** was **1625** and the last **1685** — and of roughly **25 Icelanders** ever burned about **23** were for witchcraft and the overwhelming majority were **men**.

**Kirkjugólf** is not weathered flat, it is decapitated — *jökul- og brimsorfið stuðlaberg*, columns planed off by a glacier and scoured by the sea. Protected **náttúruvætti since 1987**, with a **10-metre** exclusion zone and a **50-metre** buffer, so walk to it and do not stand on it.

**Séra Jón Steingrímsson**, **1728–1791**, is the **eldklerkur**, the fire priest, and the reason we know any of this in detail — he wrote the eruption down almost day by day. He also buried a great many of the parish he had held together, once the famine arrived.

Two footnotes the story usually loses. The charges against the nun in **1343** were not only heresy and having given herself to the devil in writing — she was also accused of having **misused the body of Christ.** And what the ground shows at the Fire Sermon is a lava front that **stalled**, held up by the terrain and by its own cooling crust. Both things are true at once, and Icelanders have never felt any pressing need to choose between them.
say: the village we're stopping at, home to a convent from 1186 to 1550
“the sisters' falls”, named for those nuns
the “church floor”, a patch of columnar basalt worn flat like tiles
the priest who preached the Fire Sermon here in 1783
the Irish monks tradition says were here before the Norse

block.title: Fjaðrárgljúfur
block.cue: You can't see it from the road — it's hidden in that low ridge on the left. We turn off for it.
block.hook: A canyon so photogenic that **Justin Bieber waded down a river here** — and accidentally loved it half to death.
block.point: Ten thousand years of patient meltwater — versus one pop star and a phone camera.
block.mic: The glacier took millennia to carve it. We nearly wore it out in a weekend.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "You cannot see it from the road on any day. It is hidden in that ridge, which is why it stayed a secret so long."
bullets: **Road position, so the running order stays honest:** the turn-off for **road 206** leaves Route 1 at **63.76274 / -18.11862**, about **5 km west of Kirkjubæjarklaustur** — so driving east we pass it *before* the village. We take the comfort stop at Klaustur first and **double back the six kilometres** for the canyon.

**Fjaðrárgljúfur** (“feather-river canyon”) is **about 1.5 km long and up to 100 m deep** — those are the figures in its own protection order — a snaking gorge with mossy green **palagonite (móberg)** walls.

Two ages, don't mix them up: the **rock is about 2 million years old** (Ice-Age palagonite), but the **cutting began about 10,000 years ago, at the end of the last Ice Age**, when meltwater from a retreating glacier sawed straight down through the soft rock — **and it is still going on today.**
The **Fjaðrá** river still does the digging, one grain at a time. That serpentine shape is just water taking the lazy route — and turning it into art.

In **2015 Justin Bieber** filmed *I'll Show You* wading through it; Instagram did the rest. So many boots trampled the moss that the site now **closes periodically to recover.** Two million years of rock, nearly worn flat by one music video.
🎬 **On screen:** this snaking canyon also stars in the *Game of Thrones* dragon-flight sequence (Season 8, Episode 1, just before the Skógafoss landing).

It is not finished. The protection notice states plainly that the cutting **is still ongoing**, and **100 metres** in **10,000 years** works out at roughly **a centimetre a year** — a hundred metres of rock removed at about the rate your fingernails grow.

“Closes periodically” has hard dates. It shut in **February 2019** for waterlogged ground and reopened **31 May 2019**; then the notice went out on **5 April 2023** and the gate shut the next morning, at **09:00 on 6 April 2023**, under the emergency power in **Article 25a of the Nature Conservation Act no. 60/2013**, reopening **20 April 2023** after two weeks of gravel being carried in and laid. That gravel is what you are standing on.

It was finally protected on **11 May 2024** by **Auglýsing nr. 555/2024**, covering **0.15 km²** — **fifteen hectares**. A patch you could walk across in ten minutes needed a legal instrument of its own.

And the closures work: after the 2019 one, **Umhverfisstofnun** recorded that the vegetation had taken **remarkably well** to being left alone — which is the whole argument for the path, in one sentence.
say: “feather-river canyon”, up to 100 m deep on your left
the river still doing the digging
palagonite, the soft mossy green rock of its walls

block.title: Foss á Síðu
block.cue: Look left — the thin waterfall down the cliff behind the farm.
block.hook: A postcard waterfall next to a cliff full of singing dwarves — and on a windy day the water forgets which way is down.
block.point: Water that runs uphill, dwarves that sing hymns, and a curse with a nine-generation warranty — all at one roadside farm.
block.mic: Blink and it's a pretty waterfall. Stay a minute and it's a folklore box-set.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Wind blows this one sideways, and in a real gale it goes back up the cliff. Worth watching for."
bullets: **Foss á Síðu** is a slender waterfall about **10 km east of Kirkjubæjarklaustur**, dropping off the cliff behind the farm of the same name — fed by the little lake **Þórutjörn** on the heath above. The farm is settlement-era, named in **Landnámabók.**
Its party trick: in a strong south wind the gusts catch the falling water and **blow it back up and sideways**, so the fall seems to **pour upward.**

Just east sit **Dverghamrar**, “the Dwarf Rocks” — a wall of **columnar basalt** said to house **hidden folk**; a local tale from **1904** has a farm girl hearing the dwarves singing a **hymn** in the cliffs.
Darker footnote: folklore ties Foss to a **curse** — a ghost-dog, **Móri**, said to hound one family for **nine generations.** Iceland doesn't do haunted houses by halves.
say: the thin waterfall behind the farm, which a strong south wind blows back upward
“the Dwarf Rocks”, the columnar basalt just east, said to house hidden folk
the ghost-dog said to hound one family here for nine generations

block.title: Orustuhóll
block.cue: Look right — the lone crag standing above the black lava.
block.hook: A hill named “Battle Hill” that took on the second-biggest lava flood in Iceland's historical time — and, somehow, won.
block.point: Estates buried, holdings abandoned, a whole district rearranged — the official counts still disagree on the exact number — and it still couldn't take one stubborn hill.
block.mic: Everything around it is 1783. This one crag is the “before” photo.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "A lone crag in flat light is hard to pick out. Look for the shape, not the colour."
bullets: **Orustuhóll** (“battle hill”) is a **rock knoll** that, before **1783**, sat as an island in the **floodplain of the Hverfisfljót river**, ringed by water and sand.

When the **Skaftáreldar** (the Laki fires) sent the **Eldhraun / Brunahraun** lava pouring east, the flow **split around the hill and left it standing** — a green survivor-islet in a sea of fresh black rock.

So it's a rare thing: a scrap of the **pre-1783 landscape** you can still see, marooned inside the lava — and the district around it was emptied. **Vatnajökulsþjóðgarður** counts **twenty estates buried outright and thirty more wrecked**; **Vísindavefur** counts **thirteen farmsteads under the lava and twenty-nine holdings abandoned**. The number depends on whether you're counting houses or land.

A **Katla Geopark** geosite; the name hints at an old battle-legend, but the real drama is geological — one crag versus **the second-largest lava flood in historical time, behind Eldgjá** (larger still, but 8,700 years before anyone was here to see it, is **Þjórsárhraunið mikla**).
say: “battle hill”, the lone crag the 1783 lava split around and left standing
the river in whose floodplain it once sat as an island
the Eldhraun lava that poured east around it

block.title: Lómagnúpur & Núpsstaður
block.cue: Look left at 11 o'clock — the black wall standing on its own.
block.hook: In **Njáls saga** this cliff **swings open like a door** and a man walks out of it reading a death list. At its foot stands a church the size of a shed whose designer the state records as **Ókunnur** — unknown.
block.point: A cliff that opens like a door in the country's greatest saga — and at its foot a church the size of a shed, built by a man the state has never been able to name.
block.mic: Everything east of here is sand. This is the last thing standing before it — and the saga knew that too.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the top has gone, you are still seeing seven hundred metres of it. That is usually enough."
bullets: That wall is **Lómagnúpur**, and it comes up before the sandur does: **Núpsstaður at route km 263.1, Lómagnúpur at 265.5**, both on the **left, north of the road**, while **Skeiðarársandur proper does not begin until km 268.6.** In **chapter 133 of Brennu-Njáls saga** the cliff swings open like a door and a man in a goatskin cloak walks out with an iron staff, names **Flosi's** men one by one, calls himself **Járngrímur**, and says he is bound for the **Alþingi** to clear the juries, then the courts, then the battlefield.

The dream at **Lómagnúpur** is a death list, read out in order. **Járngrímur** names **Grímur the Red**, **Árni Kolsson**, **Eyjólfur Bölverksson**, **Ljótur son of Hallur of Síða**, the **Sigfússynir**, then **Lambi**, **Móðólfur** and **Glúmur**, and last of all **Gunnar Lambason** and **Kolur Þorsteinsson.** Flosi had been shaken awake at **Svínafell** by **Glúmur Hildisson** and told the whole thing to **Ketill úr Mörk** — whose reading took one word, *feigir*, doomed, and whose advice took one sentence. Tell nobody.

Tucked under that cliff at **Núpsstaður** is a **bænhús**, a one-farm prayer house — a timber box **6.15 by 2.50 metres** inside a turf shell, **no pulpit, no font, unpainted throughout**, church dated **1657** and the standing timber to about **1850**. It has been in the care of **Þjóðminjasafn Íslands since 1930.**

The paperwork on the **Núpsstaður bænhús** is the best of it. **Minjastofnun** lists it as a **friðlýst kirkja** with the designer recorded, with admirable Icelandic honesty, as **Ókunnur** — unknown. The turf shell is **about 9 m long and 7.5 m wide**; side walls and the back of the chancel are **stacked turf and stone up to window height**, and the roof is **krossreist** and laid with turf. Inside: a **flagstone floor** in the nave with a bench along each wall, a chancel raised **two steps**, an altar under a small window, and **no altar rail.**
say: the black wall on the left, the cliff that opens in the dream
the farm under it, with its shed-sized prayer house
a prayer house, a private farm chapel
“Iron-Grímur”, the man who walks out of the cliff

block.title: Skeiðarársandur
block.sub: The Sand That Ate the Ring Road
block.cue: Look ahead — the vast black plain of Skeiðarársandur.
block.hook: This flat black nothing is why Iceland's Ring Road took until **1974** to close — and in 1996 a flood off the glacier took the bridge apart in an afternoon.
block.point: The last link of the Ring Road went in here in 1974 — and in 1996 the glacier came down and bit 24 metres out of it in one afternoon.
block.mic: Engineers spent decades bridging this sand. Vatnajökull started taking it apart again before lunch.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Grey sky over black sand is the default here, and it is genuinely the emptiest view in Iceland."
bullets: **Skeiðarársandur** runs to **about 760 km² on Náttúrufræðistofnun's register — one of the great sandur plains anywhere**: black sand and braided rivers, dumped grain by grain by the glaciers pouring off **Vatnajökull.**

For centuries this was **the gap in the ring**: unbridgeable rivers that could flood without warning. The **Ring Road (Route 1) wasn't finished until 1974**, when the Skeiðará bridge finally welded the country into one loop.

Then on **4 November 1996** the **Gjálp/Grímsvötn** eruption melted the ice cap and loosed a **jökulhlaup** — a glacial flood — peaking near **40,000–50,000 m³ a second, briefly rivalling the Amazon.** It **tore a 24-metre section out of Skeiðarárbrú**, twisting steel girders like wire.
Those **mangled girders now stand as a roadside monument** — Iceland's polite way of saying “we rebuilt it, but don't get comfortable.”
The piece that closed the loop was **Skeiðarárbrú**, started **1972** and finished in **July 1974** at **904 metres** — the **longest bridge in Iceland**.

For scale on **1996**: the **Ölfusá at Selfoss** averages **400 cubic metres a second**, so the flood was running at roughly **125 times** that, carrying icebergs the size of vans. Total damage came in around **1.5 billion krónur** at 2007 prices.

Rebuilding was quick and quietly humiliating: the span went back up at **880 metres** instead of **904**, and in **2017** it was retired altogether — the national record went backwards to **Borgarfjarðarbrúin at 520 metres**, because the river the big one was built for wandered off. (A national record trimmed by a river that could not be bothered to use the bridge.)
say: the vast black plain ahead, about 760 km² on Náttúrufræðistofnun's register
a glacial outburst flood, the kind that took the bridge apart in 1996
the volcano under the ice whose 1996 eruption loosed that flood

block.title: Skaftafell & Vatnajökull
block.cue: Look left — the glacier tongues spilling off Vatnajökull.
block.hook: To your left is an ice cap so big it makes **its own weather**, hides **live volcanoes**, and covers **roughly 7% of the entire country.**
block.point: One glance holds Europe's biggest ice cap, Iceland's tallest peak and a Hollywood back-lot — all quietly melting.
block.mic: It's the size of a county, hides live volcanoes, and Christopher Nolan used it as another planet.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The tongues sit low, so you often get them when the peaks have gone."
bullets: **Vatnajökull** is **Europe's largest ice cap by volume** — around **3,000 km³ of ice**, up to **~1,000 m thick**, over **about 7,500 km² by 2023 on Vatnajökulsþjóðgarður's own figure** — the last hard measured inventory, **Jökull 70**, put it at **7,720 km² in 2019.** Either way, **roughly seven percent of the country, and shrinking.** Beneath it sit active volcanoes like Grímsvötn and Bárðarbunga — fire under a very thick lid.
Poking up at **Öræfajökull** is **Hvannadalshnúkur, 2,110 m — Iceland's highest point.**

🎬 **On screen:** Svínafellsjökull — the glacier tongue here — is a Hollywood regular: the League of Shadows' ice-training in *Batman Begins* (2005) and the frozen "Mann's planet" in Christopher Nolan's *Interstellar* (2014) were both shot on this very ice.

Tucked into the green oasis of **Skaftafell** is **Svartifoss**, a waterfall framed by black **basalt columns** — the very shape that inspired Reykjavík's Hallgrímskirkja. It's a national park (2008) and **UNESCO World Heritage site (2019).**

The measured sequence for **Vatnajökull itself** is brutal: **8,723 km² around 1890**, **8,087 km² in 2000**, **7,745 km² in 2014**. And for **all of Iceland's glaciers together** — not just this one — the cover has gone from **12% of the country 130 years ago to about 10% by 2014**, thinning by roughly **a metre a year.**

Icelandic research puts the endpoint plainly — on current trends the country's glaciers will be **largely gone within two centuries**. The tongues along this road have already pulled back **around 4 kilometres** since measurements began in the **1930s**.

**Öræfajökull** in **1362** produced the **largest explosive eruption in Iceland's recorded history** — about **10 cubic kilometres** of tephra, ash on roughly **75%** of the country, **30 to 40 centimetres** deep locally, out of a caldera of **about 12 km²**. It has erupted once since, in **1727**.

Before **1362** the glacier was **Knappafellsjökull** and the district was **Litla-Hérað**, the Little District. Both names were abandoned: **öræfi** meant a harbourless coast and came to mean wasteland, and the survivors renamed their own home **The Wasteland**, where it has stayed for **664 years**.
**Svínafell**, at the foot of that film-star tongue, is where **Flosi Þórðarson** was sleeping badly when he dreamt the mountain opened — the same man who led the burning of **Njáll**.

The 1362 eruption did not merely bury Öræfi — it ran over it, with **pyroclastic flows sweeping out across the lowland** as the ash came down. And note where the summit sits: **Hvannadalshnúkur stands on the rim of that ice-filled caldera.** Öræfajökull is not a mountain with a volcano in it. It is a **volcano with a mountain on it.**
say: Europe's largest ice cap, covering roughly 7% of Iceland
the green oasis and national park tucked in at its edge
the waterfall there framed by black basalt columns
the volcano that peak pokes up from

block.title: ⛪ Hofskirkja
block.cue: Look left — the low church at Hof with grass growing on its roof.
block.hook: That building is **owned by the National Museum** — and they still hold **funerals** in it. It is an exhibit that buries people.
block.point: A museum piece that never retired — the congregation simply carried on turning up.
block.mic: Every guidebook gives you 1884 and a Viking feeling. The people who own the building give you 1883 to 85 and a Victorian carpenter — and it is a better story, because somebody's name is on it.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If it has gone in the rain — grass roof, stone walls, and a museum that has to mow it."
bullets: Everything you will ever read says this church was built in **1884.** Both the bodies that actually own and protect it — **Þjóðminjasafn Íslands** and **Minjastofnun** — say the build ran **1883 to 1885.** The joiner was **Páll Pálsson** from **Hörgsdalur.** So it is not a Viking church, it is Victorian, and it is younger than the Eiffel Tower.

Look at how it is put together, because it is three different buildings at once: a **timber frame** inside, **long walls of stacked stone with no mortar**, and a roof of **stone slabs with turf laid over the top.** Most turf buildings are turf walls. This one is drystone under a stone roof — which is the rare bit.

By the middle of the last century it was falling down. In **1953 to 54** they took it completely apart and rebuilt it in its original form. Much of what you are looking at is a careful rebuild of itself.

There has been a church on this spot a very long time: the oldest paperwork is a **máldagi of 1343**, when it was a **bændakirkja** — a farmer's own church — dedicated to **Saint Clement**, later demoted to an outlying chapel under Sandfell.
**Þjóðminjasafn took it on in 1951** under a deal with the parish: the museum pays for the repairs, the parish keeps using it. That agreement is why it is still standing and still working.
say: the church at Hof, built 1883 to 85
the National Museum, which has owned it since 1951
a church charter; the one here dates from 1343
a roof of stone slabs, the bit under the turf

block.title: 🧭 Ingólfshöfði
block.sub: The Headland Where The Date Was Invented
block.cue: Look ahead — out across the sand towards the sea, the long flat-topped headland standing on its own.
block.hook: Iceland's founding year — **874** — is **not written down anywhere.** It is a **sum.** Somebody did the arithmetic centuries later, and we have been printing the answer ever since.
block.point: The country's most famous date is a working-out, and its first address is a headland that was not even attached to the country yet.
block.mic: We passed Ingólfsfjall this morning — the mountain named after him. This is the other end of the same man's story, and neither one is where he ended up.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the sand has closed in, take my word for it — 76 metres of it out there, and it used to be an island."
bullets: Out there is **Ingólfshöfði.** **Landnámabók** says Ingólfur made landfall at the headland that now carries his name. Read the actual text and it is subtler than the postcard: the phrase is **"annan vetur" — a second winter** — and it comes *after* the business with his blood-brother Hjörleifur, not before it.

**874 comes from a calculation in Landnáma's prologue**, pinning the voyage to the reign of Haraldur hárfagri. **Íslendingabók** — written by **Ari fróði**, and the older book of the two — points at roughly **870** instead. The neat date is later arithmetic, not a record.

The **Vísindavefur** at the University of Iceland puts it plainly: Ingólfur is "first settler" **by convention.** **Hrafna-Flóki**, **Garðar Svavarsson** and **Náttfari** are all in the same sources, all here earlier. He got the title because his descendants ran the parliament and wrote the book.

The headland itself: **76 metres** high, **1,200 by 750 metres**, cliffs on every side but the west. It is **basalt lava sitting on a base of hyaloclastite** — hard cap, soft footing, which is why the sea has not taken it.
**It used to be an island.** The glacial rivers filled the gap with sand and joined it onto Iceland. The ground you are crossing built the bridge.
say: the Book of Settlements, where the landfall is written
Ari fróði's older book, pointing at about 870
the glass-and-ash rock the headland stands on

block.title: Fjallsárlón
block.cue: At Fjallsárlón.
block.hook: The glacier lagoon everyone speeds past to reach the famous one — which is exactly why it's the better stop.
block.point: Same glacier, same drama, a fraction of the crowd — the lagoon for people who read past the first page of the guidebook.
block.mic: Everyone races to Jökulsárlón. The clever ones stop here first and get the glacier to themselves.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The ice looks bluer under cloud. Bright sun actually washes it out."
bullets: **Fjallsárlón** is Jökulsárlón's **smaller, quieter sibling** — a meltwater lagoon at the snout of **Fjallsjökull**, an outlet glacier tumbling off **Öræfajökull**, Iceland's highest volcano.
Because it's tighter and less famous, you stand **much closer to the glacier wall** — the ice front looms right across the water and calves chunks into the lagoon with a crack like a rifle shot.
The icebergs here are **smaller but packed tighter**, streaked with **black volcanic ash** and that impossible **blue** — the colour of ice so compressed the air has been squeezed clean out of it.
No armada of tour boats, no crowds — just the glacier, the bergs, and **Öræfajökull** brooding behind. Like its big sister, this lagoon **didn't exist a century ago**; it's a product of the retreat.

**Ari Ólafsson**, physicist at the **University of Iceland**, gives the mechanism: in water and ice the **red** end of the spectrum fades far faster than the **blue**, and in clear dense ice daylight travels **tens of metres** through a block before it comes back out, losing red, yellow and green on the way. The white ones are white because cracks and air bubbles scatter the light straight back out before anything can be absorbed — same ice, different amount of air.

Vatnajökulsþjóðgarður dates the whole family in five words: *"Lón tóku að myndast upp úr 1930"* — **the lagoons began forming after 1930**, as the ice pulled back off the sand. There are three big ones — **Fjallsárlón**, **Breiðárlón** and **Jökulsárlón** — the same story at three different scales, and this is the one still sitting **closest to its glacier front.** (The famous one has had time to run away from its own ice. This one hasn't.)
say: the quieter glacier lagoon we're standing at
the outlet glacier calving into it
Iceland's highest volcano, brooding behind it

block.title: Breiðamerkursandur
block.sub: The Ground the Glacier Gave Back
block.cue: Look around — everything between these two lagoons was under ice when your great-grandparents were alive.
block.hook: You're driving across land that spent five hundred years under a glacier — and it only handed back the keys last century.
bullets: At its peak around **1890**, Breiðamerkurjökull reached to within **about 250 metres of the sea** — this road couldn't have existed; you'd have needed an ice axe.

As the ice pulled back, meltwater filled the hollows it had gouged — **the 1930s onwards** — leaving Fjallsárlón under Fjallsjökull behind you and Jökulsárlón waiting ahead. Two lagoons, one retreating giant.
The plain itself is **Breiðamerkursandur** — sand and gravel the glacier's rivers spread flat, now part of Vatnajökull National Park.

block.title: Jökulsárlón
block.cue: At Jökulsárlón.
block.hook: This lagoon is **Iceland's deepest lake** — and it **didn't exist** when your great-grandparents were born.
block.point: A lake that's deep, tidal, full of seals and film crews — and a living gauge of how fast the glacier is leaving.
block.mic: Your great-grandparents could have stood on solid ice right here. Now it's a 260-metre lake — and still deepening. That's the whole story, in one view.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Cloud makes the blue stronger. The photographs everyone envies were mostly taken in weather like this."
bullets: **Jökulsárlón** (“glacial-river lagoon”) only appeared around **1934–35**, when the glacier **Breiðamerkurjökull** began retreating and left a hollow that filled with meltwater. It's now **the deepest lake in Iceland — the published figure is 260 metres, and it is still deepening as the glacier retreats.** About **25 km²**, and it has **quadrupled since the 1970s.** You are looking at climate change with a boat tour on it.
The **icebergs** calving off the glacier can be **centuries old** — glowing blue, streaked with black ash from past eruptions, drifting for years before they melt. Floating archives.
It's **tidal**: a short channel links it to the sea, so the water is **brackish** and **seals** cruise in to hunt herring. Watch for heads bobbing up between the bergs.
Hollywood noticed — **two James Bond films, Batman Begins and Lara Croft** were all shot on this ice.
The bottom of it is **the lowest point in Iceland** — *lægsti staður landsins* — reaching far below sea level. Not a valley and not a cave: a hole a glacier dug and then walked out of.
For the runners-up: **Öskjuvatn** manages **220 metres**, **Hvalvatn 160**, and **Þingvallavatn** — the one on everybody's postcards — a mere **114**.

**Breiðamerkurjökull** has pulled back **about 7 kilometres** here against **around 4** for the other Vatnajökull tongues, and the reason is the lake itself — brackish water now sits against the ice front and melts it. The glacier is being eaten by its own runoff.
That salt is also why **it never sets**: even in a hard winter the surface of the lagoon does not freeze solid.
say: “glacial-river lagoon”, the deepest lake in Iceland; the published figure is 260 m, and it is still deepening as the glacier retreats
the retreating glacier that opened it in the 1930s

block.title: Fellsfjara
block.cue: At Fellsfjara, across the road from the lagoon.
block.hook: Black sand scattered with **giant diamonds** — except the diamonds are icebergs, and an hour ago they were **thousand-year-old glacier.**
block.point: A jeweller's window restocked twice a day by the tide — every gem a shard of a melting glacier.
block.mic: Diamonds that cost nothing, last an hour, and used to be a glacier. Only in Iceland.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Rain on black sand and clear ice is the whole point. Wet feet, better pictures."
bullets: When bergs in Jökulsárlón finally shrink small enough, they **float out the short Jökulsá river to the sea** — and the **tide flings them straight back** onto this black volcanic beach, **Fellsfjara** (part of **Breiðamerkursandur**).
Stranded on the black sand, the clear and blue ice glitters like **scattered diamonds** — hence the nickname. Every piece is **ancient glacier**, salt-polished and melting in front of you.
Because it's **tidal**, the beach **restocks itself every few hours** — no two visits match, and a berg you photograph now may be gone by afternoon.

One serious note: **never turn your back on the surf here.** The **Jökulsá river mouth has vicious currents and sneaker waves** — beautiful, and genuinely dangerous. Admire the ice; respect the water.
Every block out there is **old compressed glacier ice**, not frozen seawater — it was inside **Vatnajökull** for a very long time before turning up at your feet for ninety seconds of fame.

The names here are ancient and descriptive — **Breiðá**, **Breiðamerkursandur**, **Jökulsá** — and then there is **Diamond Beach**, which is English, recent and coined for visitors. It went through a very public argument in Iceland in **July 2019** about whether tourism was quietly renaming the coastline.

This sand is named after a farm. There was settlement on **Breiðamerkursandur** from about **1100 years ago**, and then the **Little Ice Age** — **Breiðamerkurjökull** advanced furthest in the **18th and 19th centuries** and at its maximum the ice front got to **within about 250 metres of the open sea**, taking everything in its path underneath it.
say: the black beach the tide throws the icebergs back onto
the black sands this beach is part of
the short river that carries the bergs out to the sea

block.title: 🏚️ Höfðabrekka
block.cue: Look right at 1 o'clock — the ridge above the sand, with the farm up on top.
block.hook: A farm that got picked up and moved because **the volcano kept aiming at it** — and the flood that did it is recorded almost hour by hour.
block.point: The volcano took the church and the farm in November 1660, so they rebuilt it further up the hill and stayed.
block.mic: In most countries a flood like that ends the settlement. Here it just changes the postcode.
block.weather: Weather pivot (if the slope is hidden): "The farm is up in that murk somewhere — which is exactly the point. It was deliberately put up out of the water's way."
bullets: **Höfðabrekka** stood on the low ground below this slope. On **3 November 1660** Katla's flood reached it — *"kom fram að Höfðabrekku jöklagangur með ofurmáta miklum vatnsþunga"* — and on the **8th–9th of November** the biggest wave *"sópaði burtu kirkju og bæjarhúsum að mestu"*: **it took the church and most of the farm buildings.**
They rebuilt it **up on the ridge itself** — where it still is, and where you are looking. The farm kept its name and changed its address.
That is the pattern along this whole coast, and it is worth naming: people here do not abandon a place, they **move it upslope and carry on.**
Everything between here and the sea is the reason — **Mýrdalssandur**, a black plain that exists because Katla has repeatedly emptied a glacier across it.
say: the farm rebuilt uphill after the 1660 flood
the glacial flood that took it

block.title: 🧊 Sveinn Pálsson
block.sub: The Country Doctor Who Worked Out How Glaciers Move
block.cue: Look ahead — Vík. He lived down there, at Suður-Vík, from 1809.
block.hook: In **1794** a country doctor stood in front of a glacier tongue and worked out something nobody in Europe had: **glaciers flow.** They are not frozen still. **They move like something thick and half-melted** — and he was about a century early.
block.point: The right answer about moving ice, written down in 1794 by a district doctor, and printed **105 years after he died.**
block.mic: He worked out how glaciers move while riding between farms in this weather — and the world got round to reading it in 1945.
block.weather: Weather pivot (if the ice is hidden): "It is all in there under the cloud. He was out in exactly this, on a horse, with a notebook."
bullets: **Sveinn Pálsson**, **1762–1840.** He took a **natural-sciences degree in Copenhagen in the spring of 1791** — the first person in Denmark to sit that exam — and went home meaning to come back and finish the medical half. He never did finish it. He doctored anyway, for the rest of his life.

In **1799** a new medical district was created covering **Árnessýsla, Rangárvallasýsla, Vestur-Skaftafellssýsla and the Westman Islands.** He took it up in **1800**, moved to **Suður-Vík in Mýrdalur in 1809** — the village we are driving into — and stayed there until he died in **1840.**

The glaciers were his own time, not the job. At **Kvíárjökull in 1794** he looked at the curved cracks running across the ice and wrote that it had moved *"hálfbráðinn eða sem þykkt seigfljótandi efni"* — **half-melted, like a thick viscous substance.** That is the modern answer: ice deforms under its own weight and creeps downhill.

Europe never got to read it. His ***Ferðabók*** and the glacier treatise ***Jöklaritið*** **stayed in manuscript and were not printed until 1945**, translated by **Jón Eyþórsson, Pálmi Hannesson and Steindór Steindórsson**; the English edition came in **2004.** By 1945 the credit for glacier flow had long gone elsewhere.

And be accurate about the one guides get wrong: **he was not Iceland's first doctor.** That was his father-in-law, **Bjarni Pálsson**, the first *landlæknir*. Sveinn stood in as acting *landlæknir* himself, briefly, in **1803–04.**
say: the glacier tongue he described in 1794
the farm in Vík he lived on from 1809

block.title: ⚖️ Kjalarnes
block.cue: At Kjalarnes, foot of Esja.
block.hook: Iceland's world-famous parliament at Þingvellir? Not even the first. The original ran right here — set up by the founder's son. Nepotism: also a Viking value.
block.point: Þingvellir wasn't Kjalarnes moved house — it was something new and national. Kjalarnes just proved Icelanders could hold a parliament without a king.
block.mic: Kjalarnes did the homework. Þingvellir took the credit, the fame, and the tourists.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Esja above it decides the visibility. If the mountain has gone, so has the headland."
bullets: **Þorsteinn Ingólfsson** — the first settler's son — held the **Kjalarnesþing** before Þingvellir's famous **930**. **Ari fróði** is the only near-contemporary source and he puts it right here: *"en áðr var þing á Kjalarnesi"*. Tradition then has him **consecrating** the big one. Build the prototype, bless the franchise. **The snag: no assembly has ever been found on Kjalarnes.** **Jónas Hallgrímsson** examined **Leiðvöllur** here in **1841** and called it a footpath; the national register still lists it *sést ekki* — nothing to see. The ruins he did find were **fourteen kilometres away at Þingnes on Elliðavatn**, protected since **1930** as *hinn forni Kjalarnessþingstaður*, and the join between the two has **never been proven**.

Laws? They sent one man — **Úlfljótr** — to Norway for **three years** to copy the **Gulating law**. He came home with Iceland's first law code, minus one feature: **the king**. Stole the software, deleted the boss.

Bonus first, same ness: Iceland's **earliest recorded church** — built by an Irishman around **900**, a century before we officially converted. Archaeologists dug: old buildings, **no church**. The paperwork outlived the building. Very relatable.

The landlord: **Helgi bjóla** — his own saga calls him "not much of a heathen sacrificer," which explains the church-building Irish tenants. His land claim? One source gives him a strip, the other the whole coast. Iceland's first property dispute. Still open.
say: sent to Norway for three years to bring back Iceland's first law code
the farm with the earliest church in the written record, built by Örlygur c. 900
the assembly held before Alþingi; Ari places it right here on Kjalarnes
the ness we're crossing, settled by Helgi bjóla
the settler, "not much of a heathen sacrificer"
the first settler's son, who set it up

block.title: 🕳️ Hvalfjörður Tunnel
block.cue: Entering the tunnel — nothing to see for a few minutes, so here's what you're inside.
block.hook: In a moment you'll have **40 metres of North Atlantic directly over your head**. Your ears will notice before you do.
block.point: Six kilometres of hole took two years and 4.63 billion krónur — and deleted an entire fjord from the driving day.
block.mic: The Hvalfjörður Tunnel — where Iceland trades picturesque fjords for efficiency and slightly damp rock faces.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Nothing to see in here whatever the weather, which is why I am talking."
bullets: The numbers, because they're the whole show down here: **5,770 metres long** — roughly **63 blue whales stacked nose-to-tail**, because Iceland loves its whales — and **3,750 of them run under the sea**. Deepest point: **165 metres below sea level**, with up to **40 metres of water** over the roof. If you're claustrophobic, just pretend you're in a very damp IKEA car park.

Blasting started from both ends in 1996, the crews met in the middle, and it opened *ahead of schedule* on **11 July 1998** — the same year *Titanic* won Best Picture. Coincidence? Probably. Cost: **4,630 million krónur** at 1996 prices… or one slightly used volcano.

Before the tunnel, driving round the fjord took **an hour**. Now: about **7 minutes** — enough time to recite the Icelandic alphabet (*good luck*), explain why Björk's swan dress was *art*, and question your life choices as you descend into literal darkness. One single tube, by the way — because why build two when you can play chicken with oncoming traffic?

Designed for 5,000 vehicles a day; now about **8,800** use it like a drive-thru for fermented shark, and the toll went in **2018**. There's serious talk of a second tube — imagine two straws in a milkshake, but the milkshake is made of basalt.
say: "Whale fjord," the water we're driving under
Iceland's currency; 4.63 billion of them, at 1996 prices, bought this hole

block.title: 🐋 Hvalfjörður
block.sub: The Whale With a Grudge and the Island of 180 Outlaws
block.cue: Emerging from the north portal — the fjord you just drove under runs away to your right, at 3 o'clock.
block.hook: How does a fjord get named "Whale fjord"? Officially: whales. In the folklore: **one specific whale** — with a red head, a grudge, and a body count.
block.point: A fjord that hunted whales, hosted a world war, and now gets skipped by everyone in a hurry. Nothing here is ordinary water.
block.mic: That little island held a hundred and eighty outlaws, according to the saga. When an archaeologist dug for their graves in 1881, he found nothing at all. The fjord kept the names and ate the evidence.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the fjord has gone in the murk, you have still driven under it, which is the more impressive fact."
bullets: The folklore — filed as folklore, from Jón Árnason's collection: a man refused to acknowledge his child by an elf-woman, and was turned into an evil whale with a red head — **Rauðhöfði**. He smashed **nineteen boats** before two priests conjured him up the fjord — thereafter **Hvalfjörður** — and into the lake above — thereafter **Hvalvatn**. Whale bones "are said" to have been found up there. *Said.*

The waterfall he was forced up: **Glymur**, named for the din. **198 metres**, long held to be Iceland's highest — a rival was measured taller in 2011, never confirmed. Glymur is contesting the ruling.

The island: **Geirshólmi**. Harðar saga puts **180 outlaws** on it, until the local farmers lured them ashore and killed them at **Þyrilsnes** — dated **986**. Hörður's wife **Helga** swam for it with her two boys; the sound is still called **Helgusund**.

The digging: **1881**, an archaeologist opens the grave-mound — *"nothing there."* The island: **no trace of any building**. A hundred and eighty men, zero evidence. The honest version — and the better story.

Then the 20th century: from **1940** the fjord hid Allied convoys — and Geirshólmi, island of outlaws, spent the war as a **gunnery target**. Aggro level: maximum. Postcard-serenity: also maximum. Very Hvalfjörður.
say: Whale lake, where the story ends
the 198 m waterfall named for the din of the whale going up
the outlaw island, dug 1881, nothing found
the sound Helga swam with her two boys
the ness where the 180 were killed

block.title: ⛰️ Akrafjall
block.sub: A Whale Bone at 85 Metres, and Two Irish Brothers
block.cue: Look left at 9–10 o'clock — Akrafjall, the free-standing mountain past the tunnel.
block.hook: There is a **whale bone in that mountain, 85 metres above the sea**. Nobody carried it up there. The sea delivered.
block.point: Read the mountain like a filing cabinet: a magnetic flip at 350 metres, a drowned-world beach at 105, a whale at 85, and two Irish farmers at the bottom. Geography keeps minutes.
block.mic: Twelve thousand years ago the sea cut a beach into that mountain, a hundred metres above where it is now — and left a whale bone at 85 metres. Sea level is not a fixed opinion.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "A free-standing mountain is the first thing the cloud takes. It will be back."
bullets: Twelve to thirteen thousand years ago, in the **Bølling** warm spell, the land was still pressed flat under the weight of the ice sheet and the sea stood correspondingly high — high enough to cut a **wave-cut notch into Akrafjall at 105–125 metres** above today's sea level. And a **whale bone has been found at 85 metres** up the mountain. That's a beach line and its residents, parked the height of a church spire above the modern shore.

Same rock as Esja: the lavas here erupted between about **4.5 and 3 million years ago**, one continuous basalt sheet with the mountain across the water — until glaciers cut **Hvalfjörður out of the middle of it, 2.5–3 million years ago**. Esja and Akrafjall aren't neighbours; they're the two halves of the sandwich the ice ate.

Hidden bonus: the **Gilbert/Gauss magnetic reversal** — the Earth's field flipping over, **3.6 million years ago** — is recorded in the mountain at about **350 metres elevation**. A compass error, archived in basalt.

The people: written tradition — Landnámabók, so tradition, not archaeology — says that shortly after **880** two brothers came **from Ireland**: **Þormóður and Ketill, sons of Bresi**, Irish-born, Norwegian descent. They claimed all of Akranes and drove out the family already living there. Þormóður farmed at **Innri-Hólmur**, the last farm before the tunnel; where Ketill settled, the sources disagree — even Akranes's own town history says "uncertain." A thousand years on, and we still haven't sorted the brothers' addresses.

The clue they left is in the names: **Akranes, Akrafjall, Akrakot, Garðar** — a cluster of grain-field place names, cited as evidence the Irish brothers actually grew corn here. The map remembers the harvest.
say: the mountain at 9 o'clock with the whale bone at altitude
"corn-field ness," the town on the ness beyond it
the Irish brother who farmed at Innri-Hólmur
the other brother, of no fixed historical address
Þormóður's farm, the last one before the tunnel
the Book of Settlements; written tradition, not archaeology

block.title: 🌉 Borgarfjarðarbrú
block.cue: Crossing Borgarfjarðarbrú — Hafnarfjall at 3 o'clock, Borgarnes dead ahead.
block.hook: Before 1981, the Ring Road took a **four-kilometre detour inland** to get across this water. Then we built **520 metres of bridge** and kept the change.
block.point: Four kilometres of detour, deleted by 520 metres of bridge — and on the far side, the town where Egils saga buries its dead.
block.mic: The bridge is 520 metres long and opened on the 13th of September 1981. Before that the Ring Road went four kilometres inland to cross the river. We are not a nation that enjoyed those four kilometres.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The bridge works in any weather. That was rather the argument for building it."
bullets: **520 metres** — preparation started in **1975**, and it opened on **13 September 1981**, at the time the **second-longest bridge in Iceland**, after Skeiðarárbrú. (Silver medal, but this one you actually drive over on the way west.)
Before the bridge, the Ring Road crossed the Hvítá about **four kilometres upstream**. Every single journey west paid that tax, both ways, for decades — until 520 metres of concrete cancelled it.

Under the water: the whole Borgarfjörður lowland was once sea floor — the flats around here are **marine sand and clay** lying between basalt knolls. You're bridging a fjord that's mostly given up being one.

And now, the pocket name. The town ahead is **Borgarnes** — but in Egils saga it's called **Digranes**, and it is, with no exaggeration, a **graveyard**. Egill's grandfather, his father, his foster-mother, his son — the saga buries its whole first act on these headlands. Full story at the stop. Yes, the stop with the toilets. We're a practical people.
say: the 520 m bridge we're crossing, opened 1981
the mountain at 3 o'clock as we come in
the river the old Ring Road crossed four kilometres upstream
the only bridge in Iceland that was longer at the time
the town ahead; in Egils saga, Digranes

block.title: 🪦 Borgarnes
block.sub: The Graveyard Chapters of Egils Saga
block.cue: At the N1, Borgarnes.
block.hook: Toilet stop, yes — but you are parked inside a **saga graveyard**. Nearly everyone in the first act of Egils saga is buried within sight of this forecourt.
block.point: The saga names every headland here — and every dig comes up empty. The names have outlasted the bones by a thousand years, which is a kind of immortality the bones never managed.
block.mic: This town is called Borgarnes now. In Egils saga it's Digranes, and it's a graveyard — Skallagrímur was rowed out at high tide and buried with his horse, his weapons and his smith's tools. People have dug into that mound. Nothing has ever been found in it.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Grey and windy is Borgarnes most days. The saga written here is not a cheerful one either."
bullets: Housekeeping before the corpses: **toilets are here**, and this is the **last stop before Arnarstapi** — a good long leg — so whatever you're debating, resolve it in favour of going. The schedule waits for nobody and neither does the coach.

The town in the saga is **Digranes**. **Skallagrímur** — Egill's father — took the land "between mountain and shore," named his farm **Borg** and the fjord **Borgarfjörður**; his man **Grani** got the land at Digranes and built **Granastaðir** — which, by the local reading, makes Grani's household the first inhabitants of what is now Borgarnes. Skallagrímur's own farm, **Borg á Mýrum**, is still there — church and farm, visible north-west of town. A settlement claim you can check from the car park.

**Kveldúlfur's coffin.** Egill's grandfather died at sea on the voyage out — and ordered his crew to put him overboard *in a coffin*, telling his son to settle wherever it washed ashore. They later found the cove where the coffin landed, carried it onto the ness, and piled stones over it. Local tradition points at **Kveldúlfshöfði**, just south of town — with the honest hedge that it's "not fully clear" where the coffin actually beached. Either way: this family's estate agent was a dead man in a floating box.

**Brák.** Skallagrímur, mid-berserk rage during a ball game, seized the boy Egill — and the woman who stepped in was Egill's foster-mother, **Þorgerður brák**. He chased her to the outer end of Digranes; she leapt from the cliff and swam for it; he hurled a great stone that struck her between the shoulders, "and neither came up again." The sound below the old town is still called **Brákarsund**. A servant woman, drowned a thousand years ago — and her name is on the water and half the street signs. Iceland picks its heroes carefully.

The town itself, in one breath: first house built **1857** by a Scot called **James Ritchie** — no relation, probably — for canning salmon; trading licence **1867** after 212 locals signed the petition. Population when Ritchie arrived: effectively zero. Now: the saga capital of the west.

**Skallagrímur's mound.** When his turn came, his body was taken out through a **hole broken in the house wall**, rowed out at high tide, and buried on the point of the ness **with his horse, his weapons and his smith's tools**. Years later Egill reopened the mound and laid his drowned son **Böðvar** beside him — the scene in the 1970 bronze relief in **Skallagrímsgarður**, two minutes' walk from here. The mound is a protected monument. It has been dug into, more than once. **Nothing — no bones, no artefacts — has ever been found in it.** That's the honest version, and it's a better story.

If the graves whet the appetite: the **Settlement Centre** down by the harbour opened on **13 May 2006** and tells this exact saga. And one closing twist — **Snorri Sturluson**, the man widely believed to have *written* Egils saga, married the heiress of Borg and lived there from **1201**. The suspected author, living on the story's home farm. Write what you know.
say: its saga name; the ness of the mound and the cliff
Egill's grandfather, who chose the family address from inside a coffin
Egill's father, buried with horse, weapons and smith's tools
Egill's foster-mother, drowned off the ness
the sound that carries her name
Egill's drowned son, laid in the mound beside Skallagrímur
Skallagrímur's farm, visible north-west of town
lived at Borg from 1201; widely believed to have written the saga
our next stop, and it's a long leg — hence the toilets

block.title: 🌋 Iceland's First Rift Zone
block.sub: The Volcanoes That Didn't Get the Memo
block.cue: Look ahead at 12 o'clock — the Snæfellsnes mountains, running west to the glacier.
block.hook: Why does this peninsula have volcanoes at all? The plate boundary **left six million years ago** — packed up, moved to Reykjanes — and Snæfellsnes **kept erupting anyway**. Most recently in the **10th century**. Some things don't take the hint.
block.point: You're driving down a plate boundary that officially closed six million years ago — and unofficially never stopped working.
block.mic: This is Iceland's *first* rift zone. It stopped rifting six million years ago, the spreading jumped south-east to Reykjanes — and Snæfellsnes kept erupting anyway, the last time in the tenth century. Retirement is a state of mind.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the peninsula has gone into cloud, you are looking at the rift anyway — you just cannot see the edges of it."
bullets: The whole ridge ahead is **Iceland's first rift zone** — the original crack, running through Snæfellsnes and north into Húnaflói. It stopped rifting about **6 million years ago**, and the spreading jumped south-east to **Reykjanes**, where all the recent fireworks are.

And then the peninsula ignored its own retirement. Volcanism restarted, and today Snæfellsnes carries **three volcanic systems**: **Ljósufjöll** in the east, little **Lýsuskarð** in the middle (**30 km by 5** — the runt of the litter), and **Snæfellsjökull** at the tip.

The eastern system is a rebel twice over: nearly every Icelandic volcanic system runs SW–NE, but this one runs **SE–NW** — at right angles to the active rift's fissures. (Iceland's spatial planning, ladies and gentlemen.)
The last eruption in any of the three: **the 10th century**, in the Ljósufjöll system. That's Settlement-era — there were farmers here watching it.
The glacier at the end of the road gets its own chapter this afternoon — we're driving straight at it. We've checked the omens; it's fine.
say: the peninsula we're driving onto; Iceland's first, officially-retired rift zone
"Light Mountains," the eastern volcanic system, the one that erupted in the 10th century
the small middle system, 30 km by 5
the glacier-volcano at the tip, last eruption about 1,800 years ago, still active
the peninsula that took over the spreading job six million years ago

block.title: 🔥 Hítardalur & Ljósufjöll
block.sub: Ninety Kilometres of One Bad Idea
block.cue: Look right at 2–3 o'clock — the hyaloclastite ridges of the Ljósufjöll system.
block.hook: Everything on your right for the next while — one volcanic system. **Ninety kilometres** of it, from Kolgrafarfjörður all the way back to Borgarfjörður. And in **1148** it hosted the deadliest fire in Icelandic history — at a **dinner party**.
block.point: One volcanic system owns ninety kilometres of this view — and its quietest valley still managed the deadliest fire in the country's history, no eruption required.
block.mic: Hítardalur is the site of the deadliest fire in Icelandic history — a bishop and roughly eighty guests, at a feast, in 1148. In Iceland, even the dinner parties make the annals.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Ridges in flat light lose their shape. Look for the skyline rather than the detail."
bullets: The **Ljósufjöll system** runs nearly **90 km** WNW–ESE, and its lavas have travelled **at least 15 km** from the mountains — as far as the mouth of Hvammsfjörður on the far side. One system, most of the horizon.

The ridge itself is mostly **móberg** — hyaloclastite. During ice ages it erupted *under* the glacier and built ridges of consolidated volcanic glass; between ice ages the lavas ran down the valleys. Same volcano, two completely different products, depending on whether there was a lid on.

Some of it is uncomfortably fresh: **Hólmshraun** in Hítardalur may have flowed **shortly before the settlement**, and its dated neighbours run about **2,600** and **3,600 years old**. In geology terms, the paint's still wet.

Now the history. **1148**, Hítardalur, up that valley on the right: Bishop **Magnús Einarsson** of Skálholt was at a feast when the building burned. The annals put the toll at **roughly eighty people**, the bishop among them — the deadliest fire in Icelandic history, and it happened at dinner.
