Hítardalur turns up again and again in **Sturlunga saga** — it was a staging post for anyone travelling to Mýrar from the west and north. Medieval Iceland's motorway services, with a body count.
say: the valley on the right where the 1148 feast fire happened
the bishop of Skálholt who died in the fire
hyaloclastite; volcanic glass welded into rock by eruptions under ice
the young lava in Hítardalur, possibly from just before the settlement

block.title: 🌋 Eldborg
block.cue: Look left at 9–10 o'clock — a low, perfectly regular ring rising out of the scrub.
block.hook: That ring on the left wasn't built by anyone. **200 metres long, 50 metres deep**, walls in places just a thin crust of lava — and the name says exactly what it looks like: **Eldborg**. Fire-fortress.
block.point: A fissure eruption that tidied itself into one perfect oval ring — so regular that the settlers just called it what it is: a fortress of fire.
block.mic: Two hundred metres long, fifty deep, and the walls in places are only a thin skin of lava crust. Eldborg is a fire-fortress — and that is literally what the name means.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "A low ring in low cloud is hard work. If it has gone, it is a crater the shape of a wedding ring."
bullets: **Eldborg** is an oval crater, about **200 m long and 50 m deep**, sitting mid-lava **38 km north of Borgarnes**. It's the textbook shape for this system: eruptions here open on a short fissure, then focus down into one big dome-shaped crater. The fissure is the draft; the crater is the final edit.

The Environment Agency records **two eruptions** here — the later one "most likely during the Settlement Age." That's the official wording, and we'll keep it: the honest answer to "when exactly?" is that nobody's published a firm date. Possibly the first settlers got a show.
Its lava, **Eldborgarhraun**, covers about **32 km²**, and the crater rim reaches **100 m above sea level** — with birch woodland around the base, which is rarer in a lava field than you'd hope.

Iceland thought enough of it to make it a **natural monument in 1974** — one of the earlier ones — **125 hectares**, protected year-round. There's a **3.4 km** trail to the rim from the farm Snorrastaðir. Not today, though. Today we have somewhere to be.
say: "fire-fortress," the oval crater ring on your left
the valley district it sits in
its lava field, about 32 square kilometres
the farm where the 3.4 km walking trail to the rim starts

block.title: 🪨 Gerðuberg
block.cue: Look right at 3 o'clock — a straight-ruled wall of basalt columns above the flowered slopes.
block.hook: Who stacked all those pillars? Nobody. That wall on the right did it to itself — and the reason it's **hexagons** is the same reason bees build hexagons: **geometry only offers so many options**.
block.point: Nobody carved these columns. Cooling rock shrinks, shrinking rock cracks, and the hexagon wins because it's the roundest shape that still fills a plane with no gaps.
block.mic: It's the same maths as a beehive. The bees do it in wax in a summer; the basalt did it in stone over years — and neither of them ever took a geometry class.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Columns show best in flat light, which is what we have. This one is improved by bad weather."
bullets: **Gerðuberg** is a belt of columnar basalt — *stuðlaberg* — running between two farms, with the slopes below it coming right down to the road. The columns look quarried, dressed, and stacked by a contractor with a level. They weren't. No hands involved.

Here's the mechanism, properly: basaltic melt is fully **solid at about 1,000 °C** — but it's still cooling after that, and cooling rock **contracts**. Shrinking solid rock has to crack. The cracks organise into columns, usually **six-sided**.

And they're hexagons because the hexagon is the shape **closest to a circle that still tiles a plane with no gaps**. Triangles and squares tile but aren't remotely circular; octagons are nicely round but leave gaps. The hexagon is the compromise candidate — and in geology, as in politics, the compromise candidate wins.

The columns always grow **perpendicular to the cooling surface** — and up close they carry horizontal "chisel marks," **1–2 cm** per groove, each one a record of a single cracking increment. The rock kept its own worksheet.

For a sense of the timescale: on Heimaey, a **40-metre-thick** lava took about **ten years** to cool and crack all the way through. A wall like this wasn't built in a day; it wasn't even *cooled* in a decade.
As for how tall Gerðuberg is exactly — I'd love to give you a number, but there's no official measurement published, and on this bus we don't invent figures, we just point at the wall.
say: the columnar basalt wall at three o'clock
the Icelandic word for columnar basalt
the island whose 40 m lava took ten years to cool and crack through

title: ⛰️ Vatnaleið
subject: vatnaleið

block.title: ⛰️ Vatnaleið
block.sub: The Quiet Leg Over the Spine
block.cue: All around — the Vatnaleið pass, Road 56.
block.hook: The road under you is exactly as old as **Wikipedia** — both launched in **2001** — and the flat-topped mountains beside it were built **under an ice sheet**. Brand-new tarmac, Ice Age scenery, no middle ground.
block.point: A road from 2001 across mountains poured under an ice sheet — Iceland keeps repaving; the geology stays put.
block.mic: A road from 2001 across mountains poured under an ice sheet — and the first waterfall of the day is waiting just over this pass.
block.weather: Weather pivot (if the mountains are invisible): "If the spine has vanished into cloud, fitting — móberg was made in the dark under an ice sheet. Being invisible is the most authentic thing it does."
bullets: **Road 56 — Vatnaleið**, "the lakes route" — is nearly the newest thing you'll touch today. The transport minister cut the ribbon on **Friday 2 November 2001**, standing down at Selvallavatn where we're headed, and the old **Kerlingarskarð** pass was retired that same day after generations of hauling traffic over the peninsula's spine. **16.4 km** of new road, topping out at **230 m** against Kerlingarskarð's **311 m** — and only **3 km** of it above 200 metres, where the old road had **ten**. We replaced the pass, not the mountains.

Those flat-topped mountains flanking the road are **móberg** — the same fought-a-glacier-and-lost rock from this morning's drive, now on both sides of you. The whole spine of Snæfellsnes is built of it, and the ice sheet that made it left ten thousand years ago. Never came back for its work.
**Baulárvallavatn** sits just west of the road — one of the lakes that gave the route its name. Quiet water, quiet leg.

Down in the bogs at the south end of **Sátudalur** two streams rise almost side by side and then immediately fall out. **Rauðusteinalækur** runs south into Baulárvallavatn and eventually reaches the sea as Straumfjarðará. **Fossá** runs north, over the waterfall we're stopping at — and then vanishes completely. I'll show you where in about ten minutes.

**Road 56 — Vatnaleið**, "the lakes route" — is nearly the newest thing you'll touch today: built in **2001**, when it retired the old **Kerlingarskarð** pass that had hauled traffic over the peninsula's spine for generations. We replaced the pass, not the mountains.
Which is the theme now: decompression. You've had the glacier, the cliffs, the black beach and the lone striped mountain. This hour is yours — the entertainment bar was set high enough this morning.
say: the old pass this road retired
the lake just west of the road

rescued: 10.0: **Road 56 — Vatnaleið**, "the lakes route" — is nearly the newest thing you'll touch today
10.0: Which is the theme now: decompression. You've had the glacier, the cliffs, the black beach

block.title: 💧 Fossá
block.sub: The Waterfall Iceland Never Bothered to Name
block.cue: At the Vatnaleið viewpoint — the fall is below the road, the lake beyond it.
block.hook: Icelandic farmers named **everything**. Seventy-nine separate features on this one abandoned farm — every gully, every boulder, the rock where the hidden people sang. They did not name the waterfall. And the name on your map today? Somebody in tourism made it up.
block.point: The postcard version gives you a name, a height and a river. **All three are wrong.** What's actually here is better: the one waterfall in a country of obsessive namers that nobody could be bothered to name.
block.mic: Land the punchline slowly: the National Land Survey maps this fall, and leaves the name field blank. Let that sit for a beat before you move to the lake.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The fall is below the road, so the cloud has to come down a long way to take it."
bullets: Start with the river, because the internet gets this wrong constantly. This is **Fossá** — literally *"waterfall river."* It is **not** Straumfjarðará. Straumfjarðará rises in Baulárvallavatn, back the way we came, and runs the opposite direction to the sea at Straumfjörður. Different river, different catchment, different ocean-facing coast.

**Landmælingar Íslands**, the National Land Survey, has this fall in its database. Mapped, plotted, classified as *foss*. The name field is **blank**. Náttúrufræðistofnun holds the same point, also blank.

So I went looking. **Zero** hits for "Selvallafoss" in Árnastofnun's national place-name archive. **Zero** in the national mapping database — the only "Selval-" name in the whole country is the lake. **Zero** across the entire Icelandic newspaper corpus, which runs back well over two hundred years. "Selvallavatn" gets 71 hits. The waterfall gets none.

Meanwhile the place-name survey of the farm above us lists **Steinkarl**, **Nóngjá**, **Krummaklettar**, **Stóriklettur** — *"where the hidden people sang."* Seventy-nine names. They named a rock for its singing elves and left the waterfall alone.
I think the old answer was just simpler than ours: the river was **already** called *the waterfall river*. Naming the waterfall on the waterfall river is like opening a restaurant called Restaurant.

And no — **nobody has ever officially measured its height.** No figure in the national survey, none in the natural history institute, none in *Íslenskir fossar*, the standard reference on Icelandic waterfalls, which records two other falls in this district and skips this one. Every number you'll find online was typed by somebody with a website and a deadline. I'd rather give you nothing than give you a number I can't stand behind.

One last thing while we're demolishing: **sel** does not mean sheep, and it does not mean seal. A *sel* is a **shieling** — the summer dairy station where the milking animals went up the valley. **Selvellir** means *"the shieling flats."* In the **1700s** the farm Horn was split in two, and the new half was built on Horn's old shieling ground. The farm went empty in the **1920s** and never came back.
say: "waterfall river"; the river the fall is actually on
"the shieling flats"; the deserted farm above us
a shieling, the summer dairy station. Not a sheep. Not a seal.
the National Land Survey, which maps the fall with no name
the river this one is not

block.title: 🌀 Selvallavatn
block.sub: The Lake With No Way Out
block.cue: Same viewpoint — the lake in the hollow between the lava and the mountain wall.
block.hook: Water pours into this lake all day long. **Nothing flows out of it.** Not a stream, not a trickle, nothing above ground. Somewhere under that lava the whole lake is quietly draining away — and nobody has ever proved where it goes.
block.point: A lake fed by a river, sitting on porous lava, with **no way out** — and the only candidate explanation is a whirlpool a farm boy noticed and nobody ever followed up.
block.mic: The "perhaps" is the whole block. Deliver it as an open question, not a solved one — because it is one.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The lake sits in a hollow and holds mist. If it looks like it is steaming, it is not."
bullets: **Selvallavatn** sits at **62 metres** above sea level in a hollow between Berserkjahraun and the mountain wall. Fossá runs in on the east, small becks run in on the south. And that is the entire hydrological story, because there is **no outflow above ground.** None.

The man who wrote down the place-names here was **Lárus Halldórsson**, born on the farm above us in **1920**. Going back over the survey he added a feature the earlier recorder had missed: **Rás** — a swallow-hole at the lava's edge *"where the water is sucked in a whirlpool down into the lava."* Then he added one careful sentence: **perhaps that is the answer to the riddle of Selvallavatn's outflow.**

*Perhaps.* He left it open. And as far as I can find, in the eighty-odd years since, **nobody has closed it.** No dye trace, no survey, no paper. A lake disappearing into a lava field, and the last word on it is a farmer's son saying "maybe."
It hasn't always been Selvallavatn either. The old name in the record is **Svínavatn** — *pig lake.* Less romantic, and it clearly lost the marketing meeting.

There's **brown trout and Arctic charr** in it — the trout run a solid **three to six pounds**, and on summer evenings shoals of small charr work along the lava edge. In a dry spell the water level can drop by **a metre and a half**.

How big is it? Genuinely nobody agrees. The standard Icelandic reference says **0.85 km²**. The national mapping database maps the shoreline at **0.30 km²**. That is a factor of nearly three, on a lake you can see the whole of from here, and I am not going to pretend I can settle it. **Maximum depth: never surveyed at all.**

The lay-by you are standing on isn't an accident, by the way. When Vatnaleið was built, an **architect** was brought in to design this viewpoint — and in **2003** the whole road took **Vegagerðin's first-ever award** for construction and finish, with the jury singling out this spot. Congratulations. You are standing on an award-winning lay-by.
The lake, Berserkjahraun and the neighbouring waters are all on the **Náttúruminjaskrá**, Iceland's nature conservation register, as item **227**.
say: "pig lake," what it used to be called
literally "channel"; the swallow-hole where the water goes down

block.title: 🪨 Berserkjahraun
block.sub: The Severance Package Was a Bath
block.cue: Crossing the rust-red lava on Road 54 — Berserkjahraun on both sides.
block.hook: Iceland's first recorded construction contract: clear a road through this lava and marry the farmer's daughter. **The contractors finished the job. They should have read the fine print.**
block.point: A 4,000-year-old lava field, a 1,000-year-old road, and the oldest lesson in construction: **get paid up front.**
block.mic: Two berserkers built the first road through here. The pay was a farmer's daughter — and the severance package was a bath they never left.
block.weather: Weather pivot (if the craters are hidden): "No red craters today — but the lumps under the moss either side of us are the berserkers' lava, and this road is doing exactly what their path did."
bullets: Erupted about **4,000 years ago** from a row of **scoria cones of the Ljósufjöll volcanic system** — **Rauðakúla, Gráakúla, Smáhraunakúla and Kothraunskúla** — rough **aa lava** that crawled to the sea at **Bjarnarhöfn** and **Hraunsfjörður** and has been gathering moss ever since.

**Eyrbyggja Saga** supplies the labour dispute: two **Swedish berserkers** were promised a farmer's daughter if they could clear a path through the lava. **They succeeded** — whereupon their master **Víga-Styrr** had them killed, **unarmed, in the bath**, and buried in the lava.

The path — **Berserkjagata** — is **still clearly visible** a thousand years on, and there is a stone cairn beside it the saga calls their grave. Careful here: the antiquarian **Sigurður Vigfússon** only **examined** it (1889 survey, published **1893**), and a local farmer **re-stacked it** in the mid-20th century. **Minjastofnun records no excavation and no bones.** The road is the evidence. The grave is the story.
say: the saga-era path they cleared, still visible
the saga that recorded the whole grim bargain
the master who ordered the bath
the volcanic system the craters belong to

block.title: 🦈 Bjarnarhöfn
block.sub: The Man Who Refused to Settle
block.cue: Look right — the farm cluster and the little white church under Bjarnarhafnarfjall.
block.hook: The man who took that land was called **Björn the Easterner** — and he got the name because he **refused to settle in the west.**
block.point: A man named for the direction he wouldn't go, a church that outlived its own siblings, and a fish that has to rot correctly before it is safe.
block.mic: Iceland's most notorious food, and the honest version is duller than the myth: no urine, no gravel, just a box with drainage and a great deal of patience.
block.weather: Weather pivot (if the farm is hidden): "You can't see it today — but it is under that mountain, and it is where the shark you may be brave enough to try tonight was hung up to dry for three months."
bullets: *Landnámabók* is blunt about it. Björn, son of **Ketill flatnefur**, was driven off the family's Norwegian estates by **King Haraldur hárfagri**, went west over the sea, *"og vildi þar ekki staðfestast"* — **and would not settle there.** So they named him for the direction he wouldn't stop facing.

He took the land between **Hraunsfjörður** and **Stafá**, kept a magnificent household — and **died unbaptised**, the only one of Ketill's children who never took the faith. No churchyard: a heathen mound by **Borgarlækur**. When an archaeologist went looking for it in **1900**, he found the stream had eaten both the mound and the farm. Nothing left to look at.
The genealogy is the gift: Björn → Óttar → Helgi → **Ósvífur hinn spaki** → **Guðrún Ósvífursdóttir**. **The most famous woman in the Icelandic sagas is his great-great-granddaughter.**

**The church is 1856–58** and is **the last of its kind standing.** One builder from Grundarfjörður put up three towered churches on this peninsula in the 1850s — Helgafell, Skarð and this one. **The other two are gone.** This one lost its tower around 1900 and survived precisely because nobody thought it worth replacing. Seven metres by four and a half, inside.

And the shark. **Everything you have heard about how it is made is wrong.** The Greenland shark **has no urinary system**, so urea builds up in the flesh and breaks down to **ammonia** — that is the toxin. **Nobody urinates on it.** Vísindavefur calls that idea *"mikill misskilningur."* At Bjarnarhöfn it ferments **six to eight weeks in slatted wooden boxes**, then hangs **six to eight weeks more** in the drying shed. Not buried in gravel, not any more.

In **2023 Matís** — the national food research institute — noted that **almost no scientific work had ever been done on how Icelanders make their national dish.** A thousand years of it, and the first proper study was a master's thesis, done with this farm.
say: 'Björn's harbour', the farm and church under the mountain
Björn the Easterner, who refused to settle in the west

block.title: ⛰️ Helgafell
block.sub: The Mountain You Walk Into When You Die
block.cue: Look right, far ahead across the lava — Helgafell sits about fifteen kilometres that way, out of sight.
block.hook: There is a mountain out there that people believed they went **into** when they died — and one autumn evening a shepherd stood on the hill and watched **the north side open up.**
block.point: A mountain people expected to be welcomed into, a chieftain who did his thinking on top of it, and a wish ritual that is younger than the Beatles.
block.mic: The honest version lands harder than the tourist one: the sagas are a thousand years old, and the bit in every guidebook was written down in 1955.
block.weather: Weather pivot (Helgafell is never visible from this road): "You won't see it from here in any weather — it's fifteen kilometres east, behind that ground. But that is the direction, and this is the story that goes with it."
bullets: **Þórólfur Mostrarskegg** held it so sacred that **no one was to look at it unwashed**, and nothing on it — beast or man — was to be harmed. *"Það var trúa þeirra Þórólfs frænda, að þeir dæi allir í fjallið"* — **he and his kin believed they would all die into the mountain.**

*Eyrbyggja saga*, chapter 11: a shepherd north of Helgafell **saw the mountain open**, saw great fires inside, and **heard Þorsteinn þorskabítur being welcomed in and told to sit in the high seat facing his father.** Next morning men rode in from Höskuldsey with the news. **Þorsteinn had drowned that day.**

**Snorri goði** — remember him — farmed there **thirty-one years**, and when he had a problem he walked up it: *"Þau ráð hafa síst að engu orðið er þar hafa ráðin verið"* — **"the plans laid up there have least often come to nothing."** It is where he and Víga-Styrr sat the day they decided what to do about the berserkers.

He is also **the man who ended the argument at the conversion.** When a messenger reported lava flowing and the heathens cried that the gods were angry, Snorri asked: *"Um hvað reiddust goðin þá, er hér brann hraunið, er nú stöndum vér á?"* — **"What were the gods angry about, then, when the lava we are standing on was burning?"** That is *Kristni saga*, and it is the same man from this hillside.

**Be careful with the three wishes.** Walk in silence from Guðrún's grave, don't look back, don't tell anyone — every guidebook prints it. **The earliest written record of it is 1955.** The Icelandic living-heritage register says so plainly. It is real folklore and it is **younger than rock and roll.** It appears nowhere in Eyrbyggja or Laxdæla.

And the grave itself: the State's own protection register calls it **"leiði Guðrúnar Ósvífursdóttur, svo nefnt"** — **the *so-called* grave.** The one man who dug there, **W. G. Collingwood in 1897**, never gave the lecture he promised and never handed the finds in. **Nobody actually knows where she lies.**
say: 'holy mountain', just over 70 m high, east of here
the settler who made it sacred
the chieftain who farmed there 31 years
the saga that records the mountain opening
where his conversion line is actually written

block.title: 🌊 Kolgrafarfjörður
block.cue: We're crossing it now — the causeway and bridge across Kolgrafarfjörður.
block.hook: On the water we are crossing right now, **about fifty thousand tonnes of herring suffocated** across two winters. **There is no comparable event recorded anywhere on Earth.**
block.point: Fifty thousand tonnes of fish drowned themselves in a fjord, twice, six weeks apart — and the second time it was the first lot's fault.
block.mic: Everyone blames the bridge. The engineers spent three years measuring and said no: the wind dropped, the fish used up the oxygen, and then the dead ones finished the job.
block.weather: Weather pivot (if it is grey and flat): "Flat calm like this is exactly the condition that did it — no wind to stir oxygen back into the water."
bullets: The fjord was crossed in **2004** — an embankment and a bridge with a water opening of about **150 metres**, shortening the road to Stykkishólmur by six kilometres. Inside it the fjord is about **10 km²** and up to **40 m** deep.

The herring came back after a long absence. They **began wintering in southern Breiðafjörður in 2006**, having been gone since roughly **1940**. By **2008** Hafrannsóknastofnun measured **800,000 to 900,000 tonnes** in the bay. **The day before it happened, close to 300,000 tonnes of live herring were sitting in this one fjord.**

**13–14 December 2012: around 25–30,000 tonnes died.** Then **1 February 2013: another 22,000.** Cause — **oxygen depletion**. Prolonged calm, cold weather, and simply too much fish in too small a space. And once December's dead began to rot, **the decomposition ate the remaining oxygen**, which is why it happened again six weeks later.

**Now the correction, because everyone blames the bridge.** Verkfræðistofan Vatnaskil reported for Vegagerðin on **21 October 2015**: **the causeway was not the cause.** It may marginally worsen oxygen levels during a huge influx in bad conditions, but the effect is **negligible** against what the herring themselves did — and **worse conditions have occurred since with no die-off.**

The aftermath was biblical. Thousands of tonnes of rotting fat coated the shore. Birds came in tens of thousands — gulls, shags, cormorants, gannets, eiders, ravens — **and a large part of Iceland's entire white-tailed eagle population.**
say: the fjord we're crossing, causeway built 2004
Iceland's Marine and Freshwater Research Institute
the Icelandic Road Administration, who commissioned the 2015 study
the great bay the herring came back into

title: ⛰️ Kirkjufell
subject: kirkjufell

block.title: ⛰️ Kirkjufell
block.cue: Ahead on the spit — the lone striped peak, with Kirkjufellsfoss by the car park.
block.hook: Half this bus already has this mountain as a screensaver. My job isn't to introduce it — **it's to correct it.**
block.point: Nobody built Kirkjufell up. The ice subtracted an entire landscape — and left the best bit standing.
block.mic: It survived the ice age and it survived HBO. It will survive your two hundred photographs — take them.
block.weather: Weather pivot (if cloud hides it): "The mountain is in there — 463 metres of it, modelling for radar today. Kirkjufellsfoss works at ground level all year; start there."
bullets: **463 metres**, standing alone on a spit — about **130 metres taller than the Eiffel Tower** — and the trick isn't height, it's **isolation**: nothing beside it to spoil the silhouette.

The stripes are the whole geology lesson: **alternating lava and sediment**, stacked through successive ice ages, then **carved by glaciers into a lone nunatak** — rock that kept its head above the ice sheet. **Not a volcano.** No crater, no magma; the ice cut everything else down around it.

The name is **Kirkjufell — 'church mountain'** — centuries older than television. *Game of Thrones* (seasons **6 and 7**) only ever calls it **"the mountain shaped like an arrowhead"** — a line in a script, not a name. Danish sailors called it **Sukkertoppen**, the sugar top. Church: original. Arrowhead: fan fiction. Sugar: the Danes were hungry.
**Kirkjufellsfoss**, the little three-tier falls, sits in the foreground like a location scout placed it. **It was ice.** Ten minutes of walking, a lifetime of screensavers.

One duty line: the climb is officially rated **very demanding and dangerous**, with **fatal accidents on record — the most recent in October 2022**. We admire from the waterfall; the summit belongs to equipped mountaineers.

The name is **Kirkjufell — "church mountain"** — centuries older than television. *Game of Thrones* (seasons **6 and 7**) only ever calls it **"the mountain shaped like an arrowhead"** — a line in a script, not a name. Danish sailors called it **Sukkertoppen**, the sugar top. Church: original. Arrowhead: fan fiction. Sugar: the Danes were hungry.
say: the three-tier falls in every postcard
the fishing town next door, roughly 900 people
the Danish sailors' nickname: "the sugar top"
rock that stood above the ice sheet while glaciers planed the rest

rescued: 10.0: The name is **Kirkjufell — "church mountain"** — centuries older than television. *Game of

block.title: 🐚 Búlandshöfði
block.sub: Where Iceland Found Out the Ice Age Had Summers
block.cue: We're driving under it now — the headland the road is cut into, sea on your left.
block.hook: This headland is where geologists proved the Ice Age **wasn't one long winter.** The evidence is seashells — sitting **high above the sea.**
block.point: A cliff full of seashells far above the waterline — and the reason we know the Ice Age came and went rather than simply lasting.
block.mic: Most roadside cliffs are scenery. This one is a textbook, and the chapter it wrote is that the ice had summers.
block.weather: Weather pivot (if the top is in cloud): "The fossil beds are up in that cloud — honest enough, because you couldn't pick them out on a clear day either without someone pointing."
bullets: High in this cliff are **marine fossil beds** — shells, laid down on a seabed — now stranded far above the present shore, and **sealed under lava dated to roughly 1.1 million years.**

That is the whole argument. Shells mean **open, ice-free sea.** Lava on top means an eruption came afterwards. Stack the layers and you are reading **warm interglacials sandwiched between cold stages** — the Ice Age switching on and off, written into a cliff face.
It made Búlandshöfði **a classic site in Icelandic Quaternary geology.** Generations of students have been driven out here to look at the rock above your window.
Honest caveat: **you cannot pick the shell beds out from the road.** They are high in the face and you need someone standing next to you pointing. Point at the cliff, not at a layer.

The road has its own reputation. Before it was rebuilt this was **one of the most notorious stretches in the country** — a narrow shelf between the mountain and a long drop — and there is a **memorial stone at the top** for the reason you would expect.
*Eyrbyggja saga* calls the screes below **Þrælaskriður** — **Slave Screes.** Not a metaphor. Two men went off here in the saga, and the saga is quite specific about why.
say: the headland the road is cut into
'Slave Screes', the saga's name for the slopes below

block.title: 🧙 Mávahlíð
block.sub: The Witch Trial That Went the Other Way
block.cue: Look left, inland — the farm under the fell.
block.hook: A woman on that farm was accused of riding a man to death in his sleep. **The case went to court — and she walked.**
block.point: Accused of witchcraft in the saga age, and the remedy was a court date rather than a fire.
block.mic: Iceland did burn people for witchcraft — three centuries later, and almost all of them men. Everything guests think they know about this is off by both.
block.weather: Weather pivot (if the fell is hidden): "The farm's in there somewhere under the cloud — still farmed, still called Mávahlíð, nine hundred years after the case."
bullets: **Geirríður** of **Mávahlíð** was accused of being a **kveldriða** — a night-rider — of riding a man in his sleep until he sickened and died. In most of medieval Europe that accusation had one ending.

Not here. The charge was brought to the **þing**, argued, and **Geirríður was acquitted** — the accuser could not make it stand. *Eyrbyggja saga* records the whole thing as a legal matter, because that is what it was.

Keep the chronology straight, because guests always ask about burnings. Iceland's actual witch-hunt was the **17th century** — the first burning for witchcraft was **1625**, the last **1685.** Of roughly **25 Icelanders** ever burned, the overwhelming majority were **men.**
So the picture people arrive with — medieval Iceland burning women — is the wrong century **and** the wrong gender. Here, in the saga age, the answer to a witchcraft accusation was a hearing.
say: 'seagull slope', the farm inland on your right
a 'night-rider', the thing she was accused of being

cuePerTour.9.0: Look left, inland — the farm under the fell.
cuePerTour.10.0: Look right, inland — the farm under the fell.

block.title: 👻 Fróðá
block.sub: The Ghosts We Took to Court
block.cue: Passing Fróðá, just east of Ólafsvík.
block.hook: How do you get rid of eighteen ghosts? Iceland's answer, year 1000: **take them to court.** Charges, pleadings, verdicts — and closing statements from the defendants.
block.point: Faced with the walking dead, our ancestors reached for the one weapon they truly trusted: **procedure**. Not the sword — the summons.
block.mic: Other nations exorcise their ghosts. We serve them papers. It's the most Icelandic thing in the entire saga corpus — and the ghosts respected the verdict.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "A haunted farm in driving rain is arguably the correct way to meet this story."
bullets: *Eyrbyggja saga*, chapters 50 to 55 — and it starts in the harbour we just left: the year **1000**, a ship from **Dublin** wind-bound **at Rif**. Aboard: **Þórgunna**, a Hebridean woman near sixty — tall, dark-browed, formidable — with bedding finer than anything Iceland had seen.

**Þuríður**, mistress of the farm **Fróðá** here — "greedy for finery and a great one for show," the saga's words, not mine — tried to buy the lot. Þórgunna's answer: **"I will not lie in straw for your sake."** So Þuríður moved her in and played the long game.

Þórgunna sickened and died. Her deathbed instruction was precise: **burn the bedding. All of it.** The husband burned the mattress and pillow — and kept the treasures. One act of greed, and the saga invoices everything that follows to it.

Then Fróðá came apart: a **seal's head rose out of the fire-pit** — out of the *fire* — staring at the hangings that should have burned, and every club-blow drove it **higher**. Drowned men walked into their **own funeral feast**, soaking wet. Of **thirty** in the household, **eighteen died** and five fled.

And the ending is *us*: **Snorri goði** sent a priest, yes — but the real remedy was a **door-court**. Every revenant formally **summoned, charged, tried and sentenced** at the door of the house. Each ghost rose as its verdict fell — Þórir wood-leg: **"We have sat while sitting could be borne."**

They burned the canopy, the priest sang the offices, the hauntings stopped — and Kjartan lived long at Fróðá and became "the greatest of champions." They didn't exorcise the ghosts. **They sued them.** And won.
say: the farm just east of Ólafsvík where the hauntings happened
the saga of this peninsula, source of the whole tale
the Hebridean woman whose bedding should have burned
the mistress of Fróðá who kept it anyway
the boy with the sledgehammer, feared by every ghost
the chieftain of Helgafell who prescribed the lawsuit
the "door-court" that tried the ghosts, one by one

block.title: ⚓ Ólafsvík
block.cue: Leaving Rif — Ólafsvík ahead in nine kilometres.
block.hook: How does a village lose everything? A river moves **once** — and a king in Copenhagen signs a licence for the neighbours.
block.point: No army touched these villages — a river moved, a licence moved, and two centuries of fortune moved with them.
block.mic: Two villages, nine kilometres apart: one's fortune was the other's loss — until the sea changed its mind. It usually does.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "A working fishing town does not close for weather. Neither does the harbour."
bullets: Housekeeping before anything else: the toilets here are the last until **Borgarnes**, roughly two hours away. If you're now re-examining your life choices, the ghost story coming up will take your mind off it.

**1687**: the Danish king licensed **Ólafsvík** as a trading place — because the harbour at **Rif** was silting up after the river **Hólmkelsá** shifted course. **Two villages, nine kilometres apart — one's fortune was the other's loss.**

Trade drained from Rif through the 1700s. Ólafsvík has held the royal licence continuously since 1687 — town rights **1983** — and the **Pakkhúsið**, the 1844 trading store, still stands by the harbour with the museum upstairs.

The kicker: around **1960** the harbour went *back* — Rif rebuilt as the district's main fishing harbour, 270-odd years after the river ruined it. Geography took three centuries to change its mind. It never apologises.

Geography took three centuries to change its mind, and it never apologises. Rif kept the boats; **Ólafsvík kept the trading licence** — and today the two villages sit **nine kilometres apart**, one fortune built on the other's loss.
say: the town ahead, royal trading licence since 1687
the river whose change of course silted Rif's harbour
"the Pack-House," the 1844 trading store, now the museum

cuePerTour.10.0: Leaving Rif — Ólafsvík ahead in nine kilometres.

block.title: 🪓 Björn the Rich
block.cue: Passing Rif on the right — the flat little harbour village on the point.
block.hook: What's more dangerous than being the richest man in Iceland? **Standing between English merchants and their cod.** In 1467, right here, the King of Denmark's own governor found out.
block.point: What's documented is one sentence: the king's governor, killed by English merchants at Rif, 1467, inside a genuine trade war over cod. Everything quotable arrived a century later.
block.mic: History gave us a sentence. Folklore gave us the barrels and the best comeback line in Icelandic history. Take both home — just keep the labels on.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Rif is flat and low, so it goes early in the murk. It is the point sticking out to the right."
bullets: **Björn Þorleifsson the Rich** — head of the Skarð family, one of the wealthiest houses in Iceland — sailed for Copenhagen in **1456**, got seized by Scots at Orkney on the way, and came out of the whole mess ennobled: **King Christian I** gave him a coat of arms — a **white bear on a blue field** — and made him ***hirðstjóri***, governor of Iceland, **for life**. "For life" turned out to be the operative clause.

In **1466** the king banned the English from trading in Iceland. The English ignored him — they had a trading post here and cod is cod. In **1467**, English merchants killed Björn at Rif. What he was doing here, nobody wrote down; later sources say his son had been seized and he came to free him. His death sat inside a real Anglo-Danish trade war, settled by treaty in **1473**. Icelandic historians file the whole era under *Ten Cod Wars, 1415–1976* — this was an early round.

Now the folklore layer, and I'll label it: the **axe-mark on Björnssteinn**, the body **cut in seven pieces and sent to his widow in barrels**, and her answer — **"Do not weep for farmer Björn — gather men instead."** Every one of those details was **first written down more than a century after the event**, in the late 1500s, with what the scholars politely call a strong folk-tale colouring. The record gives us one line; folklore wrote the screenplay.

His widow, **Ólöf the Rich Loftsdóttir**, needs no embroidery anyway: the king's own letter to the King of France calls her *mulier spectabilis* — "a distinguished woman." Royal correspondence rated her before the barrels ever entered the story.
And a footnote for the pedants (I am one): even the **information sign at the stone** gets the war wrong — its five-year war ending in 1474 doesn't stand up. Trust the stone; check the sign.
say: "Björn the Rich," the governor killed here in 1467
his widow, "Ólöf the Rich," of the famous line
"Björn's stone," where the story is anchored
the king's governor of Iceland, Björn's title
the family seat that made them "the Skarð family"

block.title: 🐦 The Tern Capital
block.cue: All around — the wetland between Rif and Hellissandur.
block.hook: Anyone here fly in from further away than the edge of **Antarctica**? No? Then every one of us has been out-travelled by the small white birds nesting beside the car park.
block.point: Two villages, **under 500 humans** between them, **17,000 nests** — the birds outnumber everyone here on a normal day. Today we brought reinforcements, and it's still close.
block.mic: You crossed an ocean to be here and you're feeling adventurous. The bird on the fence line came from Antarctica — and she does it annually.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "In wind the terns hang almost motionless. They are the easiest thing to see out there today."
bullets: This wetland holds **17,000 nests** of arctic tern — the **biggest single colony in Iceland**, by a distance, and big enough to qualify as **internationally important**. For scale: the runner-up colonies on this peninsula are Arnarstapi at **850** nests and Kvíabryggja at **500**. That's not first place. That's a different league.
The commute: some of these birds winter at the **edge of Antarctica** and fly here to breed — pole-ish to pole-ish, twice a year, every year, on a wingspan you could cover with a tea towel.

By **12 August** the breeding season is mostly done — which is the only reason we can stand this close in peace. In June, the *kría* runs an air force here, and trespassers get personally escorted out by the head. The rule stands anyway: **stay out of the marked colony area.** They've earned the fence.

One more thing about these particular birds — they weigh **about 110 grams** and they fly **pole to pole**. That commute is the longest migration of any animal on Earth, and it is being done by something lighter than a mobile phone.
One more thing about these particular birds — at **17:45 the lights go out on them too**. Hold that thought. It comes back in about an hour, and when it does, you're part of it.
say: the arctic tern; the word sounds like the noise it makes at your head
home of the peninsula's third-place colony, 500 nests

cuePerTour.9.0: Still passing Rif — look at the roadside posts for the terns.

block.title: ⛪ Hellissandur, Ingjaldshóll & the Columbus Story
block.cue: Look left at 8 o'clock — Hellissandur, with the church at Ingjaldshóll on its hill beyond.
block.hook: There's a painting of **Christopher Columbus** in the parish hall on that hill. The entire paper trail behind it runs through **a Danish short story serialised in a Winnipeg newspaper in 1889.**
block.point: Remember Guðríður, back at Laugarbrekka? This peninsula's genuine transatlantic claim was born on a farm we passed an hour ago — and the imported one arrived by short story, via Winnipeg. We'll keep the real one.
block.mic: There is a painting of Columbus in the parish hall here. The story behind it was written as a short story by a Danish novelist and printed in an Icelandic-American newspaper in Winnipeg in 1889. That is the whole documentary trail.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The church sits high on its mound, so it usually survives the cloud when the village has gone."
bullets: **Hellissandur** is reckoned **one of the oldest fishing stations in Iceland** — no founding year, because no source will stand behind one, and we don't invent dates on this bus. Named for the shore cave **Bennuhellir**, where the catch was processed.

On the hill: **Ingjaldshóll**. Church built **1903** — one of Iceland's oldest concrete churches — with tradition claiming the site back to the early 1300s. Also the farm where **Eggert Ólafsson** grew up, where the **1754 glacier climb** set out. Told you the name would come back.

The story you may have read: "Columbus wintered at Ingjaldshóll in 1477." What Columbus actually left us: one note — in February 1477 he sailed **"one hundred leagues beyond" Thule**. That's it. **He never said he went ashore**, and Iceland's own record is silent.

Where the wintering story really comes from: **fiction** — a short story by the Danish author **Sophus Bauditz**, serialised in the emigrant paper *Heimskringla* in **Winnipeg from 1889**, then translated "back" into Icelandic. One scholar's verdict, and it's the phrase to keep: **"fiction historicized."** The parish-hall painting (1998) is a 20th-century picture of a 19th-century short story.
say: the village ahead, one of Iceland's oldest fishing stations
the shore cave the village is named after

cuePerTour.9.0: Look left at 8 o'clock — Hellissandur, with the church at Ingjaldshóll on its hill beyond.
cuePerTour.10.0: Ahead at 12 o'clock — Hellissandur, with the church at Ingjaldshóll on its hill beyond.

block.title: 🪜 Saxhóll
block.cue: Approaching Saxhóll — the dark cone with the black stair bolted to its side.
block.hook: A crater staircase that won a **major international design prize**. Its own architects call it **"the stairway to heaven and hell."** It has 396 steps, and yes — somebody counted.
block.point: For eleven hundred years the question at Saxhóll was how to live beside the crater. In 2016 it became how to walk up it without wearing it out — and the answer won a design prize.
block.mic: Three hundred and ninety-six steps, and the stair itself won the biggest landscape architecture prize in Europe in 2018. The architects call it the stairway to heaven and hell.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The black stair is the giveaway. Look for the line of steps, not the cone."
bullets: **Saxhóll**: a scoria crater standing **40–45 metres** over the lava — 40 says the architect, 45 says the national park, and we're not getting between them. The **396 steps** are firm. Landscape architects count in public.

The black steel stair went in **2016** to stop the crater being trampled apart — and in **2018** won the **Rosa Barba International Landscape Prize**. The designers' own nickname: **"the stairway to heaven and hell."** Hell is presumably steps 300 through 396.

People have been here far longer than the stair: at the crater's foot lie the **ruins of Forna-Saxhóll — "Old Saxhóll" — from the settlement period**, and there was once a **church** at Saxhóll. A farm, a church, and a volcano for a back garden.

Live road note: **Route 579 to Öndverðarnes is closed to private cars today — organised buses only.** The westernmost point of the peninsula, and its Neshraun lava, belong to the coaches this afternoon.
say: the stair-wearing crater beside the road
"Old Saxhóll," the settlement-age farm ruins at its foot
the lava field running to the western tip
the westernmost point; buses only out there today

block.title: 💪 Djúpalónssandur & Dritvík
block.sub: The Job Interview Was a Boulder
block.cue: Turning down to Djúpalónssandur — the beach at the volcano's foot.
block.hook: How did you apply for a job on this coast? Four stones on a beach: **154 kilos, 100, 54 — and 23, named "Useless."** Lift the third one, or row home.
block.point: Amlóði — "Useless" — weighs 23 kilos. We named a rock after the men who couldn't lift it, and the name has outlasted every one of their bosses.
block.mic: The rusting iron is not litter. It is a war grave in effect — and it is legally protected. Leave it where it lies.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Wet black pebbles are the best they ever look. Mind your footing on the way down."
bullets: On the black pebble beach lie the four **lifting stones**: **Fullsterkur "full strength" 154 kg, Hálfsterkur "half strength" 100, Hálfdrættingur "half carrier" 54, and Amlóði — "Useless" — 23.** The park's figures — other sources disagree. Four rocks, three sets of numbers, one national argument.

Tradition: hoist **Hálfdrættingur** — the 54-kilo one — onto a ledge, or you don't row. Tradition, mind — nobody's produced the original HR paperwork. But that's the frame: the beach was the interview room.

Why the interview: **Dritvík** next door was **Iceland's largest seasonal fishing station**, mid-1500s to mid-1800s — **40–60 boats, up to 600 men** in a cove you could throw a stone across. Last boats rowed out spring 1861.

Said straight: the rusted iron on the beach is the **English trawler *Epine* GY-7**, wrecked **March 1948** with heavy loss of life. **A protected memorial — nothing may be removed.** Photos are fine. Souvenirs are not.
say: the black pebble beach down the turn-off
the cove next door; Iceland's biggest seasonal fishing station for 300 years
"Useless," 23 kg; the insult you could pick up

cuePerTour.9.0: Turning down to Djúpalónssandur — the beach at the volcano's foot.
cuePerTour.10.0: Passing the Djúpalónssandur turn-off at 9 o'clock.

block.title: 🕳️ Malarrif & Vatnshellir
block.cue: Look right at 3 o'clock — the white tower at Malarrif.
block.hook: When the farm at the lighthouse ran out of water, they didn't dig a new well. They walked to a **lava cave** and **scooped water out of the top of it for the cows.**
block.point: One small headland covers the whole vertical range of this peninsula: a lit tower for the ships above, and a drained artery of the volcano underneath — and for a while, the cows drank from the basement.
block.mic: When the well at Malarrif dried up, they walked over to Vatnshellir and dipped water for the cows out of the top of a lava cave.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The lighthouse is white and it is meant to be seen in this. That is its job."
bullets: The white tower is **Malarrif lighthouse** — concrete, **1946**, four buttresses, **about 24 metres**. About — the sources are having a disagreement over the tape measure, and we're staying out of it. First light 1917, protected since 2003.

From **1917** the farmer here was also the keeper — and in dry spells the household **dipped water for the cows out of the top of Vatnshellir**, the lava cave up the road. A cave as the backup tap. Icelandic plumbing.

**Vatnshellir** itself: a lava tube **about 200 metres long**, reaching **30 metres down**, the deeper levels called **Undirheimar** — "the Underworld." Spiral staircase, **guided tours only** — not a wander-in-with-your-phone-torch situation.
The tube formed the way all lava tubes do: the surface of the flow crusted hard while the molten interior kept draining downhill underneath — the lava left, and forgot to close the door behind it.
say: the lighthouse farm on the shore at 9 o'clock
the lava tube; "water cave," and yes, that's why
the smooth pahoehoe lava the tube runs through

cuePerTour.9.0: Look right at 3 o'clock — the white tower at Malarrif.
cuePerTour.10.0: Look left at 9 o'clock — the white tower at Malarrif.

block.title: 🪨 Lóndrangar
block.sub: The Devil Loses a Poetry Slam
block.cue: Look right at 3 o'clock — two dark pinnacles against the sea: Lóndrangar.
block.hook: Those two towers are **not** rocks the sea piled up. They're the **plumbing of a dead volcano** — and on the cliff beside them, a poet once beat the devil in a rhyming contest. We have the verses.
block.point: We're a country that keeps receipts on its folklore — the supernatural is welcome here, provided it's properly sourced.
block.mic: Lóndrangar are not rocks the sea piled up. They are the insides of a volcano — the plugs of the vent. Everything soft around them has been taken away by the Atlantic.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Two dark pinnacles against grey sea and grey sky is a harder picture, but it is a better one."
bullets: Geology first, because everyone gets it wrong: **Lóndrangar are volcanic plugs** — the solidified conduits of a vent, **75 and 61 metres**, everything soft stripped away by the Atlantic. Not stacked boulders, not "basalt columns" — the inside of a volcano with the outside removed.
A **sea eagle nested on Lóndrangar until after 1900** — prime real estate, no neighbours, fully stocked larder below.

The attested folklore — book, chapter and page in Jón Árnason's collection: on the cliff **Þúfubjarg**, the poet **Kolbeinn jöklaskáld** traded half-verses with **the devil** — fail to finish one, over the edge you go. The devil opened with *tungl*, "moon" — then couldn't rhyme it himself. Kolbeinn split the word in half, finished the verse, and the devil went into the surf. Beaten on a technicality. By an editor.
The "elf church" story you'll see online? **A modern tourist invention** — it appears in no Icelandic folklore collection. The devil story has a citation. The elf church has a marketing department.
say: the two volcanic plugs on the shore, 75 m and 61 m
the cliff where the rhyming contest happened

cuePerTour.9.0: Look right at 3 o'clock — two dark pinnacles against the sea: Lóndrangar.
cuePerTour.10.0: Look left at 9 o'clock — two dark pinnacles against the sea: Lóndrangar.

block.title: 🌋 Snæfellsjökull
block.cue: Look left at 9 o'clock — Snæfellsjökull, if it's showing.
block.hook: The most famous thing ever written about this mountain was written by a Frenchman **who never came here**. The mountain has not commented.
block.point: One mountain, three careers running at once: a volcano on pause, a glacier on a deadline, and a French science-fiction set that never checked the location.
block.mic: Verne never came here. He wrote the most famous thing ever written about this mountain from a desk in France, and it took eighty years for Icelanders to get it in their own language — 1944.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The glacier shows about a third of the days in the year. If it is out, say so loudly."
bullets: **Snæfellsjökull**: a **1,446-metre stratovolcano** wearing an ice cap. Last eruption **around the year 200** — nothing since Iceland was settled, magma chamber a few kilometres down. Not extinct — unhurried. There's a difference, and we live on it.

The ice is the fast mover — strange sentence about a glacier: **23 km² in 1890, 9 km² by 2014**, projected **largely gone by around 2050**. The postcard cap is leaving within some of your lifetimes. The volcano isn't going anywhere.

**1864**: Jules Verne put the entrance to the centre of the Earth in this crater — without ever visiting Iceland. The Icelandic translation took **eighty years** (1944). The most famous mountain in Icelandic fiction, and we got the novel last.

First recorded ascent: **1754**, by **Eggert Ólafsson and Bjarni Pálsson**, setting out from a farm called **Ingjaldshóll**. Pocket that name — it comes back within the hour with a much stranger story attached.
say: half of the first recorded ascent, 1754
the farm the 1754 climb set out from; hold that name
glacier; the word hiding at the end of the mountain's name

cuePerTour.9.0: Look left at 9 o'clock — Snæfellsjökull, if it's showing.
cuePerTour.10.0: Look right at 3 o'clock — Snæfellsjökull, if it's showing.

block.title: 🧭 Guðríður Þorbjarnardóttir
block.sub: The Farm Girl Who Out-Sailed Columbus
block.cue: Look right at 3 o'clock — Hellnar down by the shore, then Laugarbrekka.
block.hook: A woman born on that slope had a baby **on the far side of the Atlantic** — about **five centuries** before Columbus's crew ever laid eyes on it.
block.point: The Vínland story isn't only about the lovely Viking sailors with beards — the through-line is a woman from this slope who crossed the Atlantic and came back with a son and a better claim than Columbus.
block.mic: Guðríður was born within sight of this road. Her son Snorri was born on the far side of the Atlantic, about five centuries before Columbus's crew ever saw it.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "She crossed the Atlantic eight times in open boats. Today's weather is not the headline."
bullets: **Guðríður Þorbjarnardóttir** — remember this name — was born at **Laugarbrekka**, just off this road. Greenland first, then **Vínland** with her third husband **Þorfinnur karlsefni** — where her son **Snorri** was born: the first person of European descent born in the Americas outside Greenland.
Honesty clause: **the two sagas disagree.** *Grænlendinga saga* puts her on the Vínland voyage — *Eiríks saga rauða* only implies it. Two medieval sources, one woman, no agreed cut of the film.

The famous **"eight ocean crossings"**? **Tradition, not established fact.** The defensible version is still enormous: more crossings than almost any named person of her century — plus, tradition adds, a pilgrimage to Rome and a final act as an anchoress.
Her monument at Laugarbrekka — **Ásmundur Sveinsson's** Guðríður and Snorri — was **reported stolen in 2022**. Somebody stole the statue of the most travelled woman of her age. It travelled.

Hellnar below: one of the biggest fishing stations under the Glacier — about **200 people** in the early 1700s. Road note for today: **Route 574 runs one-way from noon, Búðir to Hellissandur** — nobody is coming the other way.
say: the Norse name for the North American coast
the old fishing station down by the shore
her third husband, the Vínland expedition leader

cuePerTour.9.0: Look right at 3 o'clock — Hellnar down by the shore, then Laugarbrekka.
cuePerTour.10.0: Look left at 9 o'clock — Laugarbrekka, then Hellnar down by the shore.

block.title: 🛁 Bárðarlaug
block.sub: The Half-Troll Takes a Cold Bath
block.cue: Passing Laugarbrekka — the crater pond hides until you're standing on its rim, so this one's a story.
block.hook: Time to meet the landlord of this whole coast. **Bárður Snæfellsás** — giants on his father's side, trolls in the family, raised by a creature living inside a mountain — and the first thing the saga has him do on arrival here is **take a bath**.
block.point: The saga says he bathed here and named his farm after it. The Environment Agency says the water hasn't been warm since the settlement. Both can be true — it just means the bath was freezing.
block.mic: The management plan is the driest document ever to ruin a legend: no geothermal heat since the settlement. So whatever Bárður did in that pool, he did it cold — half-troll on the outside, all Viking underneath.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The pond hides until you are on the rim, so the cloud makes no difference to this one."
bullets: The saga gives Bárður a CV like no other settler's: his father **Dumbur** was descended from **giants**, with **troll stock** in the line; his mother **Mjöll** was human. Half-troll, half-giant, part human — the saga is genuinely specific about the mix, and so are we.

From age ten he was fostered by **Dofri**, a *bergbúi* — a mountain-dweller, a being that lives *in* the mountain — who taught him genealogy, fighting skill, and "magic and ancient lore." At thirteen he married Dofri's daughter. A conventional childhood, by the standards of nobody.

Arriving on Snæfellsnes, says the saga, he came to a pond, took off all his clothes and **washed at its edge** — and the pond is called **Bárðarlaug**, "Bárður's bath," to this day. He built his farm just there: **Laugarbrekka**, "bath slope." The man named half the neighbourhood after one wash.

Now the precision point, and I love this: *laug* means a warm pool — but the official management plan for the site states there has been **no geothermal heat in that pool since the settlement of Iceland**. So whatever Bárður did here, **he did it cold**.

What the pond actually is: an oval pool in a **scoria crater planed down by a glacier** at the end of the Ice Age, protected as a natural monument since **1980** — invisible from the road, invisible until you stand on the rim. A bath with privacy walls, courtesy of the last glaciation.
say: the half-troll, half-giant settler of this coast
"Bárður's bath," the crater pond he washed in — cold, officially
"bath slope," the farm he built beside it
the mountain-dweller who fostered him from age ten and taught him magic
"rock-dweller"; the category of being Dofri is

block.title: 🐦 The Arnarstapi Cliffs
block.sub: Columns Lying Down on the Job
block.cue: At Arnarstapi — the start of the cliff path.
block.hook: Basalt columns are supposed to stand up straight. Half of the ones on this coast are **lying flat on their sides** — and the rock is following the rules by doing it.
block.point: This coast is a working census: the columns record how the lava cooled, and the nests record what the ocean is doing right now — and the second number is moving fast.
block.mic: About ten thousand pairs of kittiwakes nest along this coast — nearly two per cent of the Icelandic population. And they fell by fifty-five per cent in one year, between 2017 and 2018.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Rough sea makes the blowhole work properly. Bad weather is the good version here."
bullets: The clefts along this shore are the **Stapagjár** — columnar basalt, *stuðlaberg*, running **both vertical and horizontal**. Same maths as Gerðuberg this morning — columns grow perpendicular to whatever cooled them — except half of these cooled sideways. Read the angle and the rock tells you which way the heat left.

The ledges hold about **10,000 pairs of kittiwakes** — just under **2% of Iceland's entire population** of the species — plus roughly **12,500 pairs of arctic terns**. Now the hard number: kittiwakes here **fell 55% in one year**, 2017 to 2018. Not "declining somewhat." Fifty-five per cent. Someone counted the nests, twice.
While you're walking, look **out**, not just down: **orcas, harbour porpoises and minke whales** are regularly seen off this coast. No promises — they haven't read the itinerary.

Housekeeping: **45 minutes** here, and the **cliff path is the whole show** — statue, clefts, bird ledges, harbour. **Toilets are here**, so use them; the next stretch of road is lava, and lava is not discreet.
say: the hamlet and cliffs we're standing on
the basalt clefts along the cliff path
the kittiwake, the little gull on the narrow ledges
the arctic tern; do not test its patience

block.title: 🗿 The Bárður Statue
block.sub: The Detail Almost Every Guide Misses
block.cue: At the Bárður statue.
block.hook: Six metres of stacked stone, close to **300 tonnes** — a saga giant guarding the harbour. And the detail few guides know: it's also **a family's gravestone**.
block.point: We put up statues the way the sagas wrote — the myth on the surface, and underneath it, a real family and a real cold night.
block.mic: That statue is six metres high and close to three hundred tonnes of stone, unveiled on the seventeenth of June 1985 — and it is not only a saga monument: the family who commissioned it raised it in memory of their parents and a brother who died of exposure.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Stone troll, stone sky. He looks better in this than in sunshine."
bullets: The figure is **Bárður Snæfellsás**, by the sculptor **Ragnar Kjartansson**, unveiled **17 June 1985** — about **6 metres high** and using **close to 300 tonnes of stone**. You don't move that; you build it where it stands and let it outlast you.

You met him at Bárðarlaug an hour ago — here's his ending: he vanished **into the glacier**, and the saga says people **"believed in him almost throughout the peninsula"** and made vows to him. His title, *ás*, is the same word used of the old gods. A vow-god, not a mascot.

Now the part that changes how you look at it: the statue was **commissioned by the children of Jón Sigurðsson of Bjarg á Stapa and Guðrún Sigtryggsdóttir, as a memorial to their parents and their brother Trausti — who died of exposure young**. A saga giant on the outside; a family remembering the weather's cost on the inside.
And Arnarstapi itself is in the saga: *"Þorkell rauðfeldur took land for himself at the place called Arnarstapi."* You are standing in a named sentence from the Middle Ages.
say: the medieval saga that names Arnarstapi
the saga's word for him; the same word used of the old gods, the Æsir

block.title: 🏠 The Governor's House That Left
block.cue: At the harbour.
block.hook: This little cove was once the **seat of government for western Iceland**. Then somebody took the government building apart, put it on a boat, and **shipped it away**.
block.point: Empires file paperwork; harbours do the work. The monopoly, the governor and his house are all gone — the landing they came for is still landing fish.
block.mic: This was a monopoly-trade harbour and the seat of the district governor. His house was built here in the 1770s and 80s — and then dismantled and shipped away in 1849.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The harbour is the story and it is right in front of you, weather or not."
bullets: Arnarstapi was one of the harbours of the **Danish monopoly trade** — the *einokunarverslun* — and the landing here was reckoned **one of the best "under the Glacier."** Where the trade sat, power sat: this became the residence of the **amtmaður**, the district governor.

The house itself went up **1774–87**, built by the Royal Trading Company for its trade manager **Hans Hjaltalín** — one of the very few Icelanders ever to hold such a post under the monopoly. Trade was freed in **1787**, he bought the business and the house; he went bankrupt around **1820**; and from **1821** it housed the governor of the West Amt. One building, three careers.

Then the move: in **1849–50** the house was **taken down and carried away by sea** to Vogur á Mýrum — and moved *again* around 1983, to Korpúlfsstaðir, for storage. (We don't demolish good timber. We forward it.)

What's left is what matters now: the small-boat harbour, **rebuilt in 2002**, is today **the only harbour on the whole south side of Snæfellsnes** — motorboats since about 1933, and it still fishes year-round. The governor left; the fish didn't.
say: the district governor who resided here
the Danish trade monopoly that ran this harbour
the trade manager the house was built for, 1774–87
"under the Glacier," what this whole coast is called

block.title: ⛰️ Stapafell & Rauðfeldsgjá
block.cue: Leaving Arnarstapi — Stapafell over your left shoulder; then at 9 o'clock, a thin black cleft in the mountainside — Rauðfeldsgjá.
block.hook: Bárður again — and this time it's not a bath. Two boys, aged **eleven and twelve**. He took them **one under each arm**, walked up the mountain — and the gorge and the sea-crag where it ended **still carry their names**.
block.point: A gorge and a sea-crag, each named for the boy who died there — ages eleven and twelve, one under each arm. Icelandic place names are the country's oldest court record.
block.mic: The saga is very precise about the two boys: eleven and twelve years old. Bárður carried one under each arm up the mountain — and the gorge and the crag ahead of you both still carry their names.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The cleft is a dark line in the mountain wall — easier to find in flat light than in shadow."
bullets: The setup: the children were playing on the ice, there was a quarrel, and it ended with Bárður's daughter **Helga** adrift on an ice floe — the saga floats her all the way to Greenland in seven days. Bárður came back "very dark of countenance." The saga's phrase, and it's doing a lot of work.

The boys were **Rauðfeldur and Sölvi**, sons of the neighbour Þorkell at Arnarstapi — **one was eleven winters old, the other twelve**. The saga is precise about the ages, so we are too. Bárður took them both, one under each arm, and walked up the mountain.

**Rauðfeldur** he threw into a gorge "so deep that he was dead the moment he came down" — **Rauðfeldsgjá**, the black cleft at three o'clock. **Sölvi** he carried further and threw over a high sea-crag — **Sölvahamar**, on the coast ahead. A thousand years on, the map still files both boys exactly where they landed.

Precision point, because guides get this wrong daily: the saga **never names Stapafell**. It says only "up the mountain." The pyramid ahead certainly looks the part — but the text doesn't put Bárður on it, and we don't put words in a saga's mouth.

What Stapafell actually is: a **526 m pyramid of móberg** — same under-the-ice recipe as the Ljósufjöll ridges this morning — summit called Fellskross. As for the gorge, no official geological survey of it exists — so the only authority on Rauðfeldsgjá's origin is, for now, the saga. Make of that what you will.
say: the 526 m hyaloclastite pyramid ahead; summit Fellskross
the gorge at three o'clock, named for the elder boy
the sea-crag named for the younger, Sölvi
the twelve-year-old; his father Þorkell farmed at Arnarstapi

cuePerTour.9.0: Leaving Arnarstapi — Stapafell over your left shoulder; then at 9 o'clock, a thin black cleft in the mountainside — Rauðfeldsgjá.
cuePerTour.10.0: Look ahead at 12 o'clock — the dark pyramid of Stapafell; then right at 3 o'clock, a thin black cleft in the mountainside — Rauðfeldsgjá.

block.title: 🔪 Axlar-Björn
block.sub: The Farmer You Didn't Stop To Visit
block.cue: *Between Búðir and Arnarstapi — this one's a story, not a view.*
block.hook: Iceland has, in its entire recorded history, essentially **one serial killer**. One. He farmed on **this coast** — and the travellers who crossed his path had a habit of **not continuing their journey**.
block.point: In a country famously short of murderers, one farm on this coast produced the national serial killer — nine confessed, eighteen alleged, one execution, three graves.
block.mic: Nine confessed. Some say eighteen. Buried in 1596, in three separate pieces — because when Iceland finally gets a villain, we take absolutely no chances with the sequel.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "No view for this one. It is a story, and it is a horrible one, so mind the children."
bullets: His name was **Björn**, of the farm **Öxl** — which is why history files him as **Axlar-Björn**, "Björn of Öxl." His victims were **travellers**: people passing through this district, exactly the way we are now, minus the upholstery.
When it ended, he **confessed to murdering nine** of them — and some accounts say **eighteen**. We quote the confession, and we flag the higher figure for what it is: an account, not a count.
The bodies, it was said, went into the pond **Iglutjörn**. "It was said" is doing honest work in that sentence — that's how the record itself puts it.

He was **executed in 1596**, and the authorities took no chances with the afterlife logistics: he was **buried in three parts**, at Laugarholt near Hellnar, just along our road. Sixteenth-century Iceland's version of absolutely-definitely-finished.
say: "Björn of Öxl," Iceland's one serial killer, executed 1596
the pond the bodies were said to be dumped in
near Hellnar, where he was buried in three parts

block.title: ⛪ Búðir
block.sub: The Widow Who Rebuilt the Church
block.cue: Look right at 3 o'clock — a small black church standing alone on the lava.
block.hook: How does a small parish on a lava field get its church back? One widow. **Steinunn Sveinsdóttir** filed the paperwork with the church authorities, put up her own money, and **rebuilt it herself** — and the black church on that lava is hers.
block.point: One widow's stubbornness and 130 plant species, growing out of the same lava — the two most persistent things on this coast, side by side.
block.mic: Búðakirkja wasn't rebuilt by a bishop or a budget. It was rebuilt by one widow with paperwork and patience — consecrated in 1851, which makes this year its **175th anniversary**. She'd probably just nod.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "A black church on black lava under a grey sky. There is no bad-weather version of this."
bullets: The black church is **Búðakirkja**. First church on the site: **1703**, built by Bent Lárusson. The one you're looking at is the widow's: **Steinunn Sveinsdóttir** applied to the church authorities for permission, then led and paid for the rebuild herself — **rebuilt in the late 1840s, consecrated in 1851**. (The archives offer three build dates; the consecration is solid, so that's the one we stand on.)

Legend has it Bent Lárusson appeared to Steinunn **in a dream** and asked her to do it. That's the story as recorded — told as legend, kept as legend. She died a few years later and lies in this churchyard, gravestone still standing.

The church has been **legally protected since 1 January 1990**, was moved within the churchyard in one piece in **1984**, and today belongs to the National Museum. A museum piece that still holds services — Iceland doesn't really do "retired," see also: this entire peninsula.

Under it, **Búðahraun**: lava from the **88 m** crater Búðaklettur, about **5,000–8,000 years old**, and its beach sand is **nearly pure olivine** — the lava carries yellow-green olivine crystals, and the sea has milled the rock down to its minerals. Green-gold sand, next to a black church.

The lava is also the county's botanical garden: **over 130 plant species**, including **11 of Iceland's 16 fern species**, in a nature reserve since **1977**. Somebody counted the ferns. Eleven. They're probably still out there, counting.
say: the church itself; rebuilt late 1840s, consecrated 1851
the widow who applied, paid, and rebuilt
the lava field: 130 plant species, olivine-green sand
the 88 m crater the lava came from

cuePerTour.9.0: Look right at 3 o'clock — a small black church standing alone on the lava.
cuePerTour.10.0: Look left at 9 o'clock — a small black church standing alone on the lava.

block.title: 🦭 Ytri-Tunga
block.cue: Turning down the farm track to Ytri-Tunga.
block.hook: The staff at this stop are unionised: they turn up in June and July, lie about all day, and get photographed doing it. **Seals. The staff are seals.**
block.point: One farmer built a car park so strangers could watch seals do absolutely nothing — and it became one of the best-loved shores on the peninsula.
block.mic: The seals keep office hours, and we've arrived inside them. Act like clients, not paparazzi.
block.weather: Weather pivot (if the seals are elsewhere): "Empty rocks today — the colony commutes. Those skerries are their desks, and by June they're all back at work."
bullets: Ytri-Tunga is a working **farm** in **Staðarsveit** whose shoreline hosts one of Snæfellsnes's most reliable **seal colonies** — the **landowner built the track and the car park** so you can reach the shore without marching through the fields.

The regulars are **harbour seals** — found all along the Snæfellsnes coast, and this shore is **the best place on the peninsula to get close to them**. The bigger, shyer **grey seal** turns up *sometimes* — the wildlife survey's word, not mine (**Sólrún Þórðardóttir, 2020**).
**June and July are the office hours.** Outside them the rocks can be bare — the seals are wild, not payroll.
House rules: **keep your distance, keep it quiet, no feeding.** A seal that flees into the water because of you has paid for your photo.
say: the farm and its seal beach; "the outer tongue" of land
the farm district along this southern shore

block.title: 🦅 Löngufjörur
block.sub: The Sea Floor That Got Promoted
block.cue: Look right at 3 o'clock — flat pale sand running to the horizon; the cliffs inland on your left are old sea cliffs.
block.hook: The flat ground on your left used to be the **bottom of the sea** — and the cliffs on your *right* used to be the coastline. The land has been quietly standing up since the Ice Age ended. Iceland doesn't even hold still at the geography level.
block.point: Left of the bus: the old sea floor. Right of the bus: the old sea shore. The land stood up after the Ice Age, and one in seven of Iceland's white-tailed eagle pairs moved into the gap.
block.mic: Ten pairs of white-tailed eagles nest along this coast — about one in seven of the entire Icelandic population. If something big drifts over the flats with fingers on the ends of its wings, that's them.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Pale sand stays pale. It is one of the few things out here the cloud cannot take."
bullets: The whole lowland along southern Snæfellsnes is a **former sea floor** that has been rising since the end of the Ice Age. The cliff belts inland of us are **old sea cliffs**, now stranded well back from their own beach.

The pale flats are **Löngufjörur** — "the Long Beaches" — running from Hítarnes in the east all the way west to Búðir. The sand is **pale-yellow shell sand**, ground-up seashells, flat as far as the eye can see and almost without a stone. Note the colour; in a country famous for black beaches, we're driving past a blond one.

The register lists this coast for habitats, birds and seals — headline tenants: **10 breeding pairs of white-tailed eagles**, which is **14% of the entire Icelandic population**. One in seven of the country's eagle pairs, on this one stretch of coast — its second most important eagle breeding ground.

The small print of the same register is a little history lesson: **seal-hunting rights were once a major asset of the farms here**, and have now largely lapsed. The seals went from line item to photo opportunity in about three generations.
These days the traffic on the flats is mostly **riding tours** — horses, at low tide, on a former sea floor. There are worse commutes.
say: "the Long Beaches," the pale shell-sand flats on your left
the eastern end of the flats
the western end; we'll be there shortly
the white-tailed eagle; ten pairs breed along this coast

cuePerTour.9.0: Look right at 3 o'clock — flat pale sand running to the horizon; the cliffs inland on your left are old sea cliffs.
cuePerTour.10.0: Look left at 9 o'clock — flat pale sand running to the horizon; the cliffs inland on your right are old sea cliffs.

block.title: 🏛️ Reykjavík
block.sub: The Brook, The Hill And The Forty-Five Years Of Silence
block.cue: Look back — the green hill with the statue on it, just behind where we picked you up.
block.hook: The street you just got on the bus in is called **Lækjargata — Brook Street.** There is no brook. It is still there, running under the tarmac, and in January it is the reason the ducks in the city pond have anywhere to swim.
block.point: A buried brook that still keeps the birds warm, a parliament that stopped for forty-five years, and a church that took forty-one to build in a country that had none of the money.
block.mic: Reykjavík will tell you it has the world's oldest parliament. What it actually has is the world's oldest parliament with a very long lunch break.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the tower has gone, do not worry — you will see it again tonight, and on a morning like this the locals cannot see it either."
bullets: That hill is **Arnarhóll**, and the man on it is **Ingólfur Arnarson**, who the tradition says was Iceland's first settler. The tradition — and say it as a tradition, because that is what it is — has him throwing his **öndvegissúlur**, the carved pillars from either side of a chieftain's high seat, over the side of the ship and settling wherever they washed ashore. They came in below this hill. **What archaeology can actually pin down is different and better:** there were people here **before the ash layer dated to AD 871, give or take two years.** The statue is by **Einar Jónsson**, and it was not a gift from the state — the **Reykjavík craftsmen's guild** paid the **40,000 krónur** and unveiled it on **24 February 1924.** Arnarhóll was a working farm until the **1820s.**

Now the brook. **Lækurinn** ran from the pond down to the sea, the old town grew up on the west side of it, and the street was named **Lækjargata in 1848.** In **1911** they put the brook in a culvert and paved over it. **It is still flowing under us.** And here is the good part: the pond — **Tjörnin** — freezes in winter, except for one patch. Guides will tell you that is a natural hot spring. **It is not.** It is **warm overflow from the city's hot-water system**, coming out at the old brook outlet by Iðnó. One warm corner, and every duck in Reykjavík standing in it.

Off to the right on **Austurvöllur** is the **Alþingishúsið**, the parliament, built **1880 to 1881** by the Danish architect **Ferdinand Meldahl**, out of stone quarried up the hill in **Þingholtin.** And this is where you correct the guidebook. **Alþingi was founded at Þingvellir, traditionally in 930** — the oldest parliamentary institution in the world by date of foundation. **But it is not the oldest continuously running one, and Alþingi does not claim to be.** It was **shut down by royal decree on 6 June 1800** and did not sit again until **1 July 1845.** **Forty-five years of silence.** That gap is the whole reason the Isle of Man gets to argue about this.

Last one on the skyline: **Hallgrímskirkja**, the concrete tower you can see from most of the city. **About 74 and a half metres** — the parish's own leaflet says 73, and I am not going to pretend that is settled. It was designed by **Guðjón Samúelsson**, and the shape is meant to be **columnar basalt, mountains and glaciers** rather than anything churchy. Building started in **1945** and it was consecrated on **26 October 1986** — **forty-one years.** Guðjón died in **1950** and never saw it. The statue of **Leifur Eiríksson** out front is older than the church behind it: **a gift from the United States** for the **1930 millennium of the Alþingi**, formally handed over on **17 July 1931.**
