say: 'brook street', named 1848, with the brook culverted underneath in 1911
'eagle hill', the mound with the Ingólfur statue
'high-seat pillars', thrown overboard to choose a landing place
the parliament, founded at Þingvellir around 930, closed 1800, reopened 1845
'the pond', where one corner stays open all winter
consecrated 26 October 1986, forty-one years after work began

block.title: 🌍 Reykjanes UNESCO Global Geopark
block.cue: Look ahead — the whole peninsula opening up in front of us.
block.hook: We're driving onto the only stretch of mid-ocean ridge on Earth that pokes above the sea. Most geologists only ever see one on a diagram. You're about to spend a day standing on it.
block.point: A **constructive plate boundary** and a **mantle hotspot** overlap nowhere else on Earth. Iceland exists because both happen in the same spot.
block.mic: Today's route is basically a guided tour of a crack in the planet. Mind the step.
block.weather: Weather pivot (if it's socked in): "You will not see much of the peninsula this morning, and that is fine — everything I am about to show you is at your feet rather than on the horizon."
bullets: The whole peninsula is a **UNESCO Global Geopark** (**2015**) — one of only a handful of places where a **mid-ocean ridge climbs above sea level.** Normally the North American/Eurasian plate boundary sits **2 km down** on the seafloor. Here you can walk on it, and later today you will.

The park protects ~**825 km²** of lava, geothermal fields and rift. **Four to six linked volcanic systems** run through it — Reykjanes, Svartsengi, Fagradalsfjall, Krýsuvík, Brennisteinsfjöll, Hengill — out of ~30 Iceland-wide. We will be inside four of them before lunch.

Iceland is a **double engine**: a spreading **plate boundary** sitting on a stationary **mantle hotspot.** The oldest rock anywhere in Iceland is only **fifteen or sixteen million years** old — and out here on Reykjanes it's a tiny fraction of that. The hotspot beneath has been burning for at least **60 million.**
say: the peninsula itself, reykja = smoky and nes = headland, a UNESCO Global Geopark since 2015
one of the volcanic systems running through the geopark, and our late-morning stop

block.title: 🧝 Hafnarfjörður
block.cue: Look right — Hafnarfjörður running down to its harbour.
block.hook: When the University of Iceland actually asked — first in 1974, again in 2007 — around half of Icelanders wouldn't rule out elves. This is the town where the official ones live.
block.point: A town that built itself into an eight-thousand-year-old lava flow, and then decided the flow came with tenants.
block.mic: Other countries cancel roadworks over budgets. Iceland cancels them over elves.
block.weather: Weather pivot (if the town is in murk): "You cannot see it, which the hidden folk will consider a result."
bullets: ***Hafnarfjörður* = Harbour Fjord** — a Viking-age settlement and one of Iceland's top trading ports from the **15th century**, where English and Hanseatic merchants shipped out **dried cod.**

The town is built **into the lava** — streets and gardens threaded through **Búrfellshraun**, a flow ~**8,000 years old.** That makes it the self-declared **elf capital of Iceland.** When the University of Iceland actually asked — first in **1974**, again in **2007** — around **half** wouldn't rule out the ***huldufólk*** (hidden people) living in the rocks. The town keeps an official **elf map**, and planners sometimes call in **elf consultants** before roadworks. The lava park **Hellisgerði** is prime hidden-folk real estate.

A carpenter called **Jóhannes Reykdal** dammed the stream behind his workshop, wired in a generator from Norway, and in the first days of **December 1904** lit about **fifteen houses** — the school and the Good Templars' hall among them — and four street lamps: **Iceland's first hydroelectric station.** Reykjavík didn't manage its own until **1921.**
say: 'Harbour Fjord', the town built into a lava flow some 8,000 years old
the 'hidden people', the elves said to live in these rocks
'Cave Garden', the lava park that is prime hidden-folk real estate
the carpenter whose dammed stream lit the town in December 1904

block.title: 🏭 Straumsvík & Kapelluhraun
block.sub: A Saint Of Fire, Next Door To A Smelter
block.cue: Look right — the low silver sheds and the chimneys, and the black lava they sit on.
block.hook: That lava has a name older than the buildings: **Nýjahraun** — "the new lava." It ran in **1151.** Iceland has been calling it *new* for **875 years**, which tells you everything about the pace of things here.
block.point: An eight-hundred-year-old lava flow still called "the new one", with a medieval shrine to the patron saint of metalworkers sitting in the middle of it — and Iceland's first aluminium smelter built on top.
block.mic: Iceland's entire modern economy starts with that one deal: build a smelter, and to feed it, build a national power company. Everything you will see today is downstream of a Swiss handshake in 1966.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the plant is lost in the murk, the steam and the cloud are doing the same job. The lava under the wheels is the older story anyway."
bullets: The plant is **ISAL**, the aluminium smelter at **Straumsvík.** Built by the Swiss company **Alusuisse** under a law Alþingi passed on **13 May 1966**, it started producing in **1969** at a modest **33,000 tonnes a year.** Today it runs at about **202,000 tonnes**, with a licence for **230,000**, employs **381 people** (end of 2025) and is owned outright by **Rio Tinto.**

Here is the bit that actually matters. To run it, Iceland had to build a power station — so **Landsvirkjun was founded on 1 July 1965** and put up **Búrfellsstöð**, which started on **16 September 1969.** The smelter took **half the station's output, 105 MW.** *(In 2025 it bought **3,334 gigawatt-hours.**)* The **alumina** arrives by ship mostly from **Brazil**, the finished aluminium leaves through **Rotterdam** to around **60 customers**, and it comes out as **billet** — the stuff extruded into window frames and solar-panel rails.

Now the lava. **Kapelluhraun** poured out of the **Krýsuvíkureldar in 1151** — the same fires we will meet again in an hour. Locals call it **Bruninn**, "the burn", and the medieval name **Nýjahraun** turns up in *Kjalnesinga saga* and in an annal entry for a **1343** shipwreck. People **watched this one arrive.**

And out there in the rock is a tiny ruin called **Kapellan**, the chapel. On **21 May 1950** it was excavated by **Kristján Eldjárn** — later President of Iceland — with three colleagues. The building was **2.4 metres long.** Inside they found, broken into three pieces, a **carved claystone figure of Saint Barbara**, about **3.3 cm** of her surviving from an original of maybe **5.5 cm**, still holding her tower. Pre-Reformation. A wayside shrine where travellers stopped to pray before crossing the lava.

**Barbara is the patron saint of travellers — and of everyone who works with fire, metal and explosives.** She has been sitting in that lava for five hundred years, and then somebody built an aluminium smelter next door. *(She is now the most appropriately employed saint in the North Atlantic.)*

The chapel also carries a grim story: that a man from **Bessastaðir** was killed and buried here in the reprisals after the execution of **Bishop Jón Arason.** Kristján Eldjárn dug for it and **found nothing to support it** — and said so. Good man.
say: 'chapel lava', the 1151 flow with the shrine in it
'the new lava', its medieval name, still in use
the archaeologist who dug the chapel in 1950 and later became President

block.title: 🛣️ Vatnsskarð & Sveifluháls
block.sub: The Road Everyone Said Was A Waste Of Money
block.cue: Look ahead — the road climbing into the gap, and the long jagged ridge on our right.
block.hook: When they proposed this road in **1936**, the newspapers took it apart. Árni Óla wrote in **1940** that the project had "mostly met with condemnation" and that this exact pass would be the most expensive and difficult stretch of the lot. **We are about to drive the argument.**
block.point: A rift-built ridge, a road built to dodge the snow, and an aquifer that ties this pass to the smelter back down the coast. Everything on this peninsula is plumbed into everything else.
block.mic: Every good Icelandic road starts life as a newspaper column explaining why it should never be built.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the ridge has vanished, take a moment to enjoy the irony — this is the road they built *specifically* so weather wouldn't stop them."
bullets: The ridge on the right is **Sveifluháls.** It was built underneath a glacier — a fissure eruption erupting into ice, quenching into **móberg**, hyaloclastite, and stacking itself into a wall instead of spreading into a plain. It runs **north-east to south-west**, which is not a coincidence: that is the direction of the rift. The whole **Krýsuvík volcanic system** is about **8 km wide and 50 km long**, and this ridge is drawn along it like a pencil line on a map.

The road was **Jónas Jónsson and Jón Baldvinsson's** idea, put to Alþingi in **March 1936.** The pitch was weather. The existing route east crossed **Hellisheiði at 370 metres.** This one would top out at **168.** A **snow-free winter road** to the south. That was the whole argument.

It cost a fortune, it took years, and the stretch past **Kleifarvatn** was not finished until around **1945.** *(Which means the fastest way to make an Icelander build you a road is to point out that the other one gets snowed in.)*

One more thing you cannot see and should know. The pass is being **quarried** — for exactly the same móberg the ridge is made of. And the local objection is not about the view. **The groundwater under Undirhlíðar runs downhill and comes out at Straumsvík** — the smelter we passed twenty minutes ago. A public consultation on new extraction ran from **25 September to 6 November 2025.**
say: the móberg ridge on the right, built under the ice along the rift
'water pass', the gap we are climbing through
hyaloclastite: lava quenched by ice or water into brown, crumbly rock
the slopes being quarried, and the aquifer's route to Straumsvík

block.title: 💧 Kleifarvatn
block.sub: The Lake That Pulled Its Own Plug
block.cue: Look left — the long dark lake filling the valley floor.
block.hook: In the year 2000 this lake started emptying. Nobody drained it, nobody dammed it. **An earthquake opened a crack in the bottom and the water simply left.**
block.point: A lake with no outlet, sitting on a live fissure swarm, that lost four metres of itself to an earthquake and then quietly refilled.
block.mic: Everywhere else the lake is the stable bit of the landscape. Here it has a monster, a novel, and a habit of leaving.
block.weather: Weather pivot (if the lake is grey and flat): "This is honestly the right weather for it. It looks like the cover of the crime novel that's set here."
bullets: **Kleifarvatn** is the biggest lake on the peninsula — about **10 km²**, up to **97 metres deep**, sitting roughly **140 metres above sea level** in a closed basin on the eastern edge of the **Krýsuvík fissure swarm.** Vísindavefurinn's answer is that the basin is probably part of a **caldera around 10 km across** — a collapse, not an explosion crater — and that the lake in its present form is roughly **10,000 to 12,000 years old.**

Here is the oddity: **it has no river running out of it.** Before 2000 the water drained north into **Lambhagatjörn** and then underground, all the way to the sea at **Straumsvík.** A lake that empties itself through the floor is already unusual. Then the floor got worse.

The **earthquakes of 2000** opened and widened fissures at and near the lake's northern end, and over the **following two years the surface dropped about four metres.** Beaches appeared. The jetty ended up a long way from the water. It has since recovered a good deal, but the point stands: on this peninsula even the lakes are provisional.

It also has a monster, and the sightings are dated. In **1749**, witnesses said they watched the thing haul itself out onto a spit and lie there for **about two hours.** By **1750** people **would not fish here at all**, though the lake was full of fish, because of *"orms eða slöngu sem væri svört að lit"* — a worm or serpent, black, reckoned to be **the size of a medium whale, thirty to forty metres long.** In **1755** something surfaced *"líkasta skötu að lit og lögun"* — closest to a skate in colour and shape, and enormous.

And when the water finally did drop, Iceland's best-selling crime writer was waiting. **Arnaldur Indriðason's *Kleifarvatn* (2004)** — published in English as ***The Draining Lake*** — opens with the falling water level uncovering **a body that had been down there for decades.** He did not have to invent the setting. He just read the news.
say: the peninsula's biggest lake, 97 m deep, no river out
the fissure swarm and geothermal district we are driving into
the bay north of here where the lake's water used to surface, underground the whole way
whose 2004 novel Kleifarvatn starts with this water level dropping

block.title: 🔥 Krýsuvíkureldar
block.sub: The Fires That Shut The Door
block.cue: Look around — the whole floor of this valley is one lava flow.
block.hook: This system last erupted in the twelfth century, ran for nearly forty years, and then closed for eight hundred. It has not opened since. That is either reassuring or it isn't.
block.point: Four to six volcanic systems, taking turns across centuries. Krýsuvík has been quiet since 1188. Nobody sensible calls that finished.
block.mic: The system under this valley last went off when Iceland was still writing the sagas down. It's had eight hundred years to think about it.
block.weather: Weather pivot (if the valley is in cloud): "The lava is under the wheels rather than out the window, so you are not missing the good bit — you're driving on it."
bullets: The **Krýsuvíkureldar of 1151 to 1188** laid down **Ögmundarhraun**, **Mávahlíðahraun** and **Kapelluhraun** — three flows that between them rewrote the south coast of this peninsula and buried at least one farm.

Then the system **shut, and has stayed shut for over eight centuries.** Meanwhile its neighbours — Fagradalsfjall in 2021, Svartsengi and Sundhnúkur from 2023 — have been extremely busy. Same peninsula, same rift, completely different diaries.

That is how the **Reykjanes Fires** work. The peninsula sleeps for centuries, then wakes for decades of eruptions across several systems, then sleeps again. The last full cycle ran roughly **950 to 1240 CE** and laid most of the lava we have driven on today. We are, on the current reading, at the beginning of the next one.
say: the lava flow they left across the south coast
the 'Reykjanes Fires', the cycle that wakes this peninsula for decades at a time

block.title: ♨️ Seltún
block.sub: Where They Drilled For The Queen And Got A Crater
block.cue: At Seltún, from the boardwalk.
block.hook: In October 1999 a borehole here stopped blowing, thought about it for a bit, and then **exploded** — leaving a crater forty-three metres across and throwing mud seven hundred metres up the hillside.
block.point: A field that has been mined, drilled, blown up and rebuilt around — and the only thing that has actually changed in three hundred years is where the fence goes.
block.mic: They came here for sulphur, then for steam, and got a forty-three-metre crater by way of a receipt. Stay on the boards.
block.weather: Weather pivot (rain and low cloud, which is likely): "Honestly, this is the correct weather for Seltún. Cold air makes the steam do everything you want it to do, and the colours come up better wet than they do in sunshine."
bullets: This is a **high-temperature geothermal field** at the heart of the Krýsuvík system, and the colours are not decoration — they are the rock being eaten. Steam rises off the deep reservoir, condenses near the surface, and brings up **carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulphide.** Those gases turn the water acid, and the acid digests fresh lava into soft clay. **The mud you are photographing is bedrock that lost an argument with chemistry.**

Those pale yellow mounds have a name and a mechanism. **Brennisteinsþúfur** — sulphur mounds — form where **hydrogen sulphide reaches the surface and oxidises in open air**, dropping pure sulphur out of the gas. Vísindavefurinn puts them at **10 to 20 metres across and 1 to 1.5 metres high**, and — this is the good bit — **hollow inside.**

People mined that sulphur. According to the site's own panels there were two runs: **1754 to 1763**, and again **1858 to 1880**, and contemporary records have **72.5 tonnes of sulphur exported from Krýsuvík in the eighteenth century.** Sulphur meant gunpowder. This muddy field was, briefly, a strategic resource.

And this is where Iceland's geothermal drilling starts. **Eggert Ólafsson and Bjarni Pálsson** bored here with a hand-turned iron drill in the **autumn of 1755 and the summer of 1756** — the first attempt anywhere in the country. *(Bjarni Pálsson is a name worth keeping: he became Iceland's first* landlæknir*, the first state physician. On the South Coast run he turns up again as Sveinn Pálsson's father-in-law.)*

Fast forward two centuries. **Rafveita Hafnarfjarðar**, the Hafnarfjörður electricity utility, drilled a research hole here — remembered as **Drottningarholan**, "the Queen's Hole" — and at around **230 metres down the hole blew.** Be straight with the guests about one thing: **the sources give the year as either 1947 or 1949 and I have not been able to settle it.** What nobody disputes is what it did next.

It blew, on and off, for **half a century.** Then on **Thursday 25 October 1999** it stopped — and shortly afterwards the ground beside it detonated in a steam explosion, opening a crater **about 43 metres across** and flinging mud **700 metres to the north.** The walkways you are standing on were laid out afterwards, by people who had just watched what this ground does when it is annoyed.
say: the geothermal field we are standing in
'sulphur mounds', hollow inside, built by gas turning to solid sulphur in open air
'the Queen's Hole', the borehole that blew for fifty years and then made a crater
one half of the pair who first drilled here in 1755
the other half, later Iceland's first landlæknir
the utility whose research hole this was

block.title: 💚 Grænavatn & Augun
block.sub: The Green Lake Nobody Can Fully Explain
block.cue: Look left — the small deep-green lake below the road. And in a moment, a pool on each side of us.
block.hook: This is the crater Icelandic geology textbooks use as **the** example of its type. It is roughly **45 metres deep** in a hole only a few hundred metres across. And the reason it is green — **the sources genuinely disagree**, and I am not going to pretend otherwise.
block.point: An explosion crater deep enough to hide a fifteen-storey building, full of water whose colour two respectable Icelandic sources explain two different ways.
block.mic: We are about to drive straight between the Eyes. Wave. It is polite.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Green is a strong claim on a grey day. On a morning like this it looks like a puddle with ambitions — but it is 45 metres deep, so mind where you stand."
bullets: **Grænavatn** is a **sprengigígur**, an explosion crater — blown out in a single blast where rising magma met groundwater. Vísindavefur, the University of Iceland's own science service, lists it as the type example for the whole category. Age: **somewhere around six to seven thousand years** — one source says 7,000, another says over 6,000, and nobody has narrowed it further.

Depth: **about 45 metres**, which is the figure the geologist **Sigurður Þórarinsson** published in **1950.** The official sign at Krýsuvík says **46.** Width: "a few hundred metres" is as precise as anyone will commit to. *(A lake nobody has bothered to measure properly, in a country that measures everything. I love it here.)*

Now the colour, honestly. **Sigurður Þórarinsson wrote in 1950 that it comes from sulphur compounds in the water.** The **official information board** at the site says it comes from **geothermal algae and crystals absorbing the green light of the sun.** Both are published. Neither has been settled. Take your pick, and if a guest tells you they read something different on the internet, they are probably reading a translation of one of these two.

The properly weird bit is in the rock thrown out of it. The tephra around Grænavatn contains **gabbro nodules** — lumps of a deep, coarse-grained rock the magma tore off on its way up. **Gabbro has not been found anywhere else in south-west Iceland.** This little hole punched through something nothing else has reached.

And in a second we drive **between two more of them.** **Augun** — "the Eyes" — are two small water-filled craters, one on each side of the road, sitting on their own **300-metre crater row.** There are at least **four separate rows** in this cluster, and **Gestsstaðavatn** to the west is the oldest. This is not one volcano. It is a small committee of them.
say: 'green lake', the explosion crater on the left
'explosion crater', formed in a single blast
'the eyes', the two small crater pools the road runs between
the oldest crater in the cluster, west of the road

block.title: ⛪ Krýsuvíkurkirkja
block.sub: The Church That Burned Down And Was Built Again By Apprentices
block.cue: Look right — the small black timber church under the hill.
block.hook: That church burned to the ground in the small hours of **2 January 2010.** The fire brigade got the call at **02:04** and by the time they arrived **the building had already fallen.** What you are looking at is an **exact replica**, built by carpentry students — and the altarpiece inside is **the original.**
block.point: A church burned by a stranger and rebuilt by teenagers learning to hold a chisel. The building is new. The altarpiece, the graveyard and the argument for doing it at all are not.
block.mic: The single most Icelandic sentence available: the painting was saved because somebody always put it away for the winter.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "A black church, a grey sky and no one for miles. This is what it looked like for most of its life — the postcard version is the unusual one."
bullets: The church that burned was built in **1857** by **Beinteinn Stefánsson**, a tenant farmer and carpenter at Arnarfell, out of **driftwood.** It stopped being a parish church around **1910**, was formally abolished in **1917**, and in **1929** it was deconsecrated and turned into somebody's house. Rebuilt and reconsecrated on **Whit Sunday, 31 May 1964**, taken into the care of the **National Museum** that same year, and legally protected on **1 January 1990.**
Then the fire. It was **arson** — a man in his early twenties was later given a **one-year suspended sentence** for setting it alight. Twenty years of protected status, gone in under an hour.

Here is the part I like. The replacement was built by the **carpentry school in Hafnarfjörður** — Iðnskólinn, later Tækniskólinn — working with the **National Museum** and a volunteer society, deliberately as a **teaching project in old timber technique.** The insurance payout from the old church bought the materials. It is an **exact copy** and it **seats 40.**

It came back on **9 October 2020**, and could not be lifted onto the old foundation that day because the wind got up. They craned it into place **the next morning.** COVID then delayed the consecration by nearly two years, until **Whit Sunday, 5 June 2022, at two o'clock.** It now belongs to the parish in **Hafnarfjörður.**

And the altarpiece. It was painted for this church by **Sveinn Björnsson** — who was a painter *and* the **chief detective of Hafnarfjörður**, which is a combination I have never encountered anywhere else. Every autumn, after the September service, the picture was taken down and **stored in Hafnarfjarðarkirkja for the winter.** Which is exactly where it was on the night of 2 January 2010. **The painting survived the fire because of a filing habit.**
Sveinn died in **1997** and is buried in that churchyard — the **first burial there since 1917**, and the last. At the 2022 consecration they poured communion wine on his grave.
say: the farmer-carpenter who built the original out of driftwood
painter, chief detective, and the only man buried in that churchyard since 1917

block.title: 🌋 The Reykjanes Fires
block.cue: Look ahead — the black ground either side of the road.
block.hook: Some of the lava we are about to walk on is younger than most of the phones on this bus.
block.point: Twelve eruptions in four years, then thirteen months of silence with the ground still swelling underneath. This is not the end of anything. It is the gap between two paragraphs.
block.mic: Geologists think this peninsula has woken up for the next few decades. We are not visiting a volcano today. We are visiting its lunch break.
block.weather: Weather pivot (always usable): "You don't need a view for this one. Everything I've just described is under the tyres."
bullets: After **1240 the peninsula went quiet for about 800 years** — then on **19 March 2021** a fissure split open at **Fagradalsfjall** and the Fires restarted. That first show ran six months; **more than 50,000 people** hiked out to watch a volcano like it was a gig.

Then **Meradalir (2022)** and **Litli-Hrútur** ("Little Ram", **2023**), before the action jumped north to the **Sundhnúkur crater row** by Grindavík. **Veðurstofa Íslands counts nine eruptions there.** The ninth began on **16 July 2025** and the Met Office **formally declared it over on 5 August 2025.** That is **twelve eruptions on this peninsula since 2021.**

**And then it stopped.** As of **18 August 2026** Veðurstofan's line is *"Kvikusöfnun og landris heldur áfram við Svartsengi"* — **magma accumulation and uplift are continuing at Svartsengi**, at a rate that has held steady for weeks. Around **ten small earthquakes a day**, most of them north of Grindavík. **No eruption since the fifth of August last year** — which makes today, as we drive across it, **thirteen months of quiet.** The longest pause of the whole series.

Be careful how you say the next part, because it is the honest one. **The ground is still rising. The magma is still arriving. The Met Office's own assessment is that a new dike intrusion, and possibly a new eruption, remains the most likely outcome.** *(For the exact volume under Svartsengi and today's hazard-zone colours — check vedur.is this morning. Those numbers move and a stale one is worse than none.)*

**"Could it go off while we're here?"** You will get asked. The honest answer: it could. Here is what matters — when the magma moves it goes **sideways first**, and that dike run is the warning. **Veðurstofa Íslands puts the historic range at twenty minutes to just over four hours.** Iceland has evacuated this ground repeatedly and has **not lost a single person to lava.** If it happens today we will know before it reaches the surface, and we will be somewhere else.

Two footnotes for the geology-curious. **Kristján Sæmundsson** and **Magnús Á. Sigurgeirsson** describe **Fagradalsfjall** as unlike anything else on the peninsula — **no central volcano, no proper fissure swarm, no high-temperature field**, roughly **5 km wide and 15 km long.** Its **picrite** comes up fast and from deep without loitering in a magma chamber, which is exactly why nothing filled slowly where the instruments could watch it. And the valley the 2021 fissure opened in, **Geldingadalir**, means the **wether valleys** — named for **castrated rams**, because sheep came there for a mouthful of grass. **Hallgrímur J. Ámundason** settled that at **Vísindavefurinn** on **24 March 2021**, five days into the eruption, from the place-name register of the farm **Hraun** in Grindavík.
say: where the fissure opened on 19 March 2021 after some 800 quiet years
'the wether valleys', the 2021 eruption site, named for castrated rams
'Little Ram', the site of the 2023 eruption
the crater row by Grindavík, nine eruptions from December 2023 to August 2025
the Icelandic Met Office, the people whose numbers these are

block.title: ⛓️ Festarfjall & Ísólfsskáli
block.sub: The Giant's Chain, And A Volcano Cut In Half
block.cue: Look left — the cliff falling into the bay, with a pale vertical stripe running up it.
block.hook: That stripe has a folk tale and a geology paper, and they describe **the same object.** The story says it is a **troll-woman's silver chain.** The geology says it is the **feeder pipe the volcano erupted through.** Both are correct.
block.point: A volcano sliced open by the sea so you can see the pipe it erupted through — and a folk tale that described that pipe accurately, centuries before anyone had a word for it.
block.mic: In 2021 Iceland defended a broadband cable from a volcano using diggers. And won.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the cliff has gone, the sound has not — that is the sea doing the cutting, in real time, at the pace of about one mountain per few thousand years."
bullets: **Festarfjall** is a **stapi** — a tuya. It erupted underneath the ice sheet: móberg breccia below, a cap of grey basalt on top where the eruption finally broke the surface. About **190 metres.** And then the sea did something rare and generous — **it cut the mountain in half.** You are looking at a **cross-section of a volcano's internal plumbing**, which almost never gets exposed.

The stripe is **Festin**, "the chain": a **basalt dyke**, and — per the geologist **Kristján Sæmundsson** — the **aðfærsluæð**, the conduit the magma actually came up. Harder than the rock around it, so as the sea grinds the cliff back, the dyke stands proud. The mountain is literally wearing its own throat on the outside.

The tale is recorded in **Rauðskinna**, the folk-tale collection — *not* Jón Árnason, and guides get that wrong. A troll-woman hung a **silver chain** over the cliff and declared that when the farmer at **Hraun** had a daughter named after her, and that girl walked on the sand below, the chain would fall and be hers. **She then neglected to mention her own name.** So the chain is still up there. *(Worst-designed raffle in the North Atlantic.)*

The farm ahead is **Ísólfsskáli**, documented from **1703** as a Skálholt property. Bishop **Brynjólfur Sveinsson** ran a fishing station from it, and in **1734** the Skálholt boat was lost here with **ten men.** The 1703 land register warned the well was so bad the farm might have to be abandoned for want of water. The **earthquakes of 28–29 January 1905** brought the kitchen down, the farm stood empty **three years**, and in **1916** they rebuilt it **further back from the sea.** For decades it was the **last farm on this whole peninsula living purely off farming.**

One honest correction, because it gets repeated: **the eruptions of 2023 to 2025 did not reach Ísólfsskáli.** Those were all at the **Sundhnúkur crater row above Grindavík.** The drama on *this* road was **2021**, when lava came down into **Nátthagi** and civil protection bulldozed **eight-metre barriers** to keep it off **Suðurstrandarvegur** — because this road is **Grindavík's escape route** and it carries the peninsula's **fibre-optic cable.**
say: 'chain mountain', the half-eroded tuya on the left
'the chain', the basalt dyke running up the cliff face
'red skin', the folk-tale collection the legend comes from
the valley the 2021 lava ran into, just above this road

block.title: 🥾 Fagradalsfjall
block.cue: At the trailhead, before we set off.
block.hook: Everything from here to the ridge is younger than the year 2021. **You are about to walk on land that did not exist when you booked your last holiday.**
block.point: A four-year-old landscape, thirty metres deep, made of mantle rock that came up in a hurry — and it will look exactly like this long after everyone here is gone.
block.mic: Most of the planet is old. This bit is four. Try to be nice to it and please stay off it.
block.weather: Weather pivot (cloud, rain or wind on the path): "If the ridge is gone we shorten the walk and stand on the edge of the flow instead. The interesting rock is at your boots, not on the skyline — and the newest land in Europe is just as new in the rain."
bullets: The **19 March 2021** eruption ran **six months to the day — to 18 September 2021** — and left roughly **150 million cubic metres** of lava across **4.8 km²**, averaging **more than 30 metres thick**, peaking through May and June at around **twelve cubic metres a second.** For scale: that is a new field of rock deeper than a ten-storey building, poured out of a crack in a valley nobody had heard of.

What makes it strange is what it was made of. Fagradalsfjall's magma is **picrite**, and it came up **fast, and from deep**, without sitting in a shallow chamber first. Most eruptions are fed by magma that has been parked and stewing. This one was mantle material arriving more or less directly. Geologists were, to use the technical term, delighted.

**The rule for the next two hours: do not walk on the lava.** That is Safetravel's wording. The crust looks solid and is not, the rock is volcanic glass and will open a hand to the bone, and parts of this field are **still warm underneath** years on. Stay on the marked path, and if you want the photo, take it from the path.

The other rule is the air. **Check the gas dispersal forecast** — geothermal and volcanic ground gives off **sulphur dioxide and hydrogen sulphide**, both heavier than air, both worst in hollows and dips on a still day. **If it smells strongly of eggs in a dip, go up, not on.**

And look at what is growing. Almost nothing — and that is the lesson. There is **no acid rain here, no baking heat, no forest** to break rock down. Iceland barely weathers. **These 2021 flows will still look like this in a thousand years**, which is exactly why the medieval lava we drove over this morning also looks like last week's.
say: the magnesium-rich basalt that came up here from deep, and fast
the valley the flow pushed into, and the shortest of the marked routes
'long ridge', the viewpoint route on the green markers

block.title: ⚡ Svartsengi
block.sub: The Power Plant That Made The Lagoon
block.cue: Look right — tall white steam towers rising out of the lava field.
block.hook: That power station accidentally built the Blue Lagoon — and then in 2024 had to be walled off from lava by the metre.
block.point: Iceland pulls about **30% of its electricity** and **90% of its heating** from geothermal. Svartsengi is the textbook made real — and then defended with a digger.
block.mic: A power station that accidentally made a spa, then had to be saved by hand from the volcano it lives off.
block.weather: Weather pivot (if the towers are hidden): "You will smell it before you see it, and on a day like this the steam plume and the cloud are the same object."
bullets: ***Svartsengi* = Black Meadow**, for the scorched ground it stands on. **Geothermal water from 1976, electricity from 1978 — the first plant anywhere to make both from the same well field.** That first turbine was a modest **1 MW**, quietly running the pumps for its own boreholes.

It drills **1,000 to 2,000 m** down to water at **240°C**, and now makes **85 MW of electricity** and **190 MW of heat.** The **seventh generating unit came on line on 1 December 2025**, replacing units three and four. That heat is piped across the **Suðurnes**, a region now well over **30,000** people. The **Blue Lagoon** was never planned — just mineral-rich wastewater pooling in the lava next door.

In **2024**, the eruptions sent lava straight at it. The plant was evacuated and defended with **earthen barriers averaging seven metres**, bulldozed into place in days. **The lava stopped short. It is still running today** — and the same reservoir it drinks from is the one being refilled under our feet right now.
say: 'Black Meadow', the 1976 plant whose wastewater accidentally made the Blue Lagoon
the southern peninsula region its hot water heats

block.title: ⛰️ Þorbjörn
block.sub: The Mountain That Gave The First Warning
block.cue: Look ahead and right — the flat-topped hill standing over the town, with masts on the summit.
block.hook: On **26 January 2020** the Icelandic Met Office published a sentence it had never been able to write before: in **nearly three decades** of precise measurement, **nothing on this peninsula had ever risen this fast.** That was the first alarm of everything that followed. Grindavík was evacuated **three years, nine months and fifteen days later.**
block.point: A hill with a collapsed summit, fifteen hanged thieves, an American radar station and a Met Office GPS mast — and it is the last of those that emptied a town.
block.mic: Iceland's early-warning system for the biggest evacuation in its modern history was a lump of rock that had already been a hideout, a gallows story and a war station. It just took the promotion.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If Þorbjörn has gone, that is fine — the whole point of this story is that the thing that mattered was never visible anyway. It was two centimetres of ground, and only an instrument could see it."
bullets: **Þorbjörn** — properly **Þorbjarnarfell** — is **243 metres**, and it is **móberg**, built underneath ice like Sveifluháls this morning. But this one took **two separate glacial periods** to finish, which makes it **one of the older hills on the peninsula** — considerably older than Fagradalsfjall, where we were standing at eleven o'clock. Look at the top: it has **fallen in on itself.** There is a fault and a small rift valley up there, and — this is the odd part — **that fault runs north to south, straight across the south-west-to-north-east grain of every other crack on Reykjanes.**

The cleft splitting the summit is **Þjófagjá**, Thieves' Gorge, and *Huld* — the nineteenth-century folk collection — says **fifteen thieves** once lived in it, robbing Grindavík's sheep. Nobody could get at them. Then a farmer's son from **Hóp** noticed they all bathed at **Baðsvellir** every Saturday, taking turns guarding the clothes. Once they trusted him with the pile, **he turned one shirt-sleeve and one trouser-leg inside out on every single set**, and ran. They lost the race getting dressed, chased him across the lava in their underwear, cut their feet to ribbons, and were caught and hanged at **Gálgaklettar** — Gallows Rocks. The story ends with one of the great Icelandic shrugs: ***"the farmer's son became an unlucky man, but it is not recorded what befell him."***

There was a war up there too. **Camp Vail** was a **United States Army Air Forces radar station** — American, not British, and guides get that wrong. The road up the mountain was begun in **early October 1941** by an air-force construction unit working alongside **men hired in Grindavík**, and the station went live on **18 April 1942**: **fourteen Nissen huts** and a generator, down in the crater, with the radar on the summit. It was **the best station in the country for spotting low-flying aircraft over Faxaflói** — and it was **usable only 60% of the time**, because the antenna had to be folded down that often in the wind. Most of it was sold or demolished after the war. **A single stone hearth is still standing up there.**

Now the part that matters. On **21 January 2020** the ground started rising — **3 to 4 millimetres a day**, about **two centimetres** by the time it was announced on the **26th**. Say this next bit accurately, because almost everyone says it wrong: **the centre of the uplift was not under Þorbjörn. It was just west of it.** Underneath, roughly **a million cubic metres of magma at three to five kilometres down.** On the **22nd**, two earthquakes of **magnitude 3.7 and 3.6** were felt as far north as **Borgarnes.** At **17:19 on the 26th**, the National Commissioner declared an **óvissustig** — an uncertainty phase. That was the first alert level of this entire volcanic episode.

And then nothing happened, for years. The uplift came and went in pulses. That alert stayed in force. **On the night of 10 November 2023, at 23:48, Grindavík was evacuated** — and the eruptions we have been talking about all day began. **The warning arrived first, and it arrived from this hill.**

Two footnotes. There is a **GPS station on that summit, code THOB**, and Benedikt Ófeigsson of the Met Office **installed it at dusk at the end of January 2020** — put there because of exactly this. And note the language has moved on: **the Met Office no longer calls it the Þorbjörn signal. Every bulletin now says Svartsengi.** *(The masts you can actually see up there are telephone and aviation kit, not science. The instrument that matters is small and you cannot see it from here.)*

One thing under the wheels. The barriers protecting the town and the power plant now run **13.5 kilometres**, hold about **2.5 million cubic metres** of material — the engineers at Verkís cheerfully put that at **"more than a hundred Hallgrímskirkjas"** — and stand **seven metres on average, twenty-four at the highest point.** They cost the country around **seven billion krónur**, under a law Alþingi passed on **13 November 2023, three days after the evacuation.** And **one of them crosses this road.** *(This tarmac is also newer than most of the guests: **Suðurstrandarvegur opened on 21 June 2012** — 57 kilometres to Þorlákshöfn. The road it replaced had been in service since 1946.)*
say: 'Thór's bear', properly Þorbjarnarfell, the 243 m móberg hill above Grindavík
'thieves' gorge', the cleft in its summit
'gallows rocks', where the fifteen were hanged
'uncertainty phase', the lowest civil-protection alert level
'the south coast road', Route 427, opened 21 June 2012

block.title: 🌋 Grindavík
block.cue: In Grindavík. Doors open, but stay on made ground.
block.hook: This town stood for a thousand years. On **10 November 2023** the ground tore open beneath it in a single night — and every single person got out. **Then 874 of them moved back in.**
block.point: The full hazard case in one town — lava, ground rupture and gas, then house fires, lost roads and a relocated fleet, then the human tier: a town evacuated overnight, bought out, and slowly reoccupied. And the response that made it survivable: **real-time monitoring, hours of warning, state-funded buyouts, and barriers built in days.**
block.mic: Iceland is the only country on Earth that bought an entire town from its own citizens — and 874 of them moved back in anyway.
block.weather: Weather pivot (if it's foul): "Stay tight and stay on the tarmac. On a day like this the cracks are harder to see, and that is the only reason I am being boring about it."
bullets: **Grindavík** was settled around **934 CE** — one of the first Reykjanes communities and a major North Atlantic **cod harbour.** By December 2023 it held about **3,720 people.**

On **10 November 2023**, thousands of earthquakes in a few hours drove a **dike roughly 15 kilometres long** under the town. Fissures **metres wide** opened through roads, gardens and house foundations, the ground **subsided about a metre** and **pulled apart by around 120 centimetres.** The whole town was **evacuated in one night.** In **January 2024**, lava reached the streets for the first time — houses burned, roads buried.

Further eruptions followed through 2024 and into 2025 as the **Sundhnúkur crater row** kept reactivating. **Earthen barriers built in days** — six to ten metres by design, twenty-four at the highest point — saved some streets and were overrun on others. For all that, **none of this lava ever reached the sea.** It crossed the Grindavíkurvegur road again and again and pushed into the town on **14 January 2024**, but it never made the coast. The last time lava ran into the sea on this peninsula was the **twelfth century.**

And then people started coming back. The state buyout company **Þórkatla** bought **over 90% of the homes**, and most residents did leave for good — but at **1 April 2026** Þjóðskrá had **874 registered residents** living here again. The **school is open** for the autumn term, the **library** has been brought back to its feet, and the **harbour and the power plant never stopped at all.** In **April 2026** Alþingi debated a formal framework for rebuilding the community. *(Not a ghost town. A very small town with an extremely dramatic CV.)*

**Say this bit out loud, because it changes how people behave:** the ground here is still moving and **crevasses are still opening.** That is why we stay on made surfaces and off verges, gardens and shortcuts. People live here. They did not survive all that to have a coach party fall down a hole in their street.

One older raid, because this harbour has form. On **20 June 1627** corsairs out of **Salé** in Morocco under **Murat Reis** took **12 to 15 Icelanders** from Grindavík, along with Danish and Dutch crew, and sailed them to **Algiers** — the opening act of the **Tyrkjaránið**, the Turkish Raid. Of everyone seized around Iceland that summer, **only 27** ever made it home, **nine years later.**
say: the fishing town settled around 934, evacuated in a single night on 10 November 2023
the crater row north of the town that kept reactivating through 2024 and 2025
the state company that bought over 90% of the homes
'the Turkish Raid', the corsair raids of 1627

block.title: ⛳ Staðarhverfi & Húsatóftir
block.cue: Look right — the flat green ground running down to the shore, and the little graveyard.
block.hook: Grindavík was never one town. It was **three villages**, and this is the one that **lost.** There is a golf course on it now, and underneath the fairways are a **Danish customs post**, a **churchyard in use since about the year 1200**, and iron **mooring bolts** for tying up sailing ships.
block.point: A district that had a church, a harbour, a royal trading post and two centuries of paperwork, and now has eighteen holes and a graveyard the whole town still uses.
block.mic: Somewhere out there is a golfer who has sliced a ball into a protected eighteenth-century mooring bolt. I hope it counted as a hazard.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The reason nobody lives here any more is the weather doing exactly this, for four hundred years, plus the sea taking the sand."
bullets: The three *hverfi* were **Þórkötlustaðahverfi** in the east, **Járngerðarstaðahverfi** in the middle — that is modern Grindavík — and **Staðarhverfi**, here in the west. The middle one won because it had the better landing, and because **the area's first shop opened there around 1900.** Grindavík got its town charter in **1947.** Staðarhverfi just quietly emptied: the parsonage at **Staður** lasted until **1928**, the farm at **Húsatóftir** to about **1946**, and **Staður** itself to around **1964.**

There has been a **church at Staður since at least about 1200** — it is in Bishop Páll Jónsson's church register. It was abolished on **26 September 1909**, the day the new church at Járngerðarstaðir was consecrated. But look again: **the graveyard is still the burial ground for the whole parish.** The town moved. The dead stayed.

In the bell-gate hangs a bell reading **"SS. Anlaby 1898 Hull."** It is the ship's bell of a Hull trawler that went onto the rocks here on the night of **14 January 1902** and was **lost with all hands.**

This was also, for eighty years, **where Iceland traded with Denmark.** The 1602 monopoly assigned Grindavík harbour to **Copenhagen.** Merchants stopped coming in **1639**, resumed in **1665** with booths at **Arfadalsvík** right here, put up a proper trading house in **1731** — and then in **1745 simply stopped sailing**, blaming sand ruining the harbour. Free trade came in **1787**, the buyer went bankrupt in **1796**, and the buildings were **pulled down in 1806.**

You can still see how they moored. There is an iron bolt in **Bindisker** on one side of the bay and another in **Barlestarsker** on the other, and a **chain was run between them** to lash the trading ships down. The bolt has been **legally protected since 1930.** *(There is a protected national monument in the rough.)*

The name is the joke. **Húsatóftir** means **"the house-ruins"** — because after the merchants left, somebody built a farm **inside the foundations of their warehouses.** The golf club was founded on **14 May 1981** and the clubhouse is a **1930 farmhouse.**

And settle one thing before anyone asks: **the 1627 corsair raid did not happen here.** In 1627 the trade — and the ships — were still at Járngerðarstaðir. The merchants only moved west **thirty-eight years later.**
say: 'the Staður district', the westernmost of Grindavík's three villages
'the house-ruins', named for the merchants' foundations
the middle district, which grew into modern Grindavík
the bay where the Danish trading booths stood from 1665

block.title: 🎬 Sandvík
block.sub: The Beach That Played Iwo Jima
block.cue: Look left — the wide black sand bay.
block.hook: In the summer of **2005**, **Clint Eastwood** brought a film unit to that beach and shot most of *Flags of Our Fathers* on it. **Iceland played a Pacific island.** And this morning's stop — Krýsuvík — was the second location.
block.point: A volcanic beach on the edge of the Arctic doubling for a volcanic island in the Pacific, because the one thing you cannot fake is sand that collapses under a running man.
block.mic: Iceland's film career in one sentence: if the script needs somewhere that looks like nowhere on Earth, this is where they come. Reykjanes has been the Moon, Mars and now the Pacific — and it has not moved an inch.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Rain, black sand and a grey sea. Congratulations — you are now looking at the actual conditions they filmed in."
bullets: The reason is the sand. They started scouting in **Hawaii** and it did not work. The location manager, **Kokayi Ampah**, put it bluntly: the beaches were not long or wide enough, and *"it was very tropical — it didn't fit the look of Iwo Jima after it had been pounded by bombshells for a month."* Iwo Jima itself was out of the question — it is a war grave.

So he went looking for black sand at scale, and Eastwood's own line about flying in was: *"Flying in over the black sand beaches and lava fields, I could see that Iceland had the rugged and unusual look we needed."*

The detail that makes the whole thing work: the Marines in the film have to **climb a slope of loose black sand that gives way under them.** That is not choreography. That is what this beach does, and it is exactly what the real beach did in 1945.

Practical Icelandic footnote: the production chartered **two Icelandic Coast Guard vessels** for the landing shots at **a million krónur a day**, and hired **several hundred Icelandic extras**, organised into platoons. And **Mount Suribachi is not there** — the mountain in the film is entirely computer-generated.
The other thing on this shore, and you can walk it: the **Bridge Between Continents**, a footbridge over a rift fissure — which we will come to properly at the lighthouse.
say: 'sand bay', where Flags of Our Fathers was filmed in summer 2005
the Coast Guard vessel chartered for the shoot, named for the god

block.title: 🔌 Reykjanesvirkjun
block.cue: Look right — the second power station, and the steam behind it.
block.hook: The plant we are passing started up in May 2006. Within months the ground at our next stop began to boil harder, swallowed its own car park, and had to be rebuilt.
block.point: Take pressure out of a geothermal reservoir and the surface answers back. Gunnuhver is the receipt for the power station we just passed.
block.mic: They built a power station. The ground next door read the plans and decided to compete.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If you cannot see the plant, you will certainly see what it did — the steam at the next stop is the loud half of this story."
bullets: **HS Orka's Reykjanes power plant** began producing electricity in **May 2006** with **two 50 MW turbines.** Today it runs at **130 MW of installed capacity**, fed by **28 wells** with something like **55 kilometres of drilling** between them. This is the ridge itself being tapped — the hottest, most direct geothermal resource on the peninsula.

And there was a consequence nobody sold tickets for. As **pressure in the reservoir drew down**, steaming at the surface **increased markedly** at **Gunnuhver**, a few hundred metres away. The field surged and grew. It **destroyed the access road and the old walking platforms.** By **2008** field reports describe a **brand-new mud spring about eight metres across, flinging mud four metres into the air**, and steam rising halfway up the slopes of **Skálafell.**

New boardwalks and viewing platforms — with universal access — were **completed by summer 2010.** So when we get out in a minute and I tell you to stay on the boards, understand that the boards themselves are the second attempt.
say: the Reykjanes power plant, producing since May 2006
the hill behind, which had steam halfway up it by 2008

block.title: 👻 Gunnuhver
block.sub: The Ghost They Paid Eight Bottles To Move
block.cue: At Gunnuhver, on the boardwalk.
block.hook: This is where the peninsula stops pretending to be solid ground. And it is named after a woman who was **so angry about a stolen cooking pot** that it took a sorcerer-priest, a ball of yarn and eight bottles of brennivín to get rid of her.
block.point: Folklore doing the job of a warning sign, centuries before anyone built a boardwalk: *don't go near the hot ground, there's something angry in it.*
block.mic: Everywhere else, ghost stories are entertainment. Here it's a risk assessment with a plot.
block.weather: Weather pivot (steam and murk): "Perfect. You cannot tell where the weather stops and the ground starts — which is more or less the honest description of this place anyway."
bullets: The headline act, on the official site panels, is **Iceland's largest mud pool — about 20 metres across**, boiling behind a rim of grey mud, with steam columns you can spot from far down the road. Around it the ground has been cooked into reds, yellows and whites, and the soundtrack is pure percussion — plops, hisses, and the occasional full-throated roar.

The recipe is the same as Seltún's and just as vicious. **Steam rises off the deep reservoir, condenses near the surface, and carries carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulphide with it.** Those gases turn the water acid, and the acid **digests fresh lava into soft clay.** Everything you are photographing is bedrock that has been dissolved.

Now the ghost. The name means **Gunna's hot spring**, and Gunna — properly **Guðrún Önundardóttir** — earned it the hard way, about **four hundred years ago** by the legend preserved in **Jón Árnason's** great folk-tale collection. She was a poor woman on the Suðurnes who fell behind on a debt to a man called **Vilhjálmur**, and he confiscated the one thing she could not spare: **her cooking pot.** She died soon after, absolutely furious, and stayed that way.

At the funeral **her coffin turned suspiciously light**, and people swore they heard her say there was no need to dig deep, as she did not plan to lie there long. She kept her word. Vilhjálmur was found dead in a hollow, badly battered, and the hauntings escalated until Gunna was **riding rooftops** and terrorising people and livestock alike.

Salvation arrived in liquid form. Two men rode to **Eiríkur Magnússon**, the sorcerer-priest at **Vogsósar**, who agreed to help **for a fee of eight bottles of brennivín.** He handed over a **ball of yarn** with instructions to get Gunna to grab the loose end. When she did, she snapped that she had expected **the Devil himself, not the old man of Vogsósar.** The ball rolled, Gunna followed, and at the hot spring she circled until the yarn ran out — **then plunged in. She has been steaming about it ever since.**

**The current vents largely took shape after an earthquake swarm in 1967**, and then reorganised themselves again after **2006**, as we just discussed. Off the boardwalk the crust can be **a thin lid over boiling acid clay.** Stay on the platforms, keep children by the hand, and let the steam come to you.
say: 'Gunna's hot spring', and the Icelandic hv sounds like kv
the sorcerer-priest at Vogsósar who took the job
the silica hill with the viewing ramp
Icelandic caraway schnapps, and the going rate for ghost removal was eight bottles

block.title: 🗼 Reykjanesviti
block.sub: The Lighthouse The Ground Tried To Evict
block.cue: At Reykjanesviti — the white tower on the hill.
block.hook: Most countries build a lighthouse to warn ships about the dangerous bit. Iceland built its first one in 1878 and then discovered **the dangerous bit was the lighthouse.**
block.point: Built, broken by earthquake, rebuilt on higher ground. One small tower with the entire biography of living in Iceland written into it.
block.mic: The force that condemned the first lighthouse in 1887 is the same force that emptied Grindavík in 2023. Different century, same ground, same argument.
block.weather: Weather pivot (wind and spray, which is the default here): "This is the weather it was built for. If it were calm and sunny you would not understand why they needed it."
bullets: **Reykjanesviti is the oldest lighthouse site in Iceland**, and that comes with an asterisk worth explaining. The first tower was lit in **1878** — the country's very first — out on the wind-hammered **Valahnúkur** cliffs. It lasted **eight years** before an earthquake in **1887** cracked it up.

By **1905** quakes and surf had chewed the headland so badly that the structure was in real danger of sliding into the sea. Not "might erode eventually" — going to fall in. So a second tower went up on the safer hill of **Bæjarfell** between roughly **1907 and 1908**, and the original was finished off with **explosives on 16 April 1908** — a rare case of a lighthouse being decommissioned by demolition charge rather than a retirement party.

**Settle the argument for them:** the **site** dates to **1878**. The **tower you are photographing** is the **1907–08** model, with re-illumination cited for **1929**. Both statements are true. The architect was **Frederik Kjørboe**, the engineer **Thorvald Krabbe** — the man who effectively ran Iceland's lighthouse and harbour building for decades.

On height, **the sources disagree and I am not going to tidy it up for you** — some list the tower at about **26 metres** with the light **69 metres** above the sea, others give **31** and **73**. Either way the trick is the one every Icelander learns eventually: **you do not need to build tall if you build on a hill.** The light throws a **double flash every 30 seconds** as the landfall guide for ships steering toward Reykjavík and Keflavík. The country's front-door light, left on for the neighbours.

Walk the other way and you reach the **Bridge Between Continents**, a footbridge over a sandy rift. Cross it and you have — in the brochure version — walked from North America to Eurasia. Geologists will concede the point politely, note that the plates really are separating **at roughly the speed your fingernails grow**, and then remind you the real boundary is a **messy zone, not one photogenic gap.** The image still holds: the **Mid-Atlantic Ridge spends almost all of its 16,000 kilometres hidden under the ocean**, and here it climbs into the daylight.
Icelanders voted this **the most popular lighthouse in the country in a 2007 survey.** We do love a stubborn thing that refuses to fall down.
say: 'Reykjanes lighthouse', and viti is Icelandic for lighthouse
the coastal cliff where the 1878 original stood
the hill the current tower stands on, chosen in 1907 for being safely inland
the engineer behind half of Iceland's early lighthouses and harbours
'the bridge between continents', the footbridge over the rift

block.title: 🐧 Eldey & The Great Auk
block.sub: The Rock Where A Species Ended
block.cue: Look out to sea — the flat-topped island on the horizon. And the bronze bird on the headland.
block.hook: On that rock, in the **first days of June 1844**, two men each killed a bird, a third came back empty-handed, and **the great auk ceased to exist.** Not "became rare." **Ended.** You are looking at the exact place.
block.point: A bird that could not fly, on an island nobody could reach without ropes, hunted to the last two by three men in a rowing boat working to a collector's order — in **1844**, within the lifetime of people whose grandchildren owned cameras.
block.mic: The gannets out there are thriving — nearly fifteen thousand pairs of them. The auks are a statue. Same rock. That is the whole lesson, and it does not need a speech from me.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If Eldey is gone in the murk, that is normal — most days it is a rumour. Look at the bronze one instead. That one is always in."
bullets: **Eldey** is a **77-metre** sheer-sided cliff island about **15 kilometres** offshore. It holds **14,810 nesting pairs of gannets** — that is the last published count, from **2013–14** — which is **39.8% of every gannet in Iceland.** Be careful with the superlative: it is **Iceland's largest** gannet colony and **one of the world's largest.** The biggest are in the British Isles.

It has been protected since **1940**, by a law written specifically for it — **the first bird reserve in Iceland.** Declared a *friðland* in **1960**, re-protected in **1974.** You cannot land without permission, and **you may not fire a gun within two kilometres of it.**

Now the auks. Their real stronghold was **Geirfuglasker** — Great Auk Skerry — further out. On **6 or 7 March 1830** a submarine eruption began and **destroyed the island.** The survivors moved to Eldey, onto a ledge called **Undirlendið**. In the summer of **1834** two brothers took **thirteen** of them off that ledge and sold them to merchants in Keflavík and Reykjavík. Then it was one or two at a time.

The last hunt was commissioned by a **collector in Copenhagen** who wanted specimens. Three men climbed Eldey: **Jón Brandsson**, **Sigurður Ísleifsson** and **Ketill Ketilsson.** Jón and Sigurður each caught and strangled a bird. Ketill found nothing, because there was nothing left to find. **The egg the pair were sitting on was broken and thrown away.** The birds' internal organs are still in the natural history museum in **Copenhagen**, catalogued.

**On the date, be precise, because half the internet is wrong.** The traditional date is **3 June 1844.** The most recent peer-reviewed work narrows it only to **between the 2nd and the 5th of June 1844.** The University of Iceland's own science service says simply "early June." *(A United Nations page says 3 July. It is wrong. Do not repeat it.)*
The bronze great auk on the headland is by the sculptor **Ólöf Nordal.** It stands here, facing the island, on purpose.
say: 'fire island', the gannet rock offshore, protected since 1940
the great auk, extinct since June 1844
'great auk skerry', the colony destroyed by eruption in 1830
the sculptor of the bronze auk on the headland

block.title: ⚓ Hafnir
block.sub: A Ship With Nobody Aboard, And A Hall That Is Too Old
block.cue: Look right — the church and the scatter of houses down by the shore.
block.hook: Two things happened in this village that should not have. A **ship with no crew** delivered Iceland's biggest timber windfall of the century. And archaeologists dug up a **hall that appears to be older than the settlement of Iceland is supposed to be.**
block.point: A village that got a ninth-century hall and a free shipload of American hardwood, and is not famous for either.
block.mic: An unmanned ship crossed the Atlantic and made landfall at the only place on the coast that badly needed timber. If you want to argue that Iceland has luck, this is exhibit A.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Weather exactly like this is how the Jamestown ended up on that shore. It is the reason the story exists."
bullets: Start with the hall. In **November 2002** the archaeologist **Bjarni F. Einarsson** was looking at an aerial photograph and spotted the outline of a longhouse in the field **behind Kirkjuvogskirkja.** They dug two holes. The second hit the **long-hearth** just under a metre down. Charcoal from that hearth went for radiocarbon dating.

Say the result carefully, because it matters. The site's own museum — **Byggðasafn Reykjanesbæjar** — describes it as a **ninth-century hall, probably built before the date conventionally given for the settlement of Iceland, and in use into the tenth century.** The information board on site says only *"strong indication that the farm was built before the year 900."* That is the claim. It has not been overturned and it has not been formally endorsed. **Do not let anyone tell you it rewrites the textbooks — the excavators themselves have not said that.**

The building was about **17 metres long and 7 wide**, with two sunken structures beside it, and a geophysical survey suggested **five more buildings** around it. It has been re-turfed, with the hearth marked out in lava slabs, so you can walk the outline.

Now the ship. In **June 1881** a huge American vessel came ashore here — **three masts, three decks, about 110 metres long** — **completely empty of people.** She had been abandoned in the Atlantic months earlier, her crew taken off by a steamer, and she had drifted for something like **four months** with seventeen feet of water in her. When Icelanders reached the deck there was **grass growing on it.**

She was the **Jamestown**, fully loaded with **finished hardwood** bound for England. On the date, the sources fight: the **US Navy report says 26 June.** The **Icelandic eyewitness** — Ólafur Ketilsson, who was **sixteen and standing on the wreck**, writing it up in 1930 — says **Whit Sunday morning**, which was **5 June.** They cannot both be right and I am not going to smooth it over for you.

The locals **refused the salvage job.** Three Reykjavík men took it on, hired crews at **25 aurar an hour**, and — this detail is from the boy who was there — paid them **in gold and silver, every Saturday evening.** The timber went into houses right across Suðurnes and inland. **Þorvarðarhús**, the oldest house in Keflavík, is clad in it. A luthier has since built violins and cellos using Jamestown wood for the soundposts.
One of the ship's **anchors stands beside Kirkjuvogskirkja** in this village. The other is at Sáðgerði in Sandgerði.
say: the church, with the Jamestown's anchor beside it
the excavated hall behind the church
the archaeologist who spotted it on an aerial photo in 2002

block.title: ✈️ Keflavík
block.sub: The Airport You Arrived At, And The Base That Built It
block.cue: Look left — the terminal, the control tower, and the flat ground running away behind it.
block.hook: Almost everyone on this bus landed there. It was built by the **US military in the Second World War**, it was an **American base for fifty-five years**, and the Americans went home on **30 September 2006.** The airport you walked through is the leftovers.
block.point: A wartime airstrip became a Cold War base, became a shopping-and-housing district, became the busiest transatlantic stopover in the North Atlantic. Same tarmac. Four completely different countries' worth of history.
block.mic: Iceland is the only nation that got handed an entire American town and turned it into student flats and a business park. Somewhere on Ásbrú there is a family living in a barracks block, complaining about the parking.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If it is closed in, take comfort: this airport has one of the best weather records in the country. That is the whole reason it is here and not somewhere prettier."
bullets: There were originally **two** airfields. **Patterson Field** was started in **February 1942** up by Fitjar. **Meeks Field** — which is the one still here — was begun that summer on Háaleiti by a US Navy construction battalion, with about **3,000 men** working on it at the peak. It opened in **1943.** *(Sources give three different days in March and April 1943 for the ceremony, so I will give you the year and keep my dignity.)*

Both were named after **young American pilots killed in Iceland.** Meeks died in a crash at Reykjavík airport on **19 August 1941**, shortly after arriving in the country. The busiest month was **June 1944**: **1,050 aircraft** through the field, and on one day, **115 four-engine bombers** on the ground at once.

The airfields became Icelandic property under the **1946 agreement** and the last wartime US troops left on **8 April 1947.** Then the Cold War arrived: the **defence agreement was signed on 5 May 1951**, and the base ran for the next fifty-five years. On **1 March 1990** there were **3,294 US military personnel** here — **4,987** counting families — plus **1,086 Icelandic employees.** By January **2005** the military figure was down to **1,453.** On **15 March 2006** Washington gave notice, and on **30 September 2006** they were gone.

What happens when a foreign army hands you a town? Iceland set up a development company on **24 October 2006** and turned the base into **Ásbrú** — housing, businesses and a campus. *(The university side has just changed hands again: teaching stayed on Ásbrú but the **University of Iceland took it over on 1 January 2026.**)*

The airport itself became the country's front door. The **Leifur Eiríksson terminal** opened on **14 April 1987** at **23,000 square metres.** In **2025** it handled **8,159,461 passengers** — the fourth-busiest year in its history. **2.2 million** of those, **27%**, never left the building — they were changing planes between America and Europe, which is the entire business model of this country's aviation.
And the town is **Reykjanesbær**, created on **11 June 1994** by merging **Keflavík, Njarðvík and Hafnir** — **10,181 people** at the time.

One story for the road. On **9 October 1986**, Air Force One landed here at **five past seven in the evening** carrying **Ronald Reagan**, for the summit with **Gorbachev** in Reykjavík. The talks collapsed. On the **12th**, before flying home, Reagan stopped at this base to speak to the American personnel and explained why he was late: *"I called Nancy and told her I wouldn't be home for dinner."*
say: 'driftwood bay', the airport and the town
the municipality formed in 1994 from Keflavík, Njarðvík and Hafnir
'the bridge of the Æsir', the former base, now a district
the neighbouring town, part of the 1994 merger

block.title: 🪦 Vogastapi
block.sub: The Ghost That May Have Been Made Redundant Last December
block.cue: Look left — the long flat-topped headland dropping into the sea.
block.hook: In **1990** the folklorist **Árni Björnsson** wrote that the ghost of this headland had gone quiet since the new road was built, and predicted he would **vanish altogether once the road was finally doubled.** That doubling was completed on **11 December 2025.** So either he has retired, or he is extremely annoyed.
block.point: A headland with three recorded deaths from exposure, a fourth party who went over the cliff, and a ghost tradition that is really just an unlit road with a drop on one side and no reliable directions.
block.mic: They spent thirty-eight years arguing about doubling this road. The ghost outlasted the debate. Then in December they finished it — and by the best available folklore, that was his notice period.
block.weather: Weather pivot (ideal here): "This is the weather that killed people on this headland. On a clear day the ghost story sounds silly. Today it does not."
bullets: **Vogastapi** is about **80 metres** high, older grey basalt sitting between the young lavas either side of it. Its high point is **Grímshóll**, and there is a view-disc up there. The municipality's own website states, without hedging, that **the Stapi is haunted.**

The University of Iceland's science service is refreshingly deflating about the ghost. **Stapadraugurinn** — the Stapi ghost — has **no origin story at all.** Nobody recorded who he was or how he got there. All that survives is that he roughed travellers up. The one documented case is from the **1870s**: a man from Garður was found half-dead on the headland, carried to the farm at Stapakot, and **never once explained what had happened to him.** They blamed the ghost.

The better-attested haunting has a reason. A traveller asked for lodging in **Vogar** and was **turned away.** He set off over the Stapi in bad weather and was **found dead by Grímshóll the next morning.** They carried his body back to the very farm that had refused him, and buried him. The haunting started immediately after. *(There is a moral in there and it is not subtle.)*

The modern version is a **phantom hitchhiker.** He stands at the roadside, gets in when someone kindly stops, will not say where he is going, says nothing at all — and after a while is simply not there.

And here is why the ghost stories are so thick on this one headland: **people kept dying on it.** **28 January 1859** — Þorsteinn from Stapakot, lost in the open. Around **1865** — a fish-buyer named Egill and his companions took the wrong path in a blizzard and **went over the cliffs.** Their bodies were found broken at the bottom. Around **1870** — Sveinbjörn from Stapakot, exposure again. Árni Óla wrote the plain explanation in **1961**: *because so many died on the Stapi, it was long thought deeply haunted.*

The road is the sequel. This stretch became **Iceland's first concrete road** in the national network in **October 1965**, with **tolls charged until 1972.** Alþingi was asked to double it **six times between 1987 and 1992.** The last 5.6-kilometre section finally opened on **11 December 2025.** It now carries about **21,500 vehicles a day.**

The village below is **Vogar** — **2,005 people** as of **1 August 2026**, up from **1,308** in 2019. **The fastest-growing municipality on this peninsula**, in the decade the peninsula started erupting again.
say: 'the Stapi ghost', with no recorded origin
'Grímur's hill', the high point with the view-disc
'bays', the village below, fastest-growing on the peninsula

block.title: 🔺 Keilir
block.sub: The Cone That Only Ever Erupted Once
block.cue: Look right — the perfect triangle standing on its own out on the lava plain.
block.hook: It looks exactly like a child's drawing of a volcano, so here is the twist: **it is not one.** Not the kind you are thinking of. It erupted **once**, under a glacier, and **it will never erupt again.**
block.point: A one-shot volcano, worn down to the plug in its own throat, used as a sea-mark by people who could not read — and then the marker post for a magma dyke in 2021.
block.mic: The most volcano-looking volcano in Iceland is the one that is definitely never going to erupt. Everything on this peninsula that looks safe is not, and everything that looks dangerous is retired. Welcome to Reykjanes.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Keilir is the first thing to disappear and the first thing to come back. If you cannot see it, the locals cannot either, and they have been complaining about that for a thousand years."
bullets: **Keilir** is **379 metres** above sea level — but only about **200 metres above the ground at its foot**, which is the number to have ready when a guest checks their phone and looks at you funny. Both are true.

It is a **móbergsfell** — a hyaloclastite cone. It formed in a **single eruption beneath the ice sheet of the last glacial period.** These volcanoes erupt **once in their lifetime** and then they are finished. The University of Iceland's own science service puts it flatly: *Keilir is a hyaloclastite cone and it will not erupt again.*

The cone shape has a cause. The little cap on the summit is almost certainly the **plugged conduit** — the last of the magma, frozen solid in the pipe at the end of the eruption. The soft ash around it wore away. The hard plug did not. **You are looking at a volcano that has been eroded down to its own spine.** And nobody knows its age — it has never been dated.

Icelandic field researchers record it as a **mið**, a navigation transit: seamen lined up on Keilir to find their way in, for example running into **Hamarssund** on the approach to **Sandgerði.** A mountain used as a landmark by people who had no charts and no lights.

And it had a starring role in the modern eruptions, which is usually told wrong. In **March 2021**, a **dyke** — a blade of magma — pushed up along a line running **from Keilir south to Fagradalsfjall.** Thousands of earthquakes tracked it moving. It finally broke the surface at the **southern end** of that line, in **Geldingadalur**, on **19 March 2021 at about a quarter to nine in the evening.** So: the **magma** ran between Keilir and Fagradalsfjall. The **eruption** was at the far end of it, where we were standing this morning.
say: 'the cone', 379 m, the landmark mountain of Reykjanes
a hyaloclastite cone, formed in one eruption under ice
a navigation transit: two landmarks lined up to fix a position at sea
the valley where the 19 March 2021 eruption broke out

block.title: 🌑 Route 41
block.cue: Look ahead — Route 41 cutting through black lava.
block.hook: NASA sent thirty-two astronauts to Iceland to learn how to read rock — Armstrong among them. This is the rock.
block.point: The landscape hasn't changed in sixty years — which is exactly why NASA keeps coming back.
block.mic: The first human on the Moon practised on this lava. So will the next one.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Grey sky over black rock and no plants anywhere. If anything this is *more* like the Moon, not less."
bullets: The lava out both windows looked so alien that **NASA used Iceland as an astronaut training ground.** During the **Apollo programme (1965–67)**, **32 astronauts** — **Neil Armstrong** among them — trained on Icelandic rock. The heavy fieldwork was at **Askja** in the highlands, but the Reykjanes flows you are passing are the same **young basalt.** Volcanologist **Sigurður Þórarinsson** guided the crews.

The two lava types here — **pahoehoe** (smooth, ropy) and **aa** (rough, jagged) — are the same textures mapped on the Moon and Mars. In **2023** the **NASA Artemis** astronauts came back to the same fields to train for humanity's return to the Moon.

Reading the age of it is easy once you know the trick: **nothing grows on it.** The jet-black, plant-free fields are the new ones. The older flows toward Hafnarfjörður are ~**700 to 1,000 years old** — medieval — and still look like last week's, because Iceland has almost **no weathering**: no acid rain, no baking heat, no forest to break the rock down. *(Nothing tidies up here. It just sits there looking new for a thousand years, like a show home.)*

And a fair bit of it is hollow. **Lava tubes** form where the surface crusts over while molten rock keeps running underneath, then drains away and leaves the pipe behind. The pile is hundreds of metres thick, but the tubes sit just under the crust — sometimes **only a metre or two below the wheels.** *(You are, in a modest way, driving on a ceiling.)*
say: the smooth, ropy lava out the window, a Hawaiian word
the rough, jagged type, the other half of the pair
the volcanologist who guided the Apollo crews

block.title: 🏙️ Reykjavík
block.cue: Pulling into the city — the buildings, the bay, the hills ahead.
block.hook: The northernmost capital on Earth. Named for smoke that turned out to be steam. Heated by a hot spring that has never once posted an oil bill.
block.point: Ingólfur thought he was naming the place after fire smoke. He had actually named it after the **free energy** under the city that, 1,100 years on, makes Reykjavík one of the cleanest capitals on Earth.
block.mic: Smoky Bay. No smoke. Just steam — and a whole capital running on it.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If Esja has vanished behind us, that is the city's own weather app telling you to keep the coat on tonight."
bullets: ***Reykjavík* = "Smoky Bay."** Around **874 AD** the chieftain **Ingólfur Arnarson** sailed in, saw steam off the geothermal vents, and called it smoke. It wasn't — those **hot springs** now heat nearly every building in the city.

Archaeology backs the legend: a turf longhouse wall at **Aðalstræti** lies **under a volcanic ash layer dated to AD 871 ±2** — the founding pinned to within two years by Greenland ice cores. It is on show *in situ* at the **Settlement Exhibition.**

It is the world's **northernmost capital** at **64°N.** **Two-thirds of all Icelanders** — roughly **250,000 of 394,324** (Hagstofa Íslands, 1 January 2026) — live in the greater city, almost entirely on **geothermal heat**: **80–90°C** water piped to radiators, pools and snow-free pavements. Reykjavík was the **first major city to quit oil heating**, done by the **1970s.**

Which closes the loop on the whole day. **Everything you have looked at today — Seltún, Svartsengi, Gunnuhver, the plant at Reykjanes — is the same heat that warms the shower in your hotel tonight.** The peninsula that keeps trying to erupt is also the reason this country stopped burning oil.
say: 'Smoky Bay', the world's northernmost capital, at 64°N
the chieftain who sailed in around 874 and named the bay for its steam
the mountain behind the city, the free weather app: see Esja, good day
